structure.title: General Information
structure.heading: Section 1 - General Information [ESRS 2]
structure.start_phrase: This Sustainability Report (hereinafter also referred to as the “Report”) is prepared on a consolidated basis, in compliance with Directive (EU) 2022/2464 on corporate sustainability reporting (‘CSRD’), with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) and with Legislative Decree 125/2024, which transposed the aforementioned EU Directive into Italian law.
structure.summary:
- Prepared on a consolidated basis in line with CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), ESRS (Reg. (EU) 2023/2772), and Italy’s Legislative Decree 125/2024.
- Consolidation scope matches the Group’s Consolidated Financial Statements (parent and line-by-line subsidiaries); subsidiaries are exempt from separate sustainability reports under Art. 7(1) of Decree 125/2024.
- Coverage spans the Group’s full value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream) and integrates assessment of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IRO).
- No use of ESRS exemptions for classified/sensitive IP/know-how or for omitting forward-looking/trading-related information (per Directive 2013/34/EU, Arts. 19-bis(3) and 29-bis(3)).
- Discloses only ESRS data points deemed material via double materiality; cross-references provided, applying “Incorporation by Reference” to the Consolidated Report on Operations where possible.
- Subject to limited assurance.
- Includes information relevant to the UN Global Compact and reports progress on the Principles for Responsible Banking, adopted by the Group in 2019.

nodes.title: General Criteria for the drawing up of the Sustainability Report
nodes.heading: General Criteria for the drawing up of the Sustainability Report
nodes.start_phrase: This Sustainability Report (hereinafter also referred to as the “Report”) is prepared on a consolidated basis, in compliance with Directive (EU) 2022/2464 on corporate sustainability reporting (‘CSRD’), with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772 (European Sustainability Reporting Standards) and with Legislative Decree 125/2024, which transposed the aforementioned EU Directive into Italian law.
nodes.summary:
- The Report is a consolidated Sustainability Report of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group, prepared in accordance with the CSRD (Directive (EU) 2022/2464), ESRS (EU 2023/2772), and Italy’s Legislative Decree 125/2024, with the same consolidation perimeter as the Group’s Consolidated Financial Statements.
- Subsidiaries included in the Group perimeter are exempt from individual sustainability reporting as they are covered by the Parent Company’s consolidated report.
- Reporting scope covers the Group’s upstream, own operations, and downstream activities and reflects identified impacts, risks, and opportunities (IRO) using a double materiality approach; only ESRS-mandatory, material datapoints are disclosed.
- The Group did not use exemptions related to classified/sensitive information or forthcoming developments; the Report is subject to limited assurance.
- The Report includes information for UNEP and progress on the Principles for Responsible Banking, following the Group’s 2019 voluntary commitment.
- Value chain estimation is applied to Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions due to data access, regulatory, and quality limitations related to customers, suppliers, and partners; methodology and assumptions are detailed in Section 2 – Environmental Information.
- As this is the first year under Legislative Decree 125/2024 and ESRS, there are no changes to prior presentation and no comparative information is provided, consistent with ESRS 1; comparative data (where present) are not subject to limited review this year.
- Disclosures required by other regulations include Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy (Regulation (EU) 2020/852) within Environmental Information.
- The Report uses Incorporation by Reference per ESRS 1 to related sections of the Consolidated Financial Statements, including:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation (Notes, Part A Section 3),
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: ESG risk monitoring framework (Notes, Part E),
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate risk analysis process (Notes, Part E).

nodes.title: Value chain estimation
nodes.heading: Value chain estimation
nodes.start_phrase: The metrics reported within the Report that include estimated value chain data and are estimated through indirect data concern Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions, reported within Section 2 - Environmental Information .
nodes.summary:
- Focuses on sustainability reporting disclosures under ESRS, with emphasis on specific circumstances affecting data.
- Explains that Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions are estimated using indirect value chain data due to:
  - Regulatory constraints for financial institutions in the value chain.
  - Restricted access to and sharing of value chain information.
  - Data reliability/quality limitations stemming from limited technical expertise of some actors.
- Points to Section 2 – Environmental Information for the detailed methodology, assumptions, sources, and conversion factors used for Scope 1, 2, and 3 calculations, and discusses estimation and outcome uncertainty.
- Notes this is the first year applying Legislative Decree 125/2024 and ESRS; therefore:
  - No changes in preparation/presentation are reported.
  - No prior-year comparative information is provided (per ESRS 1, paragraph 136).
- Confirms inclusion of EU Taxonomy (Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852) disclosures in Section 2; current-year comparative data are not subject to limited review.
- States that incorporation by reference complies with ESRS 1 (paragraphs 119–120), with specific cross-references:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation in Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, Part A, Section 3.
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: ESG risk monitoring framework in Consolidated Notes, Part E (Information on risks and related hedging policies).
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate risk identification process in Part E of the Consolidated Notes.

nodes.title: Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty
nodes.heading: Sources of estimation and outcome uncertainty
nodes.start_phrase: For more details on the estimation methodology used in the calculation of Scope 3 indirect emissions, including sources of information, assumptions made and conversion factors used in the calculation, please refer to what is described in the paragraph “Methodology for calculating own direct and indirect (Scope 1 and 2) and Scope 3 indirect emissions” in Section 2 - Environmental Information.
nodes.summary:
- Explains that certain reported metrics rely on estimated value chain data, specifically for Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions in Section 2 – Environmental Information, due to difficulties obtaining direct data from customers, suppliers, and partners.
- Lists key limitations driving the use of estimates: regulatory constraints for financial institutions, restricted access/sharing of value chain information, and concerns over data reliability and technical expertise among value chain actors.
- Points to the detailed estimation methodology, assumptions, data sources, and conversion factors for Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions in the “Methodology for calculating own direct and indirect (Scope 1 and 2) and Scope 3 indirect emissions” within Section 2.
- States that this is the first year applying Legislative Decree 125/2024 and ESRS, with no changes to preparation/presentation and no prior-year comparative information, per ESRS 1 paragraph 136.
- Confirms inclusion of EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures in Section 2; notes that comparative data for the current year are not subject to limited review.
- Affirms that all incorporations by reference comply with ESRS 1 paragraphs 119–120, and specifies:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation in Part A Section 3 of the Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements.
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: environmental risk monitoring framework in the “ESG Risks” section, Part E of the Consolidated Notes.
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate risk identification process in the same “ESG Risks” section, Part E.

nodes.title: Errors and changes in the preparation or presentation of sustainability information
nodes.heading: Errors and changes in the preparation or presentation of sustainability information
nodes.start_phrase: As this is the first year that the provisions of Legislative Decree 125/2024 have been adopted, there are no changes in the preparation and presentation of information.
nodes.summary:
- Explains that certain reported metrics, notably Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions in Section 2 – Environmental Information, are estimated using indirect value chain data when direct data from customers, suppliers, and partners cannot be obtained with reasonable effort.
- Lists limitations prompting estimation: regulatory restrictions on data for financial institutions in the value chain, constraints on access/sharing of information, and concerns over reliability/quality due to limited technical expertise among value chain actors.
- Points to the “Methodology for calculating own direct and indirect (Scope 1 and 2) and Scope 3 indirect emissions” in Section 2 for sources, assumptions, and conversion factors, and acknowledges estimation and outcome uncertainty.
- States that this is the first year applying Legislative Decree 125/2024; there are no changes in preparation/presentation, and per ESRS 1 paragraph 136, no prior-year comparative information is provided.
- Confirms inclusion of Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures in Section 2 – Environmental Information; notes that comparative data are not subject to limited review for the current year.
- Confirms incorporations by reference comply with ESRS 1 paragraphs 119–120, specifically:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation referenced in Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, Part A, Section 3.
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: environmental risk monitoring framework referenced in “ESG Risks,” Part E of the Consolidated Notes.
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate change risk identification process referenced in the same “ESG Risks” section, Part E.

nodes.title: Disclosures required by other disclosures
nodes.heading: Disclosures required by other disclosures
nodes.start_phrase: The Report includes the disclosure required by Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (EU Taxonomy) within Section 2 “Environmental Information”.
nodes.summary:
- Explains use of estimated value chain data for Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions when direct data from customers, suppliers, and partners cannot be obtained, citing regulatory constraints, information access/sharing limits, and data quality/expertise issues across the value chain.
- Points to the detailed estimation methodology, sources, assumptions, and conversion factors for Scope 3 (and Scope 1–2) emissions in Section 2 – Environmental Information.
- States this is the first year applying Legislative Decree 125/2024 and ESRS; therefore, no changes in preparation/presentation and no prior-year comparatives, per ESRS 1 paragraph 136.
- Confirms inclusion of EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures within Section 2 – Environmental Information, noting that comparative data are not subject to limited review.
- Confirms compliance with ESRS 1 incorporation-by-reference rules (paras 119–120), directing readers to:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation in Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, Part A, Section 3.
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: ESG risk monitoring framework in Consolidated Notes, Part E (Information on risks and related hedging policies).
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate risk identification analysis in Consolidated Notes, Part E.

nodes.title: Incoporation by reference
nodes.heading: Incoporation by reference
nodes.start_phrase: All inclusions by reference made by the Group to other documents and contained within the Report meet the requirements of ESRS 1 - General Requirements paragraphs 119 and 120.
nodes.summary:
- Explains reliance on estimated value chain data for Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions due to challenges in obtaining direct information from customers, suppliers, and partners. Key limitations include regulatory constraints for financial institutions, restricted access/sharing of value chain data, and variable reliability/technical capability of value chain actors.
- Points to Section 2 – Environmental Information for detailed Scope 3 estimation methodology, assumptions, sources, and conversion factors.
- Notes first-year application of Legislative Decree 125/2024 and ESRS: no changes in preparation/presentation, and no prior-year comparatives per ESRS 1 paragraph 136.
- Confirms inclusion of EU Taxonomy (Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852) disclosures in Section 2; comparative data are not subject to limited review this year.
- Describes incorporation by reference in line with ESRS 1 paragraphs 119–120, specifying where to find:
  - ESRS 2 BP-1: scope of consolidation (Notes to the Consolidated Financial Statements, Part A, Section 3).
  - ESRS 2 IRO-1: ESG risk monitoring framework (Consolidated Notes, Part E).
  - E1 – ESRS 2 SBM-3: climate risk identification process (Consolidated Notes, Part E).
- Outlines Group governance: the Parent Bank provides direction, governance, and control; traditional system comprising Board of Directors, Board of Statutory Auditors, Shareholders’ Meeting, CEO/General Manager, and five committees (Appointments; Remuneration; Risk and Sustainability; Related-Party Transactions; IT and Digitalisation).
- Details Board composition and changes:
  - Board appointed on 20 April 2023 for 2023–2025.
  - 11 April 2024: appointment of a new director replacing a resignation.
  - 17 December 2024: five non-executive independent directors resigned; 27 December 2024: five new directors co-opted; 23 January 2025: eligibility checks conducted, with supervisory review ongoing.
  - Disclosures on independence and competencies refer to the pre-change Board composition given changes occurred in the last 15 days of 2024.
  - No employee/worker representatives on the Board, consistent with law and Articles of Association.
  - As of 31 December 2024: 11 of 15 directors (73.33%) independent; CEO is the only executive; 14 non-executive members.
  - Note that committee composition changed in February 2025 (reference to press release).

nodes.title: The role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.heading: The role of the administrative, management and supervisory bodies
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank, in its role as Parent Company, performs functions of direction, governance and control over the Group’s Com- panies, as part of the more general guidelines set out by the Board of Directors and in the interest of the Group’s stability.
nodes.summary:
- Describes BMPS’s traditional governance model and the Parent Company’s role in directing, governing, and controlling Group companies.
- Lists corporate bodies: Board of Directors, Board of Statutory Auditors, Shareholders’ Meeting, CEO (also General Manager), and five Board committees (Appointments; Remuneration; Risk and Sustainability; Related-Party Transactions; IT and Digitalisation).
- Details Board of Directors’ mandate (2023–2025) and changes: April 11, 2024 appointment of Raffaele Oriani; December 17, 2024 resignation of five non-executive independent directors; December 27, 2024 co-option of five new members; January 23, 2025 eligibility verification completed; supervisory review ongoing. Clarifies most metrics refer to pre-December 2024 composition.
- Notes absence of employee/worker representatives per Italian law and the Articles of Association.
- Provides independence and structure data as of December 31, 2024: 11 of 15 directors (73.33%) independent; CEO is the only executive; 14 non-executive directors; appointment of Lead Independent Director (Paola De Martini) in December 2024.
- Summarizes committee memberships as at 31.12.2024 and flags that committee composition changed in February 2025 (with link to press release).
- Covers Board of Statutory Auditors: appointed April 20, 2023 for 2023–2025; April 11, 2024 integration following resignations; current composition listed (Chair Enrico Ciai; Standing: Lavinia Linguanti, Giacomo Granata; Alternates: Pierpaolo Cotone, Paola Lucia Isabella Giordano).
- States no family or personal relationships among auditors and other key company officers; Sustainability Reporting Officer coincides with Financial Reporting Officer.
- Confirms compliance with regulatory limits on offices held (Consob Issuers’ Regulation; MEF Decree 169/2020).
- Outlines diversity governance: compliance with gender balance rules; Board 53% male/47% female; Statutory Auditors balanced by gender; adherence to Corporate Governance Code and Articles on diversity.
- Highlights diversity and inclusion policies (Code of Ethics, Sustainability and ESG Guidelines, Gender Equality Policy), equal opportunity principles, and non-discrimination.
- Provides diversity metrics and suitability: directors’ age range 48–71 (average 59) with two under 50; auditors 38–74 (average 61); tenure diversification; periodic assessment of qualifications, independence of judgment, time commitment, and interlocking prohibitions.
- Notes approval on February 24, 2025 of a formal Diversity Policy for the composition of BMPS’s corporate bodies.

nodes.title: Diversity in governance bodies
nodes.heading: Diversity in governance bodies
nodes.start_phrase: The composition of the Bank’s corporate bodies in 2024 - for the Board of Directors was 53% male and 47% female, and for the Board of Statutory Auditors, 2 male standing auditors and 1 female standing auditor, and alternate auditors, 1 male and 1 female - complied with primary and supervisory regulations on gender balance.
nodes.summary:
- Identifies the composition of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s Board of Statutory Auditors: Chairperson Enrico Ciai; Standing Auditors Lavinia Linguanti and Giacomo Granata; Alternate Auditors Pierpaolo Cotone and Paola Lucia Isabella Giordano.
- States that no Statutory Auditor is related to members of other governing bodies or top management; the Sustainability Reporting Officer is the same as the Financial Reporting Officer.
- Confirms compliance with limits on concurrent positions for control body members per Consob Issuers’ Regulation (Title V-bis, Section V, Item II) and MEF Decree 169/2020.
- Details diversity and governance practices:
  - 2024 compliance with gender-balance rules: Board of Directors 53% men and 47% women; Board of Statutory Auditors with 2 male and 1 female standing auditors, and 1 male and 1 female alternates.
  - Lead Independent Director role assigned to Paola De Martini in December 2024.
  - Adoption of legal and regulatory frameworks (including TUF, Supervisory Provisions, MEF Decree 169/2020), Corporate Governance Code, Articles of Association provisions on gender diversity (Arts. 15 and 25), and Group policies (Code of Ethics, Sustainability and ESG Guidelines, Gender Equality Policy).
  - Commitment to equal opportunities and non-discrimination across age, sexual orientation, religion, gender, ethnicity, and ability.
- Reports outcomes of diversity criteria application in 2024:
  - Board of Directors age diversification: min 48, max 71, average 59; two directors under 50.
  - Statutory Auditors age diversification: min 38, max 74, average 61; one auditor under 50.
  - Tenure diversification: directors—1 in third term, 4 in second, 10 in first; auditors—chair in second term, four in first.
  - Ongoing verification of eligibility and suitability (education, experience, independence of judgment, time commitment, and prohibition on interlocking).
- Notes that qualitative and quantitative criteria for the ideal Board composition are disclosed to shareholders prior to renewals.
- Describes the Statutory Auditors’ annual (or event-driven) verification of members’ independence and oversight of the Board’s process for assessing non-executive directors’ independence, with disclosures in governance reports.
- Provides 2024 composition snapshots and recent appointments: following 2023 resignations, the 11 April 2024 Shareholders’ Meeting appointed a new statutory auditor (Giacomo Granata) and alternate auditor (Paola Lucia Giordano) under Art. 2401 of the Italian Civil Code; also appointed Raffaele Oriani as Board Director.
- Mentions approval on 24 February 2025 of the “Diversity Policy for the Composition of the Corporate Bodies,” published on the Group’s website.

nodes.title: The Board of Statutory Auditors
nodes.heading: The Board of Statutory Auditors
nodes.start_phrase: The Board of Statutory Auditors ascertains on an annual basis or in the case of significant events, (i) the existence of the inde - pendence requirements for its members, and (ii) the correct application of the assessment criteria and procedures adopted by the Board of Directors to assess the independence of its non-executive members.
nodes.summary:
- Governance transparency: The company discloses qualitative and quantitative criteria for the ideal composition of the Board of Directors to shareholders ahead of board renewals.
- Independence oversight: The Board of Statutory Auditors annually (or upon significant events) verifies its members’ independence and the correct application of independence assessment criteria for non-executive directors, with outcomes reported in the corporate governance report or to the Shareholders’ Meeting.
- Board of Directors diversity: As of 31 December 2024, the gender diversity ratio (average female-to-male) was 88%, with a breakdown by gender and age provided.
- Board of Statutory Auditors composition: As of 31 December 2024, there were 3 regular auditors (2 male, 1 female) and 2 alternate auditors (1 male, 1 female); ages ranged from 38 to 74, average age 61, with one auditor under 50.
- Changes in auditors: Following 2023 resignations, on 11 April 2024 the Shareholders’ Meeting appointed a new statutory auditor and a new alternate auditor pursuant to Article 2401 of the Italian Civil Code.

nodes.title: Composition of the Board of Directors by gender and age
nodes.heading: Composition of the Board of Directors by gender and age
nodes.start_phrase: As at 31 December 2024, the gender diversity ratio of the board of directors, calculated as the average ratio of female to male members, was 88%.
nodes.summary:
- The company discloses qualitative and quantitative criteria for the ideal composition of the Board of Directors to shareholders prior to board renewals.
- The Board of Statutory Auditors annually (or upon significant events) verifies members’ independence and the proper application of independence assessment criteria for non-executive directors, with outcomes disclosed via the corporate governance report or the supervisory body’s report to the Shareholders’ Meeting.
- Board of Directors diversity as of 31 Dec 2024: gender diversity ratio (female-to-male) of 88%; 53% women and 47% men; majority over 50 years old (76%).
- Board of Statutory Auditors as of 31 Dec 2024: 3 regular auditors (2 male, 1 female) and 2 alternates (1 male, 1 female); age range 38–74, average 61, with one auditor under 50. Following 2023 resignations, the Shareholders’ Meeting on 11 April 2024 appointed a new statutory and alternate auditor under Art. 2401 of the Italian Civil Code.
- Governance assigns sustainability responsibilities across four areas: strategy; actions and policies; risk factor management; monitoring and reporting.
- Board of Directors responsibilities: approve sustainability/ESG strategies, policies and the Sustainability Plan in line with the Code of Ethics and voluntary commitments; approve and monitor the Group Sustainability and ESG Policy; integrate ESG factors into strategy and decision-making; approve participation in national/supranational initiatives; ensure ESG risks are embedded in risk management and define Group Risk Appetite; evaluate and approve the dual materiality analysis; set policy guidance and coordination for the Sustainability Report; approve the Sustainability Report (subject to the Risk and Sustainability Committee’s opinion).
- Board of Statutory Auditors responsibilities: ensure the Sustainability Report complies with applicable regulations; oversee the adequacy of organizational, administrative, reporting and control systems to enable a correct and complete consolidated sustainability report that reflects both the company’s impacts and how sustainability issues affect performance, results and position.
- Risk and Sustainability Committee responsibilities: evaluate strategic sustainability guidelines and macro-objectives and their consistency with overall strategy; propose environmental and social strategy, annual objectives and targets, and monitor progress; oversee sustainability evolution in light of international guidelines and principles; review and approve sustainability matters including validation of the double materiality analysis for reporting; support the Board in sustainability and ESG risk decisions; monitor Group positioning; supervise compliance with Legislative Decree No. 125 of 10 Sept 2024 regarding the Sustainability Report.
- Remuneration Committee responsibilities: provide guidelines and recommendations on remuneration for staff whose systems are set by the Board; periodically assess and monitor remuneration criteria for executives with strategic responsibilities.

nodes.title: Responsibilities of bodies with strategic oversight, management and control functions with regard to impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: Responsibilities of bodies with strategic oversight, management and control functions with regard to impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The Bank’s governance system provides for specific responsibilities regarding sustainability issues, distributed among the Bank’s bodies and functions according to four areas (strategy, actions and policies, risk factor management, monitoring and reporting).
nodes.summary:
- Overview of the Bank’s governance for sustainability, allocating responsibilities across strategy, actions/policies, risk management, and monitoring/reporting.
- Board of Directors: approves ESG strategy, Group Sustainability & ESG Policy, Sustainability Plan, and Sustainability Report; integrates ESG into corporate strategy and Group Risk Appetite; validates dual materiality outcomes; authorizes participation in sustainability initiatives; ensures ESG risk controls within the overall risk framework; sets policy guidance for reporting.
- Board of Statutory Auditors: ensures the Sustainability Report complies with regulations; oversees adequacy of organizational, administrative, reporting, and control systems to fairly represent the Bank’s sustainability impacts and how these affect performance and position.
- Risk and Sustainability Committee: evaluates sustainability strategic guidelines and macro-objectives; proposes environmental/social strategy and targets and monitors delivery; aligns with international principles; validates double materiality for reporting; advises the Board on ESG risk management; monitors Group sustainability positioning; supervises compliance with Legislative Decree No. 125/2024 on Sustainability Report preparation.
- Remuneration Committee: issues guidelines and recommendations on remuneration for personnel under Board remit; periodically reviews criteria for executives with strategic responsibilities and monitors application.
- Chief Executive Officer: executes Board resolutions and integrated sustainability strategy; oversees activities and target achievement, supported by the Steering Committee.
- Steering Committee (ESG & Sustainability session): supports the CEO in defining sustainability strategy/policies and implementing the Sustainability Plan; tracks initiatives, sponsors delivery, and resolves critical issues. Composition noted as CEO, Deputy Chief Commercial Officer, department heads, and the Financial Reporting Officer.
- CFO: responsible for the Sustainability function; promotes and integrates ESG into overall strategy; defines ESG strategies with parent-company functions; uses the Steering Committee ESG session to align on strategy/policies and address implementation challenges.
- ESG & Sustainability Function: supports the Head of Sustainability; outlines ESG strategy and the Sustainability Plan; ensures alignment with Group ESG strategy; defines policies; coordinates sustainability reporting; conducts dual materiality analysis identifying impacts, risks, and opportunities for approval by the Committee and Board.
- Sustainability Report process: integrated with financial reporting and supported by a structured system of internal controls; ESG & Sustainability Department coordinates with bank units to embed checks on impacts, risks, and opportunities within existing control frameworks.
- Formalization: governance roles and responsibilities documented in the Report on Corporate Governance and Ownership Structures (Art. 123-bis TUF), approved on 6 March 2025.
- Fitness and expertise: ECB assessed 2023 and April 2024 appointees as fit and proper; in 2024, approx. 83% of Board members have expertise in banking/financial markets and 77% in banking/financial products.
- Profile of directors: all elected directors are Italian nationals; several have international education/professional experience; strong presence of competencies in risk and banking governance and legal/regulatory matters, with about 87% of Board members having legal/regulatory expertise, many with academic/legal professional backgrounds.

nodes.title: The administrative, management and supervisory bodies: experience and expertise
nodes.heading: The administrative, management and supervisory bodies: experience and expertise
nodes.start_phrase: All the directors and statutory auditors elected in 2023 and in April 2024 were assessed by the Supervisory Authority (European Central Bank - ECB) as fit to hold office following the specific verification process, and were therefore also recognised as possessing the basic knowledge and experience required by the regulations in force in relation to the sectors (banking and financial) and products (banking and financial) in which the Bank operates, by virtue of the skills acquired through corpo- rate offices, executive or managerial positions, work or professional activities or academic and research roles.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Bank’s sustainability governance model and roles:
  - CEO ensures implementation of Board resolutions, oversees sustainability actions, and monitors objective achievement with support from the Steering Committee (ESG & Sustainability session).
  - Steering Committee supports ESG strategy and policy setting, sponsors Sustainability Plan initiatives, and resolves critical issues.
  - CFO is responsible for the Sustainability function, promotes ESG integration into overall strategy, and engages the Steering Committee on strategy and implementation issues.
  - ESG & Sustainability Function supports the Head of Sustainability, outlines ESG strategy and the Sustainability Plan, drafts policies and sustainability reporting, and conducts the double materiality analysis for approval by the Risk & Sustainability Committee and the Board.
  - Notes the Steering Committee’s composition (CEO, Deputy Chief Commercial Officer, all Department Heads, Financial Reporting Officer).

- Integrates sustainability reporting with financial reporting processes via a structured internal control system; ESG & Sustainability coordinates data collection and embeds checks on impacts, risks, and opportunities across functions.

- Formalizes responsibilities of the Board, its Committees, and the Board of Statutory Auditors in the Corporate Governance and Ownership Structures Report (Article 123-bis TUF), approved 6 March 2025.

- Details board and auditor fitness and expertise:
  - ECB confirmed fitness of directors and statutory auditors elected in 2023 and April 2024.
  - High sector expertise: ~83% in banking/financial markets and ~77% in products; strong legal/regulatory and risk governance skills (~87% for the Board).
  - Predominantly Italian nationals with international education/professional exposure.
  - Diversity of backgrounds strengthens decision-making on sustainability, climate risks, and ESG.
  - ~37% of directors have specific sustainability expertise (2024).
  - December 2024 appointments further enhanced collective suitability and practical ESG/climate risk competence and regulatory alignment.

- Embeds sustainability competencies in the annual Board self-assessment, linked to material targets and impacts in the Business Plan.

- Provides ongoing training:
  - Board Induction (29 Jan 2024) on sustainability governance and reporting evolution.
  - Information session (7 Nov 2024) on Sustainability Reporting 2024 and Double Materiality Analysis.
  - Additional induction sessions planned from January 2025.
  - Statutory Auditors participated in ABI training on sustainability/climate risk governance and IT/cyber risk governance.

- Explains oversight of material impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - Regular information flows and controls keep governance bodies informed.
  - Board, supported by the Risk & Sustainability Committee, reviews/approves double materiality results and evaluates policy effectiveness for ESG risk management and opportunity capture.
  - Risk & Sustainability Committee oversees ESG topics and stakeholder relations, assesses strategy consistency, proposes environmental/social strategies, sets targets, monitors execution, and defines/requests information flows per supervisory rules and Group policies.
  - Board integrates ESG factors into corporate strategy and Risk Appetite, with continuous monitoring to ensure alignment with long-term objectives and regulatory requirements.

nodes.title: Roles and responsibilities of management bodies in exercising oversight of the process for managing material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.heading: Roles and responsibilities of management bodies in exercising oversight of the process for managing material impacts, risks and opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Governance bodies are informed about material impacts, risks and opportunities through regular information flows and control mechanisms.
nodes.summary:
- Composition and expertise: In 2024, the Board of Directors and Board of Statutory Auditors of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena exhibited diverse and complementary skills across education, managerial experience, technical expertise, and ESG/sustainability knowledge, ensuring collective suitability to understand key risks and opportunities, including climate impacts.
- Sustainability competence: About 37% of directors have explicit sustainability expertise gained through board/committee roles, ESG commissions, academic engagement, cross-sector ESG guideline work, and external training.
- Strengthening in 2024: December 2024 appointments further enhanced the Board’s collective suitability, adding professionals with practical board/auditor experience and strong ESG exposure from companies where ESG risks and opportunities are integral to strategy.
- Ongoing assessment: Sustainability-related skills of both Boards are evaluated in the annual self-assessment, linked to the Bank’s Business Plan, targets, and material impacts.
- Board education: Induction and information sessions were held on 29 January 2024 (Sustainability governance and the evolution of reporting) and 7 November 2024 (2024 Sustainability Reporting: Double Materiality Analysis), with additional induction sessions commencing January 2025.
- Statutory Auditors’ training: In 2024, members attended advanced ABI Formazione programs on governance of sustainability and climate risk, and governance of IT and cyber risk.
- Governance roles on impacts, risks, and opportunities: The Board of Directors, supported by the Risk and Sustainability Committee, receives regular information flows and control inputs, reviews and approves Double Materiality Analysis outcomes, and evaluates policy effectiveness in managing ESG risks and opportunities.
- Committee responsibilities: The Risk and Sustainability Committee oversees sustainability matters and stakeholder relations, ensures ESG strategy alignment with overall strategy, proposes environmental and social targets, monitors progress, and defines required risk-related information flows (subject, format, frequency).
- Strategy integration: ESG factors are embedded in corporate strategy and Risk Appetite; the Committee’s continuous monitoring supports alignment with long-term objectives and regulations, integrating sustainability across strategies.
- Material IROs disclosure: Material impacts, risks, and opportunities approved by the Board are detailed by ESRS chapter, including time horizons (short/medium/long term) and boundaries (own operations, upstream, downstream).
- Supervisory oversight of sustainability reporting: The Board of Statutory Auditors monitors compliance with consolidated sustainability reporting regulations and adequacy of internal control and risk management systems for ESG risks.
- Process and controls: The Supervisory Board verifies the sufficiency of organizational resources, systems, and procedures for timely, complete, reliable reporting; oversees administrative/accounting systems and periodic quantitative/qualitative information flows; and confirms process correctness, obtaining certifications from the Delegated Administrative Body and the Sustainability Reporting Officer.
- Coordination with control functions and auditors: It reviews work by the Sustainability Reporting Officer (including EU Taxonomy disclosures), second- and third-level control functions (Internal Audit), and maintains information exchanges with the external auditing firm on the scope and planning of sustainability report assurance.
- Legal compliance and reporting: It monitors compliance with disclosure and publication requirements (Italian Civil Code Articles 2429 and 2435), and reports to the Shareholders’ Meeting on its supervisory activities under Legislative Decree No. 125/2024, including the independent auditors’ conformity certification per Article 8(1) of the same decree.

nodes.title: Role of the Supervisory Board in the Monitoring of Sustainability Reporting
nodes.heading: Role of the Supervisory Board in the Monitoring of Sustainability Reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The Board of Statutory Auditors monitors compliance with the provisions of the regulations on consolidated corporate sustainability reporting and the sustainability reporting process, with the support of the corporate control functions.
nodes.summary:
- Materiality and ESRS framing: The report references ESRS-specific chapters that summarize material Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs), their time horizons (short/medium/long term), and relevant boundaries (own operations, upstream and downstream value chain).

- Supervisory oversight of sustainability reporting: The Board of Statutory Auditors monitors compliance with regulations on consolidated sustainability reporting, ensures the internal control and risk management system adequately addresses ESG risks, and verifies the adequacy of organization, resources, processes, and IT for reporting. It oversees administrative/accounting systems, ensures timely and reliable information flows, reviews the correctness of the reporting process, and obtains internal certifications from the Delegated Administrative Body and the Sustainability Reporting Officer (including EU Taxonomy-related information). It coordinates with second- and third-line control functions and the external auditor, monitors assurance work, and ensures publication and disclosure meet Italian Civil Code deadlines and Legislative Decree requirements. It reports to the Shareholders’ Meeting on its supervisory activities and on the independent auditor’s certification.

- Integration of sustainability into remuneration and incentives: Group remuneration policies aim at sustainable long-term value, merit, and inclusion, with a balanced fixed/variable pay mix to prevent excessive risk-taking and aligned with regulatory guidance. Variable pay for senior managers and Key Staff is tied to economic, financial, risk, and ESG objectives set ex ante; non-executive directors and Statutory Auditors have no performance-linked incentives. Pay determinations consider role, market benchmarks, skills, location, education, scarcity, contract type, experience, and certifications.

- ESG-linked incentives since 2023: ESG objectives aligned with the Business Plan are embedded via the Board-approved, annually updated Sustainability Plan. For 2024, the CEO/General Manager’s scorecard weights are economic-financial 80%, risk 10%, ESG 10%. ESG KPIs include: ESG financing volumes to target, percent achievement of the ESG Programme, share of the less represented gender in leadership roles, and definition of the ESG strategic roadmap. For other relevant functions in 2024, a composite ESG KPI includes at least three shared and function-specific indicators aligned to the Sustainability Plan.

- Climate-related incentive elements: The composite ESG KPI incorporates climate considerations, including sub-targets for green financing volumes supporting decarbonisation, and objectives tied to defining decarbonisation targets, a climate transition plan, and associated monitoring.

nodes.title: Remuneration policies
nodes.heading: Remuneration policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s remuneration policies are geared towards the creation of sustainable value over time, the enhancement of merit, the growth of all employees, entirely in keeping with the risk governance and diversity and inclusion policies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on integrating sustainability and ESG performance into remuneration and incentive schemes across the Group.
- Remuneration policies aim for long-term sustainable value creation, merit enhancement, employee growth, and alignment with risk governance and diversity and inclusion; ensure fair, competitive pay with a balanced fixed/variable Pay Mix to avoid conflicts of interest and excessive risk-taking.
- For senior managers and personnel, pay may include fixed and variable components with ex-ante conditions tailored by sub-category; non-executive directors and the Board of Statutory Auditors receive no variable pay and no incentive plans.
- Pay determination considers role weighting, market benchmarks, skills, commitment, location and cost of living, education, market scarcity for specialized roles, contract type, experience, and professional certifications.
- Variable incentives are tied to pre-defined economic-financial and qualitative objectives; since 2023, ESG objectives aligned with the Business Plan and embedded in the annually updated Sustainability Plan are included.
- CEO/General Manager 2024 incentive system: fixed plus annual variable deferred over a long-term horizon, with a scorecard weighted 80% economic-financial, 10% risk management, 10% ESG.
- 2024 ESG KPIs include: ESG lending volumes to targets; percentage achievement of the ESG Programme; percentage of the less represented gender in positions of responsibility; and definition of the ESG strategic roadmap.
- 2024 update: for other relevant entities/functions, the composite ESG KPI must include at least three common indicators plus business-specific indicators aligned with the Sustainability Plan.
- Climate-related integration: ESG KPIs contain climate sub-objectives; ESG financing volumes include green volume sub-targets supporting decarbonization; ESG Programme achievement covers setting decarbonization targets, establishing a climate transition plan, and related monitoring.
- Clarification of “Key Staff”: individuals whose activities materially impact the Bank’s or Group’s risk profile.

nodes.title: Main characteristics of incentive systems
nodes.heading: Main characteristics of incentive systems
nodes.start_phrase: In compliance with supervisory provisions, the remuneration packages for Group senior managers and personnel may consist of a fixed and a variable component.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Integration of sustainability (ESG) performance into remuneration and incentive schemes at Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena.
- Remuneration philosophy: Create long-term sustainable value, reward merit, support employee growth, align with risk governance and diversity & inclusion; ensure fair, competitive pay and a balanced fixed/variable “Pay Mix” to avoid short-termism and excessive risk-taking.
- Incentive structure: Fixed plus variable components for senior managers and relevant staff; variable pay conditions set ex ante by personnel sub-category; non-executive directors and statutory auditors have no incentives and no linkage to Group results.
- Determinants of pay: Role weighting and market benchmarks, plus skills, commitment, work location/cost of living, education, scarcity of specialized skills, contract type, experience, and certifications.
- Variable pay metrics: Economic-financial and qualitative objectives defined ex ante; since 2023, ESG objectives integrated and aligned with the Business Plan and annually updated Sustainability Plan.
- CEO/General Manager 2024 incentive scorecard: 80% economic-financial, 10% risk management, 10% ESG; variable component paid over a long-term horizon upon verification of objectives.
- 2024 ESG KPIs: ESG lending volumes to target, percent completion of the ESG Programme, percent of less represented gender in leadership roles, and definition of the ESG strategic roadmap.
- 2024 enhancement: Composite ESG KPI for other relevant entities/functions includes at least three shared indicators plus business-specific indicators aligned with the Sustainability Plan.
- Climate integration: ESG composite KPI embeds climate-related sub-objectives; ESG financing volumes include Green Volumes to support decarbonisation; ESG Programme targets cover defining decarbonisation goals, a climate transition plan, and ongoing monitoring.
- Definition of Key Staff: Roles with material impact on the Bank/Group risk profile, identified per regulatory criteria.

nodes.title: Incentive systems - climate considerations
nodes.heading: Incentive systems - climate considerations
nodes.start_phrase: The definition of the composite ESG KPI for the CEO/General Manager, and all relevant personnel, includes considerations and sub-objectives related to climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Integration of sustainability (ESG) performance into remuneration and incentive systems at Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, aligned with risk governance, merit, fairness, competitiveness, and D&I.
- Pay structure: Balanced fixed and variable “Pay Mix.” Variable remuneration applies where requirements are met and is set ex ante by personnel category to discourage excessive risk-taking.
- Scope of objectives: Scorecards for the CEO/General Manager and Key Staff tie incentives to economic-financial, ESG, and risk objectives. Non-executive directors and statutory auditors receive no variable incentives and have no link to Group results.
- Remuneration determinants: Role weighting, market benchmarking, skills, commitment, location/cost of living, education, scarcity for specialized roles, contract type, experience, and certifications.
- ESG integration: Since 2023, ESG targets linked to the Business Plan have been embedded in remuneration policies and aligned with the annually updated Sustainability Plan.
- CEO/GM 2024 Incentive System: Fixed plus annual variable paid over a long-term horizon after verification. Scorecard weights: 80% economic-financial, 10% risk management, 10% ESG. 2024 ESG KPIs: ESG lending volumes to target, % achievement of the ESG Programme, % of less represented gender in leadership roles, and definition of the ESG strategic roadmap. For other relevant roles, the composite ESG KPI includes at least three shared and role-specific indicators aligned with the Sustainability Plan.
- Climate considerations: Embedded within the ESG component (10%). Sub-targets include green lending volumes supporting decarbonization; defining decarbonization targets, transition plan, and monitoring; integrating climate/environmental risks into risk management and credit processes; building a Group ESG database; and climate-focused elements in the ESG strategic roadmap and business-specific indicators.
- Governance and approvals: 2024 remuneration policies approved by the Shareholders’ Meeting on 11 April 2024. The Ordinary Shareholders’ Meeting approves remuneration and incentive policies and any instrument-based plans; it may authorize raising the variable-to-fixed cap above 1:1 (up to 2:1) only if permitted by the Articles. As of 31 December 2024, the Bank’s Articles do not allow exceeding 1:1; group-level decision rules are specified.
- Board of Directors’ role: Proposes and implements remuneration policies; sets systems for top executives, key business/function leaders, direct reports to governing bodies, and control functions; ensures alignment with risk appetite, strategy, long-term goals, governance, and internal controls; ensures legal and ethical compliance.
- Key Staff definition: Personnel whose activities have, or may have, a material impact on the Bank/Group risk profile, identified per applicable regulations.

nodes.title: Approval and updating of incentive systems
nodes.heading: Approval and updating of incentive systems
nodes.start_phrase: The remuneration policies for 2024 were approved at the Shareholders’ Meeting of 11 April 2024.
nodes.summary:
- Integration of climate and environmental risks into the Group’s risk management framework, credit standards and processes, and structuring of a Group ESG database; ESG strategic roadmap includes decarbonisation strategies and climate-change support, with climate considerations embedded in business indicators and a 10% ESG goal component in scorecards.

- Governance of remuneration and incentive systems for 2024: Shareholders’ Meeting (11 April 2024) approves remuneration and incentive policies and instrument-based plans; per Articles of Association and Bank of Italy Circular 285, the Shareholders’ Meeting may set variable/fixed pay ratios within regulatory limits, though the Bank’s Articles as of 31 Dec 2024 do not allow increases above 1:1. The Board of Directors drafts, submits, and implements policies; defines incentive systems for key executives and control functions; and ensures consistency with risk appetite, strategy, long-term objectives, governance, internal controls, and legal/ethical standards. The Remuneration Committee gives independent opinions and proposals, evaluates criteria for managers with strategic responsibilities, oversees control function remuneration with Risk Management involvement, and prepares related documentation. Compliance, Risk Management, and Internal Audit ensure regulatory alignment and support risk-consistent design and implementation, particularly regarding customer relations.

- Due diligence statement: a process integrated into the business model and strategy, not a standalone procedure, used to identify, manage, and report actual and potential negative impacts on people and the environment. The 2024 Double Materiality Analysis identifies material impacts, risks, and opportunities across topics/subtopics. Core due diligence elements are mapped to ESRS 2 and topical ESRS, covering governance integration, stakeholder engagement, impact identification and assessment (climate change, workers in the value chain, consumers/end users, business conduct), mitigation measures (decarbonisation of financed emissions, own-operations and downstream value chain actions, worker and privacy actions, corporate culture initiatives), and monitoring effectiveness through transparency, targets and metrics for own operations and the downstream value chain, and objectives for workers, privacy, and culture.

nodes.title: Statement on due diligence
nodes.heading: Statement on due diligence
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s due diligence process is fully integrated into its business model and the overall strategic framework adopted by the bank, although it does not constitute a separate, formalised procedure.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Bank’s due diligence approach as integrated into its business model and strategy, focused on identifying, managing, and reporting current and potential negative impacts on people and the environment.
- Highlights the 2024 Double Materiality Analysis, which identifies material impacts, risks, and opportunities by topic, sub-topic, and sub-sub-topic, with a summary of material negative impacts.
- Maps core due diligence (duty of care) elements to ESRS 2 and topical ESRS disclosures, covering:
  - Governance integration: roles and responsibilities of management bodies, links to incentive schemes, and the IRO identification process.
  - Stakeholder engagement processes and oversight by management bodies.
  - Identification and assessment of negative impacts across climate change, workers in the value chain, consumers and end-users, and business conduct.
  - Measures to mitigate impacts: decarbonisation levers and actions for own operations and the downstream value chain; actions for workers, privacy, and corporate culture.
  - Monitoring effectiveness: climate targets and metrics, objectives for workers and corporate culture, and privacy actions.
- Explains risk management and internal control framework for sustainability reporting, integrated with financial reporting and led by the Sustainability and ESG Function.
- Notes centralized oversight of sustainability reporting regulations, projects, and disclosures at the Parent Company level.
- Details a Group-wide control model aligned with the Internal Control System (Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013) with:
  - First-level line controls by Bank departments to ensure completeness, accuracy, reliability, and timeliness of data.
  - Subsidiary responsibilities for data quality and Board approval of their sustainability reporting contributions.
- Outlines the Sustainability and ESG Function’s annual double materiality analysis per CSRD and EFRAG IG1, and its role in defining policies, actions, and targets.
- Describes roles of corporate control functions:
  - Chief Risk Officer: integrates ESG risks into risk frameworks and appetite, internal risk reporting, and ESG risk materiality assessment.
  - Chief Compliance Executive: ensures compliance with EU/national rules, evaluates regulatory changes, and oversees correct application of sustainability regulations.
  - Chief Audit Executive: assesses adequacy of internal controls for ESG policies, procedures, and actions.
- Notes ICT’s responsibility for data integrity in the reporting process.
- States that the Financial Reporting Officer and CEO issue a compliance statement with Directive 2013/34/EU and Italy’s Legislative Decree No. 125/2024; the report is certified for alignment with EU Taxonomy Regulation 2020/852 Article 8(4).

nodes.title: Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.heading: Risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting
nodes.start_phrase: The process of preparing the Sustainability Report is integrated into the financial reporting process and is the responsibility of the Sustainability and ESG Function, in interaction with the Bank/Group’s various entities.
nodes.summary:
- Sustainability reporting is integrated with financial reporting and overseen by the Parent Company’s Sustainability and ESG Function, coordinating Group entities.
- A Group-wide internal control model, aligned with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013, ensures structured, ongoing controls and prompt anomaly detection.
- First-level (line) controls:
  - Parent Company Departments ensure completeness, accuracy, reliability, timeliness, and regulatory compliance for their sustainability disclosures.
  - Subsidiaries provide and approve their sustainability contributions via their Boards of Directors.
- The Sustainability and ESG Function conducts an annual double materiality analysis per CSRD and EFRAG IG1, and coordinates related policies, actions, and targets.
- Corporate control functions’ roles:
  - Chief Risk Officer: integrates ESG risk into risk frameworks and appetite, internal aggregated risk reporting, and performs ESG risk materiality assessments.
  - Chief Compliance Executive: ensures compliance with EU/national sustainability regulations, evaluates regulatory changes, and monitors proper application.
  - Chief Audit Executive: evaluates adequacy of ESG-related internal controls, policies, and procedures.
- ICT Function ensures data integrity across the IT component of reporting.
- The Financial Reporting Officer (FRO) and CEO issue a compliance statement on adherence to reporting standards (Directive 2013/34/EU and Italian Legislative Decree 125/2024) and certify alignment with EU Taxonomy Regulation (Article 8(4)).
- Law 262 Control Function supports FRO certification via a mixed model:
  - Analytical checks (own testing and reliance on other control functions’ results).
  - Synthetic checks (checklists and sub-certifications from contributing departments and subsidiaries).
- This approach mitigates risks of non-compliance with ESRS qualitative characteristics (relevance, faithful representation, comparability, verifiability, understandability) and risks in data processing, storage, and transfer.
- Post-controls, the FRO assesses the overall Internal Control System for sustainability, accounting, and financial reporting, defines remediation actions, and formalizes them in the “Report for Issuing Certification.”
- Control functions regularly brief the Board of Directors and Board of Statutory Auditors on sustainability reporting risks and controls; these bodies review the FRO’s certification report.
- Strategy and business model highlights:
  - Purpose centered on the well-being of customers and local areas, linking economic, social, and environmental value creation.
  - Focus on opportunities and risk management from the sustainability transition, climate change, and environmental protection; reinforcement of social role.
  - Distinctive positioning: centuries-long heritage, strong brand, locally entrenched network; bank for families and businesses.
  - Customer approach combining technology and human touch with hybrid channels (digital, face-to-face/in-branch).
  - Progressive, structural integration of ESG into strategy and business model, with voluntary adherence to international sustainability initiatives and goals.

nodes.title: Strategy
nodes.heading: Strategy
nodes.start_phrase: Consistent with its historical focus as a bank that revolves around the needs of families and the territories in which it operates, the Group recognises the connection between economic development, social development and environmental protection in order to generate sustainable value over time.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s sustainability-driven strategy and customer-centric business model:

- Purpose and positioning: A bank with deep local roots focused on families and territories, aiming to create long-term shared value by putting people, local areas, and sustainability at the center, combining technology with human touch across hybrid customer journeys (digital and in-branch).

- ESG integration: Sustainability is structurally embedded in strategy and the 2024–2028 Business Plan (“A Clear and Simple Commercial Bank, Revolving Around Customers, Combining Technology With Human Touch”), aligning with international initiatives (SDGs, PRB, NZBA) and regulatory guidance (ECB climate and environmental risk).

- Environmental (E): 
  - NZBA member since 2022; net zero Scope 1 and 2 (market-based) by 2030.
  - Portfolio decarbonization with targets and transition plans for high-emission sectors; coal phase-out achieved; further sector targets added through Feb 2025 and management targets for non-priority sectors.
  - No direct operations or revenues in fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) or chemical production; restrictive lending/exclusions for coal, unconventional oil and gas, and harmful ecological impacts; biodiversity and protected-area screening (UNESCO, Ramsar, IUCN I–VI).
  - Support SME transition (notably agrifood) to renewables; expand green financing, investment, funding, and insurance offerings.

- Social (S):
  - Workplace wellbeing, safety, skills development, inclusion, and culture programs.
  - More restrictive lending for sectors harmful to societal welfare (tobacco cultivation/production, gambling, controversial weapons).
  - Screening against human rights violations, child/forced labor, H&S breaches, fraud, AML/CFT, and corruption; no direct Group activities or revenues in controversial weapons, tobacco cultivation/production, or gambling.
  - Products supporting equitable and inclusive business models; offerings for disadvantaged individuals and companies; financial education initiatives.

- Governance (G):
  - Promotion of ESG culture via training and ESG-linked variable remuneration.
  - Integration of ESG in credit policies, risk measurement, and overall strategy.
  - Strengthening ESG data quality, monitoring, and transparency.

- Execution framework:
  - A Board-approved Sustainability Plan and cross-functional ESG Programme define initiatives, timelines, responsibilities, and monitoring, with periodic reporting to top bodies and an ESG Steering Committee to address deviations.
  - Forward-looking information prepared under ESRS with acknowledgment of uncertainty.

- Business model:
  - An Italian commercial bank delivering a hybrid, secure, and accessible customer experience through branches and advanced digital platforms.
  - Five strategic guidelines: customer-centric service models; optimized omnichannel digital platform; “zero-based” risk management; expansion of fee-based products/services; enhanced household lending and SME solutions focused on sustainability and innovation.
  - Key inputs: financial resources, technology, digital infrastructure, specialized expertise, and vetted suppliers.
  - Operations: retail and commercial banking with activities in factoring, corporate finance, investment banking; insurance/pensions via AXA partnership; asset management via independent third-party products.
  - Workforce: 16,727 employees (as of 31 Dec 2024).
  - Client segments: Retail, Private Banking, Companies (SMEs to large), and Large Corporate.
  - ESG-aligned products: Sustainability-Linked Loans; Green/Social Loans; EU Taxonomy-aligned Green Loans.

nodes.title: Business model
nodes.heading: Business model
nodes.start_phrase: Banca MPS is a commercial bank characterised by a business model strongly rooted in the reference territories, which combines the solidity and expertise of the branch network with an advanced digital platform in order to guaran- tee a hybrid customer experience and value in step with available technologies.
nodes.summary:
- Includes a forward-looking information disclaimer noting potential significant deviations between projections and actual results.
- Describes Banca MPS’s business model: a territorially rooted commercial bank in Italy combining a strong branch network with an advanced digital platform to deliver a hybrid, secure, inclusive customer experience; transformation anchored in technological innovation and skilled people.
- Outlines five strategic pillars for value creation: customer-centric, high value-added service models; optimized omnichannel digital platform with high security and accessibility; “zero-based” risk management using advanced analytics; development of fee-based products to diversify revenues and strengthen advisory; enhanced lending for households and tailored SME solutions with a focus on sustainability and innovation.
- Lists key inputs: financial resources, technology, digital infrastructure, and specialized expertise sourced via vetted, reliable suppliers and partners.
- Details business scope: primarily Italian retail and commercial banking, with activities in factoring, corporate finance, and investment banking; insurance-pension via strategic partnership with AXA; asset management through third-party investment products.
- Notes scale and customer focus: 16,727 employees as of 31 Dec 2024; segments served include Retail, Private Banking, Companies (SMEs to large), and Large Corporate with tailored offerings.
- Highlights ESG-integrated products: Sustainability-Linked Loans, Green/Social Loans, and Taxonomy-Aligned Loans, aligned with LMA guidelines and EU Taxonomy; expanded savings/insurance offerings (funds/SICAV with unit-linked and multi-segment policies) including more ESG options.
- Covers digital and inclusion initiatives: ATM audio guides extended to international-card users for visually impaired accessibility; Google Pay and Apple Pay enabled for Banca Widiba credit cards.
- Emphasizes transversal integration of sustainability: clear indicators, targets, cascading processes, and monitoring to ensure delivery of sustainable, long-term value for diverse customer segments.
- Describes the value chain: 
  - Upstream: suppliers, commercial partners (e.g., AXA), and non-commercial partners providing inputs and services.
  - Own operations: resources (employees, property, hardware) and core products/services (credit, wealth management, bond issuances, payments, consulting, deposits, digital).
  - Downstream: customers (deposits, loans) and distributors (agents, networks, promoters).
- Positions the Group as a financial intermediary linking capital providers with companies and individuals, supporting communities and sustainable, resilient growth.
- Points to related sections for further detail on sustainable products, environmental and social information, and the consolidated operational overview.

nodes.title: Value chain
nodes.heading: Value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Group value chain can be broken down into two main segments: upstream and downstream, which together describe the processes and players involved in the Group’s creation of value.
nodes.summary:
- The Group expanded sustainable finance offerings aligned with the LMA Green and Sustainable Lending Glossary and the EU Taxonomy (Regulation 2020/852).
- Savings/insurance products were revamped, combining funds/SICAV with unit-linked and multi-segment policies and adding ESG-focused solutions.
- Accessibility and digital payments advanced: ATM audio-guide functionality was extended to international cards for blind/visually impaired users; Apple Pay and Google Pay enablement was extended to Banca Widiba credit cards.
- Sustainability is embedded across the business model with defined indicators, targets, and cascading monitoring to drive long-term value and serve diverse customer segments.
- The report signposts further detail in Environmental and Social sections and refers to the Consolidated Report for group overview, customer assets, and distribution channels.
- A comprehensive value chain model is outlined across upstream, own operations, and downstream segments.
- Upstream: suppliers provide operational/infrastructure services (hardware, software, energy, real estate), technology and digital services, payment infrastructure, risk management software, financial/insurance, legal/tax/advisory, logistics/administration, and outsourcing. Business partners add insurance products and advisory, payment and card services (including SEPA and SWIFT, mobile payments), and support real-estate financing. Non-commercial partners (associations and public financial institutions) collaborate on public funds, government bond placement, and programs for development, digitalisation, and sustainability.
- Own operations: resources (employees, property, hardware); products (credit, wealth management, bond issuances); services (payments, consulting, deposits, digital).
- Downstream: processes for delivering banking services, distributing financial products, customer relationship management, lending, and investment finalisation, involving customers (funding and borrowing) and distributors (advisors, agents, credit brokers, promoters).
- The Group’s ecosystem role is emphasised as an intermediary connecting capital providers with companies and individuals through financial solutions and services.

nodes.title: Upstream Segment
nodes.heading: Upstream Segment
nodes.start_phrase: The upstream segment groups the players involved and the processes aimed at collecting the resources needed to carry out business operations.
nodes.summary:
- Defines the Group’s value chain through two segments: Upstream (inputs enabling operations) and Downstream (delivery of banking services).
- Upstream segment:
  - Describes suppliers providing operational and infrastructure services: hardware/software, electricity and gas, real estate maintenance/management, logistics and administrative support, outsourcing for non-core activities.
  - Details technology and digital providers: IT systems, digital infrastructure, payment systems, online platforms, and risk management software supporting banking infrastructure.
  - Covers financial and insurance service providers for corporate asset insurance, financial risk management, and legal/tax/advisory services.
  - Highlights strategic business partners offering:
    - Insurance products (life, non-life, credit-related) and advisory for asset protection and savings.
    - Payment and card services (prepaid, contactless, international and real-time payments via SEPA and SWIFT, mobile payments).
    - Real estate financing promotion via partnerships with agencies and real estate firms.
  - Notes non-commercial partners (associations and public financial institutions) supporting public fund management, financing of economic/infrastructure projects, government bond placement, and regional/government programs (including EU funds, digitalization, and sustainability initiatives).
- Downstream segment:
  - Outlines processes for direct service delivery: provision of banking services, financial product distribution, customer relationship management, loan disbursement, and investment finalization.
  - Identifies main actors:
    - Customers on both funding (deposits/raising capital) and borrowing sides.
    - Distributors: financial advisors, financial agents, credit brokers, and reporters.

nodes.title: Downstream Segment
nodes.heading: Downstream Segment
nodes.start_phrase: The downstream segment groups together the players involved and the business processes, as well as the related support processes aimed at operations involving the direct provision of banking services, the distribution of financial products, customer relationship management, loan disbursement and the finalisation of investments.
nodes.summary:
- Maps the Group’s value chain, distinguishing the upstream and downstream segments.
- Upstream: details key players and services provided by suppliers (IT, digital infrastructure, facilities, utilities, logistics, outsourcing, financial and insurance services), strategic business partners (insurance products and advisory, payment and card services including SEPA and SWIFT, and real-estate financing promotion), and non-commercial partners (associations and public financial institutions supporting public funds management, government bond placement, and regional/EU programs for digitalization and sustainability).
- Downstream: outlines core processes for delivering banking services and identifies main actors—customers (funding sources and borrowers) and distributors (financial advisors, agents, credit brokers, reporters).
- Explains the evolution to a double materiality approach: from impact analysis in 2022, initial double materiality alignment with GRI in 2023, to a 2024 ESRS-aligned methodology integrating impact and financial materiality, with stakeholder engagement, to guide strategy, risk management, and objectives.
- Describes a four-step materiality process: 1) understand context and define boundaries; 2) identify potential impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs); 3) assess IROs using qualitative-quantitative metrics with internal and external stakeholder input; 4) aggregate and validate material topics with governance approval.
- Specifies Step 1 inputs: the 2024–2028 Business Plan, feedback from analysts/investors/ESG raters, Italy’s environmental-social-economic needs and SDG/EU recommendations (per PRB), and key regulations and guidance (EU Taxonomy, ESRS, CSRD, SFDR, ECB climate risk guidelines, EFRAG).

nodes.title: Double materiality analysis
nodes.heading: Double materiality analysis
nodes.start_phrase: Over the past few years, the double materiality analysis, consistent with the evolution of the concept of sustainability, has become increasingly important, requiring the gradual integration of sustainability considerations into corporate strategies, risk management and investment decisions of companies.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s double materiality analysis and its evolution as a core component of strategy, risk management, and long-term sustainability.
- Timeline of methodology updates: 2022 shift from single materiality to impact analysis; 2023 first adoption steps aligned with GRI Standards; 2024 rollout of a new double materiality methodology aligned with ESRS and internal developments.
- Definition and scope of double materiality:
  - Impact materiality: assessment of positive/negative, current/potential impacts on society, economy, and the environment from activities and business relationships.
  - Financial materiality: assessment of risks and opportunities with material effects on financial position, results, cash flows, access to finance, and cost of capital.
- Material topics are those meeting impact and/or financial relevance criteria; outcomes feed into strategy, policies, actions, and objectives.
- A structured four-step decision process:
  1) Understand the organization’s context and define boundaries.
  2) Identify potentially material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).
  3) Assess IROs using qualitative-quantitative metrics with internal and external stakeholder engagement.
  4) Identify and validate material topics, aggregating findings and obtaining approval from control bodies.
- Step 1 details (context setting) consider:
  - The Group’s 2024–2028 Business Plan and objectives.
  - Material issues and feedback from analysts, investors, and ESG rating agencies.
  - Italy’s environmental, social, and economic needs per Principles for Responsible Banking, progress toward SDGs, and EU recommendations for the 2030 Agenda.
  - The regulatory framework: EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852), ESRS (Delegated Reg. 2023/2772), CSRD (Dir. 2022/2464), SFDR (Reg. 2019/2088), ECB climate risk guidelines, and EFRAG materiality assessment guidance.

nodes.title: Step 1 - Understanding the context
nodes.heading: Step 1 - Understanding the context
nodes.start_phrase: Understanding the context consists of identifying the scope of the Group’s own activities, business relationships and the context in which they take place, and defining the necessary inputs for identifying impacts, risks and opportunities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s transition to a double materiality analysis, integrating both impact and financial materiality into strategy, risk management, and decision-making.
- Evolution: Shift from Single Materiality to impact analysis in 2022; initial double materiality reflections in 2023 aligned with GRI; full methodology rolled out in 2024 aligned with ESRS and EFRAG guidance.
- Objective: Identify material sustainability topics based on either impact relevance (on people, environment, economy) or financial relevance (risks/opportunities affecting financial performance, position, cash flows, financing, cost of capital).
- Governance link: Results feed into the Group’s strategy, policies, actions, objectives, and are validated by control bodies.
- Four-step process:
  1) Understand organizational context and define boundaries (activities, relationships, operating context).
  2) Identify potentially material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) across ESRS sub-topics, over short/medium/long terms and across the value chain.
  3) Assess IROs using qualitative/quantitative methods, engaging internal functions and external stakeholders.
  4) Aggregate, identify, and validate material topics per regulatory areas.
- Context inputs (Step 1): 2024–2028 Business Plan; analyst/investor/ESG rater feedback; Italy’s environmental, social, economic needs (PRB, SDGs, EU recommendations); EU and national regulations (EU Taxonomy, ESRS/CSRD, SFDR, ECB climate risk guidance, Delegated Regulation 2023/2772, EFRAG IG 1); internal sustainability policies; sector benchmarking.
- Boundary: Own operations (e.g., HR), upstream (procurement), downstream (product marketing/distribution).
- IRO mapping (Step 2): Captures positive/negative, actual/potential impacts including human rights; considers market, social, economic, regulatory trends and client characteristics; notes interlinkages (e.g., community initiatives → reputation/trust; ESG financing → product innovation; financing of exposed sectors → credit/market risk).
- Assessment approach (Step 3): Data-driven where available; otherwise qualitative based on internal policies/initiatives; structured stakeholder engagement for consolidation and validation.
- Impact metrics used: severity/benefit (entity), extent, irreparability (for negative impacts), and probability (for potential impacts).

nodes.title: Step 2 - Identifying Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: Step 2 - Identifying Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: An effective identification of potentially material impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to short-, medium- and long-term time horizons cannot disregard an understanding of the internal and external dynamics that may affect the bu- siness, while providing a clear view of emerging challenges and opportunities, constituting a key step in guiding the review of processes, policies and objectives.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the sustainability reporting approach in the 2024 Annual Report, grounded in internal ESG regulations (e.g., Sustainability and ESG Directive, Environmental Policy, Inclusion Plan and Rules) and a benchmark of peer banks’ disclosures.
- Defines the double materiality boundary across the full value chain: Own Operations (e.g., human resources), Upstream (procurement of materials and services), and Downstream (marketing, distribution, sales of products and services).
- Describes Step 2: identification of Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) over short-, medium- and long-term horizons, informed by internal/external dynamics, market, social, economic and regulatory trends, stakeholder expectations, and the Bank’s business and client profile; maps IROs at ESRS sub-topic granularity (including human rights), covering the value chain and highlighting linkages between impacts, risks and opportunities (e.g., community initiatives enhancing reputation; ESG financing expanding offerings; financing in ESG-exposed sectors creating financial risk from concentration).
