- Describes Step 3: assessment of potentially material IROs using qualitative and/or quantitative analyses aligned with business processes and data availability, with stakeholder engagement (internal and external) incorporated in the consolidation of assessments.
- Details impact assessment metrics per relevant legislation: Entity (severity/benefit), Extension (scope), Irreparability (negative impacts only), and Probability (for potential impacts).

nodes.title: Step 3 - Assessing potentially material IROs and stakeholder engagement
nodes.heading: Step 3 - Assessing potentially material IROs and stakeholder engagement
nodes.start_phrase: Each impact, risk and opportunity was analysed using qualitative and quantitative information, taking into account the assessments developed as part of the contextual understanding and engagement process of internal and external stakeholders.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the Group’s double materiality process aligned with ESRS, starting from internal regulations (Sustainability & ESG Directive, Environmental Policy, Inclusion Plan and Rules) and a benchmark of banking sector disclosures.
- Defines the assessment boundary across the entire value chain: Own Operations (e.g., HR), Upstream (procurement of materials and services), and Downstream (marketing, sales, and distribution).
- Describes Step 2: identification of impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs) over short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, grounded in internal/external context analysis, including market, social, economic, and regulatory trends, stakeholder expectations, business characteristics, and customer needs.
- States that IROs cover actual and potential, positive and negative impacts (including human rights) at the maximum ESRS granularity (Sub-Topics/Sub-Sub-Topics), without defining entity-specific issues, and include the whole value chain.
- Highlights linkages among IROs: community/non-profit initiatives can enhance reputation and trust; ESG financing strategies can expand product offerings; financing in ESG-exposed sectors can create financial risks (e.g., credit and market) due to concentration.
- Details Step 3: assessment of potentially material IROs using both qualitative (based on internal initiatives, policies, strategies) and quantitative approaches (data aligned with business specifics and availability), with internal and external stakeholder engagement in the consolidation phase.
- Specifies impact assessment metrics per legislation: Entity (severity/benefit), Extension (spread), Irreparability (negative impacts only), and Probability (for potential impacts only).
- Emphasizes that proactive IRO management strengthens resilience and supports positive environmental and social outcomes.

nodes.title: Assessing potentially material Impacts
nodes.heading: Assessing potentially material Impacts
nodes.start_phrase: The assessment of impacts involved the use of the following metrics defined in relevant legislation:
nodes.summary:
- Establishes the inputs and context for a double materiality assessment, drawing on internal sustainability regulations (e.g., Sustainability and ESG Directive, Environmental Policy, Inclusion Plan and Rules) and a benchmark of banking-sector disclosures.
- Defines the assessment boundary across the full value chain: own operations (e.g., human resources), upstream procurement (materials and services), and downstream marketing and distribution (sale of products and services).
- Describes Step 2 (Identifying Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities) with a time-horizon lens (short/medium/long), grounded in analysis of market, social, economic, and regulatory dynamics, customer characteristics, and stakeholder expectations.
- Maps IROs to ESRS at maximum granularity (Sub-Topics and Sub-Sub-Topics), covering actual and potential, positive and negative impacts (including human rights), and bringing the value chain into scope without adding entity-specific topics.
- Illustrates IRO interlinkages: community initiatives can enhance reputation and trust; ESG financing strategies can expand product offerings; financing in ESG-sensitive sectors can elevate financial risks (e.g., credit, market) via concentration.
- Details Step 3 (Assessing potentially material IROs) using qualitative and quantitative approaches based on data availability, internal initiatives, and strategies, with stakeholder input (internal and external) integrated in the consolidation phase.
- Sets impact assessment metrics: severity/benefit, extent, irreparability (negative impacts only), and probability (potential impacts only); determines materiality via scored averages tailored to actual/potential and positive/negative impacts, applying a threshold >3; identifies material impacts from own activities and business relationships.
- Assesses risks and opportunities under financial materiality, aligned with the Group’s risk framework and regulations, detailing risks at ESRS Sub-Sub-Topic level; opportunities stem from ESG initiatives that can broaden products, strengthen brand and trust, and attract talent.
- Applies ESRS/EFRAG-aligned parameters—magnitude of financial effects and probability—using a 1–5 scoring scale; combines existing internal qualitative/quantitative metrics with supplementary analyses; classifies risks and opportunities with scores >3 as material.
- Notes that risk assessment leverages inherent risk logic and considers current and prospective assets/costs; opportunity assessment evaluates financial effects tied to specific products.
- Emphasizes stakeholder engagement as integral to the double materiality process, enabling insight into trends, expectations, impacts, and perceived sustainability-related risks/opportunities; priority stakeholders are identified via a two-pronged approach based on business characteristics, context, sustainability strategy, initiatives, and global trends.

nodes.title: Assessing Potentially Material Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: Assessing Potentially Material Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: Within the framework of financial materiality, risks and opportunities are analysed taking into account the specific characteristics of the Group’s financial intermediation activity.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the Group’s double materiality methodology and scoring framework for impacts:
  - Actual positive impacts: relevance based on significance (average of Scale and Scope) versus a threshold
  - Actual negative impacts: relevance based on significance (average of Scale, Scope, Irreparability) versus a threshold
  - Potential positive impacts: relevance based on significance (average of Scale and Scope) and probability versus a threshold
  - Potential negative impacts: relevance based on significance (average of Scale, Scope, Irreparability) versus a threshold
- Sets a materiality threshold for the sustainability statement: topics with an impact rating above 3 are included
- States that material impacts were identified from both the Group’s own activities and its business relationships
- Details assessment of potentially material risks and opportunities under financial materiality:
  - Uses ESRS parameters: magnitude of potential financial effects and probability of occurrence
  - Applies EFRAG guidance, combining existing qualitative/quantitative metrics with additional assessments scored 1–5
  - Determines final scores by averaging assessed magnitudes; risks and opportunities with ratings above 3 are deemed material
- Aligns risk assessment with the Group’s established risk management system and regulatory requirements, enhanced to meet CSRD granularity
- Evaluates opportunities by estimating current and prospective financial effects from ESG-related products and strategies
- Describes stakeholder engagement as integral to double materiality:
  - Continuous dialogue to understand trends, expectations, impacts, and perceived sustainability-related risks and opportunities
  - Identification of priority stakeholder categories based on business characteristics, context, sustainability strategy, initiatives, and global sustainability trends, using a two-pronged approach

nodes.title: Stakeholder Engagement
nodes.heading: Stakeholder Engagement
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s engagement with stakeholders is a crucial step of the double materiality assessment; through an ongoing dialogue with stakeholders, it allows for a deeper understanding of industry trends, expectations related to social, environmental and governance aspects, significant impacts related to the Group’s business and its value chain, and to gather Stakeholder perceptions also on risks and opportunities related to sustainability issues for financial institutions and the Group, in a flexible and customised way.
nodes.summary:
This partial document from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s Sustainability Reporting explains the Group’s double materiality assessment approach under ESRS and CSRD, aligned with EFRAG IG 1 guidance. It outlines:
- How materiality is scored for actual and potential positive/negative impacts using significance (averages of Scale, Scope, and Irreparability where applicable) and probability, with a materiality threshold set at ratings above 3 for the sustainability statement.
- The assessment of financially material risks and opportunities using magnitude and probability parameters, leveraging existing risk management methodologies, qualitative and quantitative metrics, and a 1–5 scoring scale; items averaging above 3 are deemed material.
- Integration of inherent risk logic, current/prospective asset and cost exposures, and supplemental analyses to meet CSRD granularity; opportunities are evaluated based on current and prospective financial effects tied to specific products.
- A structured stakeholder engagement process as a core input to double materiality, using:
  - Stakeholder Management via internal interviews with functions that interface with customers, employees, and suppliers.
  - Direct Stakeholder Engagement via one-to-one interviews in 2024 with academia, sustainability associations, and customer associations.
- The validation rule that a topic is material if at least one mapped impact, risk, or opportunity is material.

It then lists material sustainability topics and subtopics and indicates where each is material across impacts, risks, and opportunities, including:
- E1 Climate change: Climate change adaptation; Climate change mitigation; Energy.
- E5 Circular economy: Resource outflows related to products and services.
- S1 Own workforce: Secure employment; Working time; Adequate wages; Social dialogue; Freedom of association/collective bargaining; Work-life balance; Health and safety; Gender equality and equal pay; Training and skills development; Employment and inclusion of persons with disabilities; Measures against violence and harassment; Diversity; Privacy.
- S2 Workers in the value chain: Secure employment; Working time; Adequate wages; Social dialogue; Freedom of association/collective bargaining.

Overall, the excerpt details the methodology, thresholds, stakeholder inputs, and the set of material topics identified across impacts, risks, and opportunities.

nodes.title: Step 4 - Identifying and validating material topics
nodes.heading: Step 4 - Identifying and validating material topics
nodes.start_phrase: The relevance of sustainability issues was determined in a manner consistent with relevant regulations.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s stakeholder approach used to inform ESRS/CSRD-aligned double materiality:  
  - Stakeholder Management via internal interviews with functions that maintain ongoing dialogue, indirectly covering customers, employees, and suppliers.  
  - Stakeholder Engagement via direct, one-to-one interviews in 2024 with external stakeholders (academia, sustainability associations, and customer associations) to assess and validate impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).

- Explains that stakeholder input is integrated with internal data, external benchmarking, and regulatory analysis to consolidate the relevance of sustainability topics.

- Sets the materiality rule: if at least one of impact, risk, or opportunity is material for a topic, the topic is deemed material for the Group.

- Lists the material topics identified across ESRS areas, with materiality mapped across impacts, risks, and opportunities:
  - E1 Climate change: adaptation, mitigation, energy.
  - E5 Circular economy: resource outflows related to products and services.
  - S1 Own workforce: secure employment, working time, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association/collective bargaining, work-life balance, health and safety, gender equality and equal pay, training and skills, inclusion of persons with disabilities, measures against violence/harassment, diversity, privacy.
  - S2 Workers in the value chain: parallel labor topics including secure employment, working time, wages, social dialogue, FOA/CB, work-life balance, health and safety, child and forced labor, privacy.
  - S3 Affected communities: land-related impacts.
  - S4 Consumers/end users: privacy, freedom of expression, access to quality information, health and safety, non-discrimination, access to products/services, responsible marketing.
  - G1 Business conduct: corporate culture, whistle-blower protection, prevention/detection (including training) and incidents.

- Notes that detailed IROs, time horizons, and scopes will be provided in subsequent ESRS-specific chapters.

- Highlights strategic resilience: alignment of the materiality results with Stakeholder Engagement outcomes, the 2024–2028 Business Plan, and analyses of ESG risk factors on traditional risks, supporting the Group’s ability to manage material risks/impacts and capture opportunities.

- Emphasizes increased rigor versus the 2023 Non-Financial Statement due to CSRD/ESRS requirements, including more granular topics and explicit assessment of risks and opportunities.

- Confirms validation and governance: results shared and consolidated by competent Group entities and presented to the ESG session of the Management Committee, the Risk and Sustainability Committee, the Board of Statutory Auditors, and the Board of Directors.

nodes.title: Validation of material topics
nodes.heading: Validation of material topics
nodes.start_phrase: The process of mapping and assessing impacts, risks and opportunities was shared and consolidated by the competent Group Entities through the Stakeholder Management process mentioned above.
nodes.summary:
- Presents Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s double materiality assessment conducted under ESRS/CSRD, mapping impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs) with greater granularity than in 2023 and aligning results with stakeholder engagement, the 2024–2028 Business Plan, and analyses of ESG risk factors on traditional risks to support strategy resilience.
- Lists key sustainability topics assessed across:
  - Workforce: work-life balance, health and safety, child labour, forced labour, privacy.
  - Affected communities: land-related impacts.
  - Consumers and end users: privacy, freedom of expression, access to quality information, health and safety, non-discrimination, access to products and services, responsible marketing practices.
  - Business conduct: corporate culture, whistle-blower protection, prevention and detection (including training), incident management.
- Describes validation governance: results shared and consolidated through Stakeholder Management and presented to the Management Committee (ESG session), Risk and Sustainability Committee, Board of Statutory Auditors and Board of Directors.
- Identifies non-material environmental standards for the Group: ESRS E2 (Pollution), ESRS E3 (Marine Waters and Resources), ESRS E4 (Biodiversity and ecosystems), while detailing the analytical approach used (qualitative-quantitative methods, expert consultations, internal analyses) across own operations and the value chain.
- Summarizes findings for E2–E4:
  - E2: Potential downstream pollution impacts via financing/investment; operational/reputational risks from inadequate controls; counterparty credit/market/liquidity risks; opportunity to expand product offerings to meet counterparties’ needs.
  - E3: Potential inefficient water use in own operations and downstream water-related impacts via financing; associated operational/reputational and financial risks; product offering opportunities.
  - E4: Potential biodiversity impacts from own sites and downstream exposure to sectors with direct biodiversity risks; operational/reputational and financial risks; product offering opportunities; recognition of positive contributions via internal policies/initiatives.
- Concludes that financial materiality for E2–E4 shows no reportable material risks, but the Group maintains prudential safeguards and continuous monitoring of direct and indirect environmental risks.
- Notes risk management integration: 2025 Risk Appetite Statement to include internal thresholds and two KRIs for non-climate environmental risks (transition and physical), with operational limits on exposure in the non-financial corporate portfolio.
- Points to additional details available in Part E of the Notes.

nodes.title: In-depth study of non-material topics
nodes.heading: In-depth study of non-material topics
nodes.start_phrase: Following the analyses conducted, the following issues were found not to be material for the Group:
nodes.summary:
- The Group’s double materiality assessment deems ESRS E2 (Pollution), E3 (Water and Marine Resources), and E4 (Biodiversity and Ecosystems) non-material for reporting. Assessments covered own operations and the upstream/downstream value chain using qualitative-quantitative analyses, expert input, and internal studies.
- E2 findings: potential negative impacts via financing companies with weak pollution controls; operational/reputational risks from inadequate internal controls; financial risks (credit, market, liquidity) from counterparty exposure; opportunity to expand products to meet counterparties’ needs.
- E3 findings: potential inefficient water use in own operations and lack of dedicated policies; downstream risks via financing entities that may waste water or cause harmful discharges; associated operational/reputational and financial risks; product development opportunities.
- E4 findings: potential negative impacts from sites in high-biodiversity areas and positive contributions via internal climate/biodiversity policies; downstream risk of biodiversity loss through lending to high-impact sectors; operational/reputational and financial risks; product expansion opportunities.
- Financial materiality for E2–E4 was not identified; however, the Group will monitor environmental risk thresholds via the 2025 Risk Appetite Statement with KRIs for E‑non‑climate Transition and Physical Risks and set operational limits for the non-financial corporate portfolio.
- A detailed ESRS disclosure index maps where topics are reported: 
  - Section 1 (ESRS 2) on general information, governance roles, due diligence, risk controls, strategy, stakeholder engagement, and IRO processes.
  - Section 2 Environmental: Climate change (ESRS E1) is material with disclosures on transition plan, policies, actions, targets, energy, GHG emissions, and phased-in financial effects; Resource use/circular economy (ESRS E5) largely not applicable/not material.
  - Section 3 Social: Own workforce (S1), Workers in the value chain (S2), Affected communities (S3), Consumers and end-users (S4) with policies, actions, targets, metrics, and grievance mechanisms; many items are material.
  - Section 4 Governance: Business conduct (G1) including policies, anti-corruption controls, incidents, with some items not material.
- A cross-reference table flags which EU regulatory-related ESRS data points are material, immaterial, not applicable, or phased-in: climate metrics and targets (E1) largely material; E2–E4 disclosures immaterial; selected social and governance indicators material (e.g., human rights, H&S, gender pay gap, anti-corruption incidents).
- The climate change section (ESRS E1) outlines:
  - Methodology and internal frameworks (Environmental Policy, ESG Directive, Credit Policies, Risk Governance Directive).
  - Material positive impacts through supplier and customer awareness initiatives aligned with decarbonization strategy.
  - Material negative impacts from own Scope 1–2 emissions and energy use, and from financing high-emitting clients lacking transition plans.
  - Material risks concentrated downstream: credit risk from counterparties’ transition misalignment and physical climate events, and reputational risk.
  - Opportunities: expanding transition-supporting products (downstream) and enhancing brand reputation (own operations).

structure.title: Environmental Information
structure.heading: Section 2 - Environmental Information
structure.start_phrase: This section provides, in relation to the management of “climate change”, a description of the impacts, risks and oppor - tunities found to be material from the double materiality analysis.
structure.summary:
- Context and scope: ESRS E1 climate change section of the 2024 Sustainability Report outlining material impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), the Group’s transition plan, related policies and actions, and the targets/metrics used to monitor effectiveness.
- Mapping approach: Double materiality assessment tailored to the Group’s operations, commercial activities and decarbonisation strategy; review of internal governance and policy documents (Environmental Policy, ESG Directive, Credit Policies, Risk Governance Directive); safeguards applied across own operations and the value chain.
- Value chain dynamics: Interactions with suppliers and customers create both risk (counterparties’ difficulty managing climate issues) and opportunity (expanding transition-supportive products and raising customer awareness); setting climate targets may enhance reputation.
- Material positive impacts:
  - Upstream: Supplier awareness raised via selection criteria that evaluate climate adaptation/mitigation policies and safeguards.
  - Downstream: Customer awareness and transition acceleration supported by an ESG questionnaire assessing environmental profile; results inform tailored commercial offerings aligned with the Group’s decarbonisation and credit strategy.
- Material negative impacts:
  - Own operations: Scope 1 and 2 emissions (e.g., heating, fossil-fuel fleet with low hybrid/electric uptake) and direct energy consumption; mitigation via internal policies and corporate strategies to reduce emissions and energy use.
  - Downstream: Potential financing of highly emissive counterparties lacking transition plans and emission-reduction initiatives.
- Material risks:
  - Credit risk in the downstream value chain from counterparties’ deteriorating creditworthiness due to transition misalignment and physical climate impacts (acute/chronic events), material to climate adaptation, mitigation and energy.
  - Reputational risk from financing highly emissive clients without transition plans.
- Material opportunities:
  - Downstream: Expansion of product range relating to climate mitigation and energy.
  - Own operations: Reputation enhancement linked to climate mitigation progress.
- Oversight and performance: Targets and metrics are set to track and evaluate the effectiveness of policies, actions and the transition plan.

nodes.title: Climate change
nodes.heading: Climate change [ESRS E1]

Climate change

tunities found to be material from the double materiality analysis. Next, the section outlines the Group’s transition plan,

nodes.title: Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard takes into account the specific aspects related to the Group’s operational and commercial activities and its decarbonisation strategies.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: ESRS E1 Climate Change section of the Sustainability Report outlining double materiality results, transition planning, policies/actions, targets and metrics related to climate change.
- Mapping approach: Assessment grounded in internal governance and policy documents (Environmental Policy, ESG Directive, Credit Policies, Risk Governance Directive), covering own operations and the value chain; recognizes both risks and business opportunities from counterparties’ transition challenges; potential reputational gains from climate targets.
- Material impacts:
  - Positive: Upstream supplier engagement through selection criteria that assess climate adaptation/mitigation; downstream customer awareness via an ESG questionnaire that informs tailored commercial offers aligned with the Group’s decarbonisation and credit strategy.
  - Negative: Own operations’ Scope 1–2 emissions (heating, fossil-fuel vehicle fleet, energy use) with reduction measures in place; downstream exposure from financing highly emissive counterparties lacking transition plans.
- Material risks: Credit risk from counterparties’ financial deterioration due to transition misalignment and physical climate events; reputational risk from financing high emitters without credible plans; material across adaptation, mitigation, and energy topics.
- Opportunities: Expansion of transition/energy-related product offerings and enhancement of brand reputation through climate mitigation efforts.
- Resilience and risk management: Built per ECB November 2020 guidelines within the broader Risk Management Framework, covering physical (CCA) and transition (CCM) risks; includes identifying transmission channels, defining exposure metrics and indicators, scenario-based impact analysis on P&L and asset values, and setting tolerance thresholds with operational limits and escalation processes.
- Model integration: Physical and transition risk drivers embedded in credit models to produce PD/LGD-based risk add-ons at counterparty level.
- Stress testing and limits: Tolerance margins informed by internal and institutional climate stress tests; ESG limit breaches trigger governance escalations and corrective actions.
- Scenario foundations: Physical risk uses open and commercial datasets (ISPRA, IPCC, Copernicus, Cerved) with Hot House World/Current Policies projections; transition risk uses Net Zero 2050 scenarios aligned with the Paris Agreement.
- Time horizons: Short-term (≤1 year), medium-term (1–5 years, 3-year buckets), long-term (>5 years, 10-year buckets).

nodes.title: Resilience analysis
nodes.heading: Resilience analysis
nodes.start_phrase: The process of identifying and assessing risks related to climate change, with respect to the taxonomy areas defined as Climate Change Mitigation (or CCM) and Adaptation (CCA), was developed as part of a process undertaken in the wake of the November 2020 ECB Guidelines, and within the broader Risk Management Framework with the risk factors related to the topic under analysis.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: E1 Climate Change (adaptation, mitigation, energy) across the Bank’s operations and value chain (upstream and downstream), covering impacts, risks, opportunities, and related policies, actions, and targets.

- Resilience and risk management:
  - Developed per ECB 2020 Guidelines and integrated into the Group Risk Management Framework.
  - Methodology includes: identifying transmission channels and materiality for core risks; defining exposure measures and key indicators; scenario analysis on P&L and asset values; setting tolerance thresholds and operational limits with escalation processes.
  - Integration of physical and transition risk variables into PD/LGD to produce risk add-ons.
  - Climate stress testing (internal and institutional) informs tolerance margins; ESG limit breaches trigger corrective actions.

- Climate scenarios and horizons:
  - Physical risk scenarios use open and commercial data (ISPRAmbiente, IPCC, Copernicus, Cerved) with “Current Policies/Hot House World” assumptions.
  - Transition risk scenarios align with “Net Zero 2050” and the Paris Agreement.
  - Time horizons: short-term (≤1 year), medium-term (1–5 years, 3-year bucket), long-term (>5 years, 10-year bucket), with references to RAS/ICAAP horizons (25–30 years, 2050+).

- Material risks identified and monitored:
  - Physical climate risk for credit risk in non-financial corporate portfolios.
  - Physical climate risk for credit risk in retail mortgage portfolios.
  - Transition risk for credit risk in non-financial corporate portfolios.
  - Transition risk for credit risk in retail mortgage portfolios.
  - Transition risk affecting operational and reputational risk (e.g., exposure to brown lending and stakeholder perceptions).
  - All linked to KRIs in the Risk Appetite Statement with operational limits; quarterly monitoring and reporting to top management.

- Strategic integration and disclosure:
  - Embedding climate risk factors into risk and strategic processes to support transition, mitigate risk, and maintain financial stability.
  - Further methodological details referenced in the Financial Statements, Part E (risks and hedging policies).

- Transition plan for climate change mitigation:
  - Commitment to net-zero by 2050, recognizing the role of financing and products.
  - Emissions profile: ~99% Scope 3 financed emissions (lending to non-financial corporates); ~0.05% Scope 1–2 from own operations.
  - Decarbonization strategy for financed emissions aligned with NZBA (member since 2022), including 2030 interim targets and actions based on science-based climate scenarios.

nodes.title: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
nodes.heading: Transition plan for climate change mitigation
nodes.start_phrase: Aware of the important role of financial institutions in supporting the transition to a zero net emission economy by 2050 through their financing, investment and product and service offerings, the Group is committed to doing its part to mitigating climate change.
nodes.summary:
- Establishes the bank’s climate and environmental risk framework: multi-horizon materiality analysis (including ICAAP 25–30 years and post-2050 end-horizon), updated risk maps, horizon analysis, and climate stress testing tied to the Risk Appetite Statement (RAS).
- Identifies material risks under continuous monitoring: physical and transition climate risks for credit risk in non-financial corporates and retail mortgages; transition risk for operational and reputational exposure linked to “brown” lending.
- Embeds climate risks in risk management, strategy, and lending processes; assigns KRIs with operational limits in the RAS; monitors quarterly and reports to top management.
- Outlines a climate transition plan aligned with net-zero by 2050 and NZBA guidelines, using science-based scenarios (IEA, NGFS) and setting 2030 interim targets.
- Confirms emissions profile: ~99% Scope 3 (financed emissions from lending to non-financial corporates); ~0.05% Scope 1 and 2 from own operations.
- Defines NZBA sectoral targets covering ~90% of financed emissions in emission-intensive sectors: Oil & Gas, Power Generation & Distribution, Iron & Steel (announced Aug 2023) and Cement, Aluminium (announced Feb 2025); coal sector phase-out already achieved.
- Sets additional 2030 interim management targets (in 2024) for residual high-impact sectors, with sector-specific transition levers guiding credit policies and commercial offerings; alignment with Paris Agreement and EU policies.
- Commits to zero Scope 1 and market-based Scope 2 emissions by 2030; actions include energy efficiency, dematerialization, reduced fossil fuel use, and 100% renewable electricity; further measures to be defined in 2025.
- Details governance: transition plan and targets discussed in the ESG Steering Committee, approved by the Board of Directors with binding Risk & Sustainability Committee opinion; latest update January 2025.
- Integrates counterparty-level transition and physical risk indicators into lending; Risk Management and Sustainability functions conduct regular monitoring, identify deviations, and define mitigation actions; NZBA sector targets reported to UNEP and published online.
- Describes client transition support: engagement and ESG profiling via questionnaires; green products (Sustainability-Linked Loans, Taxonomy-aligned Green Loans) with incentive pricing; protocols with institutions; ESG-based credit policies incorporating emission intensity and transition risk.
- Enhances transparency and execution: ESG training programs; financed-emissions data systems; periodic cross-functional forums (Commercial, Sustainability/ESG, Credit, CRO) to review progress and corrective actions; simulation tools and KPIs for green products.
- Notes ESG Program/Project (since 2023) coordinating cross-functional initiatives to implement the decarbonization strategy, with quarterly updates to top management.
- Invests in ESG infrastructure: centralized ESG database and dashboards for regulatory and voluntary reporting (CSRD, Pillar 3, bond frameworks, NZBA); tools for climate risk models and stress testing; indicates limited CapEx/OpEx for certain share-plan items.

nodes.title: Decarbonisation levers and key actions for reducing indirect emissions from the credit portfolio
nodes.heading: Decarbonisation levers and key actions for reducing indirect emissions from the credit portfolio
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has developed an organic approach to support its customers’ transition to climate neutrality in order to pursue its goals of reducing emissions from its lending portfolio to non-financial corporations
nodes.summary:
- The Group outlines an organic, sector-differentiated strategy to reduce financed (indirect) emissions in its lending portfolio while managing climate risks, recognising contributions from all sectors, with specific focus on high-emissions priority sectors.
- Core transition levers include shifting to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, adopting renewable-based technologies, increasing use of recycled materials, and employing emissions offsetting and capture.
- Activation mechanisms:
  - Client engagement using ESG assessments and questionnaires to share emissions/environmental profiles and tailor financing frameworks.
  - Offering green products (Sustainability-Linked Loans and Taxonomy-aligned Green Loans) with differentiated pricing to incentivise credible transition plans and optimise portfolio emission intensity.
  - Protocols and guidelines in collaboration with institutions and industry associations to accelerate sectoral transitions.
  - ESG-integrated credit policies that embed counterparty ESG scores, transition risk exposure, and emissions intensity into lending decisions.
- Transparency and monitoring framework:
  - Targeted ESG training and capability-building across roles; cross-functional ESG expert teams to support the network.
  - Systematic data collection and analysis of financed emissions with dedicated monitoring and reporting systems.
  - Regular interdepartmental governance (Commercial, Sustainability/ESG, Credit, CRO) to review progress, enact corrective actions, and design new initiatives.
  - Use of simulation tools and definition of KPIs to structure and monitor green products.
- Cross-functional support (ESG, ESG Risk, Sustainable Finance) to relationship managers for designing green operations and solutions for Corporate and SME clients.
- Investment program focused on integrating and monitoring ESG factors within business processes as part of the Bank’s ESG Programme; share-plan CapEx/OpEx deemed insignificant.
- 2024 CapEx priorities:
  - Building a centralised ESG data platform and dashboards to enhance internal and mandatory reporting (CSRD, Pillar 3, Social and Green Bond, NZBA) and to enable accurate identification and KPI tracking of green products in line with regulation.
  - Developing applications for internal climate risk management models supporting C&E risk monitoring, climate stress testing, and regulatory compliance.

nodes.title: Transparency and monitoring progress
nodes.heading: Transparency and monitoring progress
nodes.start_phrase: To effectively support the transition to a sustainable economic model, the Group has adopted a number of integrated measures aimed at fostering the dissemination of climate strategies, the achievement of set targets and the use of dedicated operational levers.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the Group’s strategy to reduce financed (indirect) emissions by supporting clients’ transition to climate neutrality, differentiated by sector (priority high‑emitting, other climate‑intensive, and remaining sectors).
- Defines cross‑sector and sector‑specific transition levers: shifting to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency and renewable-based technologies, increasing use of recycled materials, and deploying emission offsetting and capture.
- Details activation tools:
  - Client engagement via ESG questionnaires and sharing of ESG/emissions profiles to tailor support and financing.
  - Green lending products (Sustainability‑Linked Loans, Green/Taxonomy‑aligned loans) with incentive pricing to favor credible transition plans and optimize the loan portfolio by emissions intensity.
  - Protocols/guidelines with institutions and trade associations to accelerate transition.
  - ESG‑integrated credit policies embedding counterparties’ ESG scores, transition risk exposure, and emissions intensity into decisions, aligned with the Group’s decarbonisation strategy.
- Describes transparency and monitoring measures: ESG training by role, financed‑emissions data collection and reporting systems, periodic cross‑function reviews (Commercial, Sustainability/ESG, Credit, CRO) to track progress and corrective actions, simulation tools and KPIs for green products, and a cross‑functional ESG/ESG Risk/Sustainable Finance team supporting relationship managers on green transactions for corporates/SMEs.
- Explains 2024 ESG investments:
  - CapEx: centralized ESG data platform and dashboards, regulatory/mandatory reporting (CSRD, Pillar 3, Social/Green Bond, NZBA), tech to structure and monitor green products and KPIs, climate risk models and climate stress‑testing capabilities.
  - OpEx: external ESG datasets, expert advisory for decarbonisation strategy and transition plan, training and awareness programs, and development of ESG governance/process framework with external support.
  - Objective: embed ESG into risk management and reporting, aligned with ESRS and EU sustainability regulations.
- Notes the Group’s inclusion in EU Paris‑aligned benchmarks due to its key role in financing the low‑carbon transition.
- Presents climate‑related policies: an organizational model integrating ESG across strategy, business model, and policies for mitigation and adaptation, approved by the Board with oversight from risk/sustainability governance bodies.
- Highlights the Group’s Sustainability & ESG Guideline: commitment to measure and progressively reduce Scope 1, 2, and 3 emissions and increase renewable energy use; support client transitions through:

nodes.title: Policies, Actions and Targets relating to climate change
nodes.heading: Policies, Actions and Targets relating to climate change

Policies, Actions and Targets relating to climate change
This section includes a description of the policies the Group has adopted in relation to climate change mitigation  
and adaptation, actions and targets in relation to both its own operations and the value chain.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group adopts an organisational model that aims to progressively integrate the principles of environmental, social and governance sustainability into the definition of its strategy, business model and corporate policies in line with the changing with the changing regulatory framework and the context in which it operates.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on OpEx investments to accelerate decarbonisation: acquisition of external ESG/climate data, tools to issue and track ESG financial instruments, expert support for a decarbonisation strategy and broader transition plan, staff training on climate risk and ESG, and external support to configure ESG governance and business processes.
- Objective: embed ESG principles in risk management and reporting, aligning with ESRS and European sustainability regulations; reaffirm the Group’s role in Paris-aligned EU benchmarks as a financier of the low‑carbon transition.
- Policy framework and governance: an organisational model integrates ESG into strategy, business model and corporate policies; all key policies approved by the Board after review by the Risk & Sustainability Committee and Management Committee (ESG session), with periodic updates.
- Group Guideline on Sustainability and ESG: commitments to measure and progressively reduce Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, increase renewable energy use, and support clients’ transition via:
  - Green credit with ESG-integrated credit standards and dedicated financing solutions;
  - Advisory and investment/insurance products with sustainability strategies;
  - Issuance of green bonds.
- Code of Ethics: treats environment as a primary asset; drives reduction of direct/indirect impacts, climate risk management, and alignment with SDGs and the Paris Agreement; informs conduct standards and stakeholder alignment.
- Environmental management policies: EMS oversight aligned with ISO 14001; Environmental Policy and Safety & Environment Policy set principles, compliance duties and apply to all Group companies (and relevant third parties); availability on website/intranet.
- Alignment with major frameworks: SDGs, Paris Agreement, EU Action Plan, European Green Deal, PNIEC, EU Taxonomy, IDD, MiFID II ESG, SFDR, UN Global Compact, UNEP FI/PRB.
- Actions in own operations: longstanding Scope 1–2 reductions; 100% renewable electricity target since 2012 and zero market-based Scope 2; IPMVP-based Measurement & Verification Plan (baseline 2019) certified by Tor Vergata University recorded 6,018 MWh savings in 2024; consolidation of a network energy management platform.

nodes.title: Climate-change actions relating to own transactions
nodes.heading: Climate-change actions relating to own transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has specific actions aimed at managing the climate change mitigation related to its business.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and policy framework:
  - Group Directive on Environmental Management System Oversight: defines the EMS oversight model to ensure regulatory compliance; applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies; approved by the Board of Directors with annual management review; aligned with UNI EN ISO 14001; available on the corporate intranet.
  - Environmental Policy: sets guiding principles for managing significant environmental impacts in line with the Code of Ethics; overseen by the Parent Company; approved by the Board after committee reviews; aligned with applicable regulations and external codes (UNEP FI Declaration, UN Global Compact); available on the corporate website.
  - Group Policy on Safety and Environment: establishes group-wide rules on safety and environment; applies to the Parent Company, all Group companies, and relevant third parties (suppliers, consultants); Board-approved after committee reviews; implemented per Italian Legislative Decrees 152/2006 and 121/2011 and UNI EN ISO 14001:2015; available on the intranet.

- Climate actions in own operations:
  - Longstanding program to cut Scope 1 and 2 impacts by reducing fossil fuel use, improving efficiency, and increasing renewables; target since 2012 to use 100% renewable electricity and achieve zero market-based Scope 2 emissions.
  - Measurement & Verification Plan (since 2019) aligned with IPMVP to verify energy, water efficiency and renewables results; baseline 2019 with ordinary/extraordinary adjustments; certified by Tor Vergata University; 6,018 MWh consumption reduction in 2024 vs. 2019 from projects.
  - Energy Management Platform active across more than 1,200 branches nationwide; real-time monitoring of energy and environmental parameters; AI/ML-driven optimization of HVAC set-points and predictive maintenance.
  - Continued climate system adjustments guided by the “National plan to reduce natural gas consumption” (Decree no. 383/2022), though no longer in force.
  - Participation in public energy-saving initiatives in 2024 (“M’illumino di meno” on 16 Feb; International Energy Saving Day on 18 Feb), switching off illuminated signage and minimizing night lighting at HQ (Piazza Salimbeni 3, Siena).

- Climate actions in the downstream value chain:
  - Transition Plan-driven approach with sector-specific strategies, exclusionary guidelines, credit processes integrating ESG assessments, and ESG products/advisory to support counterparties’ transition and national climate measures.
  - Sector clustering and targets:
    - Priority high-emission sectors: Oil & Gas; Electricity Production & Distribution; Iron & Steel; Cement; Aluminum.
    - Non-priority high-emission/high-impact sectors: Real Estate; Transportation; Automotive; Agriculture; Chemicals (high climate impact).
    - Other sectors: lower transition risk/intensity.
    - For the first two clusters: 2030 intermediate decarbonization targets consistent with NZBA, portfolio approach, and defined credit/trade policy directions delivered via ESG offerings. For other sectors: counterparty-level actions based on ESG profiles.
  - Exclusion and restriction criteria (per Sustainability and ESG Guideline):
    - Coal extraction: no new exposures; no funding for exploration/new mines or expansion of existing mines; no renewal at maturity (full phase-out by 2025). Exceptions only for site redevelopment/reclamation with documented due diligence.
    - Power generation: recognized as highly emission-intensive but a key decarbonization opportunity via renewables; sector subject to evolving regulation and technology.

nodes.title: Climate change actions in relation to the downstream value chain
nodes.heading: Climate change actions in relation to the downstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has identified specific actions aimed at managing negative impacts on climate change mitigation consistent with the objectives of its Transition Plan, for details of which see the section “Transition Plan for Climate Change Miti- gation”.
nodes.summary:
- The bank’s operational energy management: deployment of a nationwide, AI- and machine-learning–enabled platform across 1,200+ branches to monitor real-time energy use and environmental parameters, optimize HVAC set-points, and enable predictive maintenance; ongoing 2024 actions to curb consumption via climate-condition monitoring and system adjustments aligned with Italy’s (now-lapsed) National plan to reduce natural gas consumption.
- Awareness and savings initiatives: participation in “M’illumino di meno” (16 Feb 2024) and International Energy Saving Day (18 Feb 2024), with signage switched off and night lighting minimized at the Siena headquarters.
- Downstream value chain climate strategy: actions aligned with the Group’s Transition Plan, including sector- and risk-based credit strategies, ESG due diligence standards to steer lending, and provision of ESG-linked products and advisory to support clients’ transition and adoption of national climate measures.
- Sectoral approach and targets: segmentation of client sectors into three clusters by emission intensity, climate risk, technology availability, and portfolio impact; 2030 intermediate decarbonization targets for high-emission sectors consistent with NZBA guidance, with specific credit/commercial directions; cross-cutting, counterparty-level ESG actions for lower-risk sectors.
- Exclusion and restriction policies: stringent criteria to limit exposure to activities misaligned with EU/Italian climate plans—particularly coal mining, coal-intensive power, and new unconventional oil and gas projects—governed by the Group’s Sustainability and ESG Guideline.
- Coal phase-out: no new exposure to coal mining; exclusion of funding for exploration, new or expanded mines; non-renewal of existing exposures to achieve full exit by 2025; possible financing only for mine site reclamation/redevelopment subject to rigorous environmental due diligence.
- Power generation stance: recognition of renewables as a Net-Zero opportunity while acknowledging the sector’s current high emissions, regulatory pressure, and fast-evolving technologies.

Climate change actions in relation to the downstream value chain
The Group has identified specific actions aimed at managing negative impacts on climate change mitigation consistent 
with the objectives of its Transition Plan, for details of which see the section “Transition Plan for Climate Change Miti-
gation”. These actions take the form of defining strategic actions differentiated by sector of economic activity, emission 
intensity and exposure to climate risks, exclusionary and/or more restrictive guidelines for certain sectors and economic 
activities, credit strategies and processes and standards aimed at assessing the client’s ESG profile and directing the pro-
vision of credit, and offering credit products and advisory services aimed at encouraging the transition of counterparties 
and the underwriting of nationally planned climate and environmentally friendly measures.

nodes.title: Strategic Actions differentiated by sector
nodes.heading: Strategic Actions differentiated by sector
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has divided its business sectors, based on indicators assessing aspects of emission intensity, exposure to climate risk, and available technologies on climate change and impact on the Group’s emission profile, into three clusters:
nodes.summary:
- The Group implemented a real-time energy and environmental monitoring platform across 1,200+ branches, using AI and machine learning to correlate environmental parameters with HVAC set-points and enable predictive maintenance.
- In 2024 it continued targeted energy-saving actions by closely tracking climate conditions and adjusting systems accordingly, aligning with Italy’s (now lapsed) National plan to reduce natural gas consumption (Decree no. 383/2022).
- It joined national and international energy-saving initiatives (“M’illumino di meno” and International Energy Saving Day), reducing illuminated signage and night lighting at its Siena headquarters.
- For downstream value chain climate action, the Group set sector-specific strategies aligned with its Transition Plan, integrating ESG into credit assessment and offerings to steer clients toward decarbonization and adoption of climate-friendly measures.
- Business sectors are clustered into:
  - Priority high-emission sectors (Oil & Gas; Power; Iron & Steel; Cement; Aluminum) with 2030 interim decarbonization targets consistent with NZBA and specific credit/trade policy directions delivered via ESG products.
  - Non-priority high-emission and high climate-impact sectors (Real Estate, Transportation, Automotive, Agriculture, Chemicals) with targeted strategic directions.
  - Other sectors addressed through a counterparty-by-counterparty approach based on ESG profiles.
- Restrictive guidelines and exclusions are applied to minimize exposure to activities misaligned with national/EU climate plans:
  - Coal extraction: no new exposures; no funding for exploration, new mines, or expansion; non-renewal of existing exposures to achieve a full phase-out by 2025. Possible exceptions for site redevelopment/reclamation with documented environmental due diligence.
  - Coal-intensive power generation/distribution and new unconventional oil & gas projects are subject to exclusionary criteria.
- The Sustainability and ESG Guideline (publicly available) governs these criteria.
- The power generation sector is highlighted as both highly emission-intensive and a key opportunity for net-zero via the growth of renewables, amid evolving regulation and technologies.

nodes.title: Guidelines and/or exclusion criteria
nodes.heading: Guidelines and/or exclusion criteria
nodes.start_phrase: The Group, in addition to the strategic actions differentiated by sectors, has also introduced restrictive exclusion criteria for certain sectors, due to their high impact on the environment and inconsistency with national and European climate action plans, in order to minimize exposure to projects and counterparts that could undermine climate and environmental objectives.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on energy efficiency in operations: deployment of a real-time platform across 1,200+ branches using AI/ML to monitor environmental parameters, optimize HVAC set-points, and enable predictive maintenance; continued 2024 actions to cut consumption through climate monitoring and system adjustments, aligned with Italy’s now-expired National plan to reduce natural gas consumption (Decree 383/2022).
- Participation in national/international energy-saving campaigns in February 2024 (“M’illumino di meno” and International Energy Saving Day), including switching off most illuminated signage and minimizing night lighting at the Siena headquarters.
- Downstream value chain climate strategy aligned with the Group’s Transition Plan: sector-based strategic actions, exclusionary/more restrictive guidelines, credit strategies/standards integrating ESG assessments, and ESG products/advisory to support counterparties’ transition and national climate measures.
- Sector segmentation for decarbonization:
  - Priority high-emission sectors: Oil & Gas; Electricity Production & Distribution; Iron & Steel; Cement; Aluminum.
  - Non-priority high-emission and high climate impact sectors: Real Estate; Transportation; Automotive; Agriculture; Chemicals.
  - Other sectors with lower transition risk/emissions.
  - For the first two clusters: 2030 intermediate decarbonization targets (NZBA-aligned), portfolio approach, and specific credit/trade policy directions; for other sectors: cross-cutting, counterparty-level actions based on ESG profiles.
- Exclusion and restriction guidelines (per Sustainability and ESG Guideline):
  - Coal extraction: no new exposures; no funding for new/expanded mines; non-renewal of existing exposures to phase-out by 2025; possible funding for site remediation with documented environmental benefits.
  - Power generation: promote renewables via financial solutions; restrictions for counterparties planning to expand coal capacity, build new coal plants, generate >30% of electricity from coal without a Paris-aligned plan, or lacking plans to reach ≥40% renewables by 2030.
  - Oil & Gas: support transition with sustainability-linked loans, green bonds, and advisory; exclusions for financing unconventional exploration/production (fracking, tar sands, Arctic, Amazon Sacred Headwaters, ultra-deep waters) and for companies with >20% revenue from unconventional extraction/transport or those pursuing new oil exploration/infrastructure (aligned with COP-28); provisions to reduce exposure where emission-reduction pathways are structurally limited.
- Integration of ESG into credit processes:
  - Since 2022, adoption of an ESG Outlook to guide credit strategies (ordinary, ESG guidelines, specific guidelines), combining sectoral transition alignment and a counterparty ESG score from an ESG questionnaire.
  - Negative ESG Outlook triggers conservative business plan assumptions (sensitivity add-ons) and steers financing toward improving clients’ emission profiles; influences overall stress applied to plans.
  - ESG questionnaire integrated into systems, expanding data on client ESG profiles and assessing transition and physical climate risks.
- Cross-references to decarbonization levers and actions to reduce indirect emissions in the loan portfolio.

nodes.title: ESG strategies, processes and credit standards
nodes.heading: ESG strategies, processes and credit standards
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2022, the Group has introduced an additional assessment element called the “ESG outlook” for the purpose of defi- ning its credit strategies, which are divided into three levels: ordinary strategy, ESG guidelines, and specific strategic guide- lines.
nodes.summary:
- Decarbonization strategy: The Group promotes renewable energy and supports clients’ emissions reduction to stay on a Net-Zero trajectory, with targeted financial solutions and actions to curtail exposures where transition progress is structurally limited.
- Coal sector exclusions: Criteria exclude counterparties that plan to expand coal-fired capacity, build new coal plants, produce over 30% of power from coal without a Paris-aligned transition plan, or lack plans to reach at least 40% renewable generation by 2030.
- Oil & Gas approach: Provides Sustainability-linked loans, Green Bonds, and advisory to support low-carbon transitions; defines exclusions for financing unconventional oil and gas (fracking, tar sands, Arctic, Amazon Sacred Headwaters, ultra-deep waters), for companies deriving >20% of revenues from unconventional extraction/transport, and for new oil exploration and new oil infrastructure (aligned with COP28).
- ESG integration in credit: Since 2022, uses an ESG Outlook (sectoral transition alignment and client ESG score) to shape credit strategies and business plan stress. Negative ESG Outlook triggers conservative assumptions and directs financing to improve clients’ emissions profiles. An ESG questionnaire, integrated into systems, assesses counterparty ESG, transition risk, and physical risk.
- Green products: Offers Sustainability-Linked Loans, Green Loans, and EU Taxonomy-aligned loans. In 2024, disbursed about EUR 904.5 million in green finance (EUR 424.5 million SLL; ~EUR 480 million green loans).
- SME support – Nuova Sabatini: Provides loans/leases for low-impact capital investments via the Capital Goods ceiling, eligible for MIMIT interest-equivalent grants (2.75% ordinary; 3.575% for Industry 4.0 and green investments), loan sizes EUR 20,000–4,000,000, up to 5 years, with SME Guarantee Fund coverage up to 80%. In 2024, disbursements totaled ~EUR 47.5 million (EUR 30 million for 4.0, EUR 3.2 million for green).
- SACE Green New Deal: Participates in SACE public guarantees for green projects; cumulative disbursements of EUR 232.8 million since 2022, including EUR 40.4 million in 2024.

nodes.title: Green product and service offerings
nodes.heading: Green product and service offerings
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has actively contributed to activately supporting its customers in the transition towards more sustainable economic models by developing and promoting financial products that comply with sustainability and green criteria.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group’s green products and services, aligned with the Group’s Sustainability and ESG Directive, LMA guidance, and the EU Taxonomy.

  - Sustainability Linked Loans (SLL): general-purpose loans tied to ESG KPIs, including climate mitigation targets, rewarding improved performance.
  - Green Loans: financing for projects with positive environmental and/or social impacts (e.g., renewable energy, sustainable mobility, sustainable agriculture).
  - Taxonomy-Aligned Loans: Green Loans meeting EU Environmental Taxonomy criteria.
- 2024 green finance disbursements: approximately EUR 904.5 million total, including EUR 424.5 million in SLLs and about EUR 480 million in Green Loans.
- SME support via “Nuova Sabatini” (Capital Goods Measure) with a new “Green” contribution for low-impact investments:
  - Loans/leases from EUR 20,000 to EUR 4,000,000, up to 5-year term, eligible for up to 80% guarantee by the SME Guarantee Fund.
  - Operating grant from MIMIT based on notional interest over 5 years at annual rates: 2.75% (ordinary), 3.575% (Industry 4.0), 3.575% (green).
  - 2024 disbursements: about EUR 47.5 million total, including EUR 30 million for Industry 4.0 and EUR 3.2 million for green investments.
- Partnership with SACE under the Green New Deal to provide public guarantees for green projects:
  - Total disbursed since 2022: EUR 232.8 million, including EUR 40.4 million in 2024.

nodes.title: SACE Green New Deal
nodes.heading: SACE Green New Deal
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2022, the Group has entered into the Green New Deal agreement with SACE, the Italian Export Credit Agency that has been supporting Italian companies in export and internationalisation projects for over forty years.
nodes.summary:
- Overview: The Group expands green products and services to support customers’ transition to sustainable models, guided by its Sustainability and ESG Directive and aligned with LMA definitions and the EU Taxonomy.

- Financing products:
  - Three categories: Sustainability-Linked Loans (SLL) tied to ESG KPIs; Green Loans for projects with positive environmental/social impact; Taxonomy-Aligned Loans meeting EU environmental criteria.
  - 2024 disbursements: approx. EUR 904.5 mln (EUR 424.5 mln SLL; ~EUR 480 mln Green Loans).

- SME support (Nuova Sabatini – Capital Goods ceiling):
  - Loans/leases EUR 20,000–4,000,000, up to 5 years, potentially guaranteed up to 80% by the SME Guarantee Fund and backed by CDP resources.
  - Grants from MIMIT equal to interest on a 5-year loan at 2.75% (ordinary), 3.575% (4.0 and green investments).
  - 2024 disbursed: ~EUR 47.5 mln (EUR 30 mln for 4.0; EUR 3.2 mln for green).

nodes.title: Climate change targets on own operations
nodes.heading: Climate change targets on own operations
nodes.start_phrase: Since 2012, the Group has embarked on a journey to reduce its own emissions in order to limit its negative impact on climate change and has identified, with an evidence-based approach, progressive targets to reduce direct and indirect emissions from its operations, initially setting a target to reduce Scope 1 emissions by 60 percent by 2026 compared to 2017 and to adopt 100%39 electricity from renewable sources, and subsequently to pursue Net Zero Operation (Scope 1 and Scope 2 market based) on its own operations by 2030.
nodes.summary:
- Green bonds: The Group supports large corporates in structuring and placing green bonds aligned with ICMA guidelines and the EU Taxonomy to finance/refinance green or social projects or KPI-linked sustainable activities; EUR 500 million placed in 2024.

- UCITS and asset management: Issued over 130 new UCITS classified under SFDR Articles 8 and 9; by year-end, 74% of catalogue funds aligned with Articles 8 and 9. ESG funds represented 40% of total placed funds (approx. EUR 10 billion), meeting the 2024–2028 target. Developed rules to assess ESG characteristics of UCITS in asset management; on 2 January 2024, revised four asset management lines with ESG strategies and new benchmarks; in June 2024 launched six ETF lines and two ESG bond lines (four for Retail, four for Premium).

- Insurance products: Launched InvestiSemplice, a multi-branch investment policy linked to segregated management and funds focused on responsible/sustainable companies. Introduced CAT Guarantee coverage for companies to meet compulsory natural catastrophe insurance requirements under the 2024 Budget Law, supporting climate adaptation.

- Own-operations climate objectives and performance: Since 2012, progressing on emissions reduction with a 2017 baseline. Initial targets: reduce Scope 1 by 60% by 2026 and use 100% renewable electricity; strengthened to Net Zero for Scope 1 and Scope 2 (market-based) by 2030.
  - Scope 1: ~75% reduction vs 2017, exceeding the 2026 target; fossil fuel consumption down 48%; used carbon credits to offset ~69% of 2024 natural gas emissions (reductions include offsets).
  - Scope 2 (market-based): Achieved 100% renewable electricity in 2024 for the defined consolidation scope, zeroing market-based emissions; total energy use down 35% vs 2017; Scope 2 location-based emissions down 36%.
  - Combined Scope 1 and 2: 15% reduction as of 31 December 2024, with year-on-year improvement vs 2023.
  - Governance and systems: ISO 14001-certified environmental management system since 2003; Energy Manager role since 2009.

- Downstream value chain climate targets (financed emissions): Commitment to align with a 1.5°C pathway as an NZBA member. Interim 2030 targets set for priority high-emitting sectors—Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Iron & Steel, Coal (exposure-based target), Cement, and Aluminum. Cement and Aluminum targets defined in 2024 and reported February 2025; monitoring to begin end-2025 per NZBA guidance. Two-phase rollout: August 2023 targets for Oil & Gas, Power, Iron & Steel, and coal phase-out; February 2025 targets for Cement and Aluminum plus internal management targets for other emission-intensive sectors. Public reporting for NZBA targets; internal monitoring for management targets.

- Methodology for target setting: Analyzed exposures to non-financial companies (loans, bonds, equity) and defined baselines using external emissions data; set sector boundaries via NACE codes including upstream/downstream; included Scope 3 where relevant; identified priority vs non-priority emission-intensive sectors. Alignment paths based on climate scenarios: NGFS Net Zero 2050 (baseline 2022) for Oil & Gas, Power, Iron & Steel; IEA NZE2050 (baseline 2023) for Cement and Aluminum.

nodes.title: Climate change targets in relation to the downstream value chain
nodes.heading: Climate change targets in relation to the downstream value chain
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has embarked on a path to contribute to the goals of the Paris Agreement by aligning its financial activities with the trajectory of limiting global warming to 1.5°C.
nodes.summary:
- The Group strengthened its climate commitments, targeting net zero Scope 1 and 2 (market-based) emissions by 2030; as of 31 Dec 2024 it achieved a 15% reduction versus 2023.
- Environmental governance includes an ISO 14001-certified management system (since 2003) and a dedicated Energy Manager (since 2009), with objectives informed by stakeholder input.
- Downstream (financed emissions) strategy aligned with the Paris Agreement and NZBA:
  - Interim 2030 targets set for priority high-emitting sectors: Oil & Gas, Power Generation, Iron & Steel, Coal (phase-out via financial exposure), Cement, and Aluminum.
  - Two-phase rollout: Aug 2023 (O&G, Power, Iron & Steel; coal phase-out) and Feb 2025 (Cement, Aluminum; plus internal management targets for other emission-intensive sectors).
  - Methodology: portfolio analysis using external emissions data, PCAF for financed emissions (business loans and unlisted equity; data quality score 2), sector boundaries via NACE, selective inclusion of Scope 3, and climate scenarios (NGFS NZE2050 for O&G, Power, Iron & Steel; IEA NZE2050 for Cement, Aluminum).
  - 2030 reduction targets vs baselines: O&G -40%; Power -77%; Iron & Steel -29%; Cement -23.6%; Aluminum -9.1%; Coal: zero financial exposure.
  - 2024 performance vs 2022/2023 baselines: O&G financed emissions +264% (off-track); Power -73% and Iron & Steel -69% (on-track), supported by shifts toward lower-intensity and renewable-heavy counterparties.
  - Mitigation actions for O&G include integrating emissions and transition risk into client assessment, exclusion of financing for unconventional O&G and new deposits, active engagement with high emitters, KPI-linked transition financing, and close exposure monitoring; targets to be reviewed at least every five years.
- Supporting finance objectives to enable client transition by 2028:
  - 7.6% green loans share within NZBA sectors (stock).
  - 30% of annual disbursements with ESG purposes (2024: 18%, EUR 1,858m—EUR 904m green; EUR 954m social).
  - 25% of bond issuance as Green/Social (2024: EUR 750m social, 25% of total).
- Upstream value chain: no specific climate targets yet; effectiveness ensured via supplier governance and audits. In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria.

nodes.start_phrase: For the purpose of calculating direct Scope 1 and indirect Scope 2 emissions for 2024, conversion factors from the “ABI Lab Guidelines” (December 2024 version) were used.

- Defines the Group’s 2024 greenhouse gas accounting approach for Scopes 1, 2, and 3, including sources, factors, and estimation methods, covering Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena and subsidiaries (e.g., MPS Banque).
- Scope 1 and 2: applies ABI Lab Guidelines (Dec 2024) for CO2, CH4, N2O; CO2e factors from ISPRA NIR 2024; CH4/N2O GWPs from IPCC 2021 (AR6). Company/personal cars: 70% of fuel use treated as business. MPS Banque uses ADEME Guide.
- Scope 2 accounting: uses both location-based (grid average factors; all purchased electricity, renewable and non‑renewable) and market-based (contract-specific factors; electricity with Guarantee of Origin = zero emission factor).
- Scope 3 categories included and methods:
  - Category 1 Purchased goods/services and Category 2 Capital goods: spend-based approach with EEIO coefficients by NACE code.
  - Category 3 Fuel- and energy-related (not in Scopes 1–2): Group consumption data times DEFRA 2024 factors; apartment-block utilities estimated from reimbursements using national average commodity prices.
  - Category 4 Upstream transport/distribution: only MPS Tenimenti; otherwise transport costs embedded in Category 1 (EEIO).
  - Category 5 Waste and Category 6 Business travel: DEFRA 2024 factors (by waste treatment and travel mode/vehicle type).
  - Category 9 Downstream transport: MPS Tenimenti and MPS Banque only (EEIO).
  - Category 13 Downstream leased assets: estimates for Group-owned properties leased to third parties via clustered specific-consumption coefficients by property use (residential, garage/warehouse, industrial—leather processing, tertiary comparable to banking). Sources include Enel, ARERA, and AbiLab 2022 benchmarks; energy conversion per ABI Lab 2024 (location-based for electricity).
  - Category 15 Financed emissions: PCAF Standard (Dec 2022), Score 2 option 1b; attribution = (exposure/borrower total assets) × borrower emissions; calculated for loans to non-financial corporates only, with plans to expand coverage and improve data quality.
- Confirms no biogenic CO2 within Scope 3 as of 31 Dec 2024.
- Scope 3 categories excluded and reasons: 7 Employee commuting (not reproducible for 2024; prior coverage only >100-employee sites); 8 Upstream leased assets (already in Scope 1); 10 Processing of sold products, 11 Use of sold products, 12 End-of-life of sold products, and 14 Franchises (all not material).
- Details estimation procedures for Scopes 1 and 2 where data are incomplete:
  - Apartment-block utilities: derived from reimbursement amounts using national average energy prices.
  - Residual utilities (LPG, district heating): based on bills; missing months extrapolated using Parent Company/Banca WIDIBA natural gas monthly ratios (e.g., December assumed 27% of Jan–Nov consumption).
  - District heating renewable status assigned by site; renewable-fed systems listed for Turin (waste-to-energy), Ferrara (geothermal, two sites), Monterotondo Marittimo (geothermal steam), Pomarance (geothermal steam).
  - For Monterotondo Marittimo and Pomarance (lump-sum billing), consumption estimated from indoor area using an average intensity of 51.0324913 MWh/m2.

nodes.title: Calculation methodology - estimated data focus
nodes.heading: Calculation methodology - estimated data focus
nodes.start_phrase: In relation to the scope of reported consumption, details are given of the calculations and estimates made by the Group for the following consumption:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Methodologies and estimations used in the Sustainability Reporting for energy consumption (Scope 1 and 2), district heating/LPG data completion, funded emissions (Scope 3 category 15), and GHG intensity versus net revenues.
- Scope 1 and 2 consumption estimation:
  - Apartment block utilities: estimated from reimbursement amounts using national average commodity prices.
  - Residual utilities (LPG and district heating): primarily from bills; missing months estimated using a seasonal ratio derived from the natural gas consumption profile of the Parent Company and Banca WIDIBA (e.g., applying December’s 27% share to Jan–Nov totals when December data are absent).
  - Real estate owned and leased to third parties: estimated based on floor area, climate zone, and tenant activity.
- District heating treatment:
  - Classification of district heating as renewable or non-renewable is determined by each building’s supply source.
  - Listed renewable systems include: Turin (waste-to-energy), Ferrara (geothermal hot water, two sites), Monterotondo Marittimo (geothermal steam), and Pomarance (geothermal steam).
  - For Monterotondo Marittimo and Pomarance, billed on a lump-sum basis with no metered data; consumption estimated from indoor surface area using an average Bank factor of 51.0324913 MWh/m2.
- Scope 3 category 15 (funded emissions) estimation:
  - Emissions data sourced from an external provider; either company-reported (accurate) or estimated.
  - Scope 1 estimates use Eurostat emissions intensity per value added by NACE and country, refined with granular ISPRA/EU ETS data, recalibrated to sector value added and revenues, and benchmarked against accurate peer samples.
  - Scope 2 estimates use sectoral electricity consumption (Terna) and ENEL conversion factors to CO2e.
  - Scope 3 estimates adapt Eurostat’s consumption-based accounting tool to cover full value chains, then deduct estimated Scope 1–2 to derive Scope 3.
- GHG intensity versus net revenues (2024):
  - Total GHG emissions (position-based) per net revenues: 2,965 tCO2e.
  - Total GHG emissions (market-based) per net revenues: 2,961 tCO2e.
  - Revenue reconciliation used for intensity: net revenues used 6,923,029 (€ thousands); balance sheet net revenues 6,872,986 with 50,042 from non-current assets held for sale.

nodes.title: Indirect Scope 3 category 15 emissions - estimation methodology
nodes.heading: Indirect Scope 3 category 15 emissions - estimation methodology
nodes.start_phrase: For the calculation of counterparties’ funded emissions (Scope 1, Scope 2, Scope 3), the absolute emissions data of coun - terparties are provided by an external provider and are calculated on the basis of the provider’s own proprietary estimation methodology.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Methodology and outcomes for estimating financed emissions (Scope 1, 2, 3) for counterparties, GHG intensity vs net revenues, and use of carbon credits for mitigation.
- Data source: Counterparty absolute emissions are supplied by an external provider, either directly reported by companies (corporate sustainability reports) or estimated via the provider’s proprietary methods.
- Scope 1 estimation: Based on Eurostat emissions intensity (tCO2/€ value added) by NACE code and EU country; refined with more granular NACE/ATECO data (ISPRA/ETS), recalibrated to revenues using sector value-added/revenue ratios, and benchmarked against averages from firms with accurate data.
- Scope 2 estimation: Uses electricity consumption at 2-digit NACE level (Terna) and a conversion factor to CO2e (ENEL).
- Scope 3 estimation: Adapted from Eurostat’s consumption-based accounting tool to capture full product-chain emissions (adjusted for intermediate goods); Scope 3 derived by subtracting Scope 1–2 from total emissions.
- GHG intensity vs net revenues (2024):
  - Total GHG emissions per net revenues (position-based): 2,965 tCO2e
  - Total GHG emissions per net revenues (market-based): 2,961 tCO2e
  - Reconciliation: Net revenue used 6,923,029; non-current assets held for sale 50,042; total net revenue on balance sheet 6,872,986 (euro thousands).
- Carbon credits and mitigation (2024):
  - Offsetting >69% of natural gas use (2 million Sm3) via VER credits from the Vishnuprayag Hydro-electric Project (India), verified under Verra’s VCS, displacing fossil-based grid electricity.
  - Credits retired: 4,064 tCO2e, 100% from reduction projects; no absorption projects; no EU share indicated; no future retirements reported for 2024.
- Strategy: The 2022–2024 plan includes purchasing carbon credits to meet Scope 1 reduction targets, addressing hard-to-abate emissions.

nodes.title: GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed with carbon credits
nodes.heading: GHG removals and GHG mitigation projects financed with carbon credits
nodes.start_phrase: In 2024, the Group offset emissions for the use of 2 mln Sm3 of natural gas, equal to more than 69% of total natural gas consumption, by purchasing VER (Verified Emission Reduction) Credits for joining the Vishnuprayag Hydro-electric Project (VHEP) by Jaiprakash Power Ventures Ltd.
nodes.summary:
- The Group offset emissions associated with 2 million Sm3 of natural gas use in 2024—over 69% of its total natural gas consumption—by purchasing Verified Emission Reduction (VER) credits linked to the Vishnuprayag Hydro-electric Project (VHEP) in India.
- The VHEP, verified under the Verra VCS standard, supplies renewable electricity to India’s grid, displacing fossil-based generation (noting that over 70% of the northern grid’s electricity comes from fossil fuels), thereby reducing anthropogenic GHG emissions.
- Carbon credits written off in 2024 totaled 4,064 tCO2e, entirely from reduction projects (0% from absorption projects), with no credits from EU projects and no matching adjustments; no credits are expected to be written off in the future for 2024.
- The Group’s Scope 1 emission-reduction target (as per the 2022–2024 business plan) includes the use of carbon credits to address hard-to-abate emissions.
- Under ESRS E5 (Resource use and circular economy), the report outlines:
  - A double materiality assessment process considering internal and public documents (e.g., Environmental Policy, Decarbonisation Strategies) and initiatives such as waste management, reduced paper use, separate waste collection, and use of sustainable materials.
  - Material opportunities identified primarily in the downstream value chain, centered on expanding products and services that support resource reuse and circular economy solutions (e.g., financing recycling initiatives, contributing to circular systems, especially for output resources).
  - A mapping of impacts, risks, and opportunities across the value chain, with impacts tied to the Group’s operations and opportunities concentrated downstream.
  - A note that detailed policies, actions, and targets for this material topic follow in subsequent sections.
