nodes.start_phrase: The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard takes into account the specific aspects related to the Group’s operational and commercial activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS E5 (Resource use and circular economy) within Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s sustainability reporting.
- Approach: Double materiality analysis covering impacts, risks, and opportunities across operations and the value chain, based on internal/public documents (Environmental Policy, Decarbonisation Strategies) and initiatives (waste management, paper reduction, separate collection).
- Material outcome: A key opportunity in the downstream value chain to expand offerings that support resource reuse and recycling (circular economy), notably via financing for recycling initiatives and systems tied to output resources.
- Scope of impacts/risks/opportunities: 
  - Impacts in own operations (positive/negative).
  - Risks in the upstream value chain.
  - Opportunities in the downstream value chain related to outflows of resources tied to products and services.
- Policies and governance:
  - Group Sustainability and ESG Policy guiding integration of ESG into strategy, business model, and processes, with commitments on responsible resource use, circular economy, pollution prevention, and biodiversity restoration.
  - Credit Policy (Board-approved, Feb 2025) including investment support for companies transitioning to circular economy and efficient resource management.
  - Policy oversight and validation by the Board of Directors, relevant Board Committees, Executive Committee; implementation led by CFO and Sustainability & ESG Staff, with organizational functions involved.
- Strategic actions: Support corporate clients’ transition via dedicated credit solutions and investment strategies aimed at long-term sustainable projects/products in material recovery and reuse.
- Standards and regulatory alignment: References to EU Sustainable Finance context and product governance rules (IDD, Directive (EU) 2016/97, EU Delegated Directive 2021/1269—MiFID II ESG).
- Transparency: Sustainability and ESG Policy available on the Group’s corporate website.
- Monitoring: Processes in place to track the effectiveness of policies and actions related to resource use and the circular economy.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: In line with its strategy, market trends and new European regulations in the area of sustainable finance, the Group is commit- ted to working to support sustainable development through the incremental integration of sustainability principles into strategies and operational processes.
nodes.summary:
- Focus and scope: Addresses outflows of resources tied to products and services in the downstream value chain, within the Group’s broader sustainability strategy and EU sustainable finance context.

- Policy framework and governance:
  - Group Sustainability and ESG Policy defines how ESG principles are integrated into strategy, business model, product development and distribution, with emphasis on responsible resource use, circular economy, pollution prevention, biodiversity, human rights, labor standards, health and safety, and good governance.
  - Policy applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies; approved by the Board of Directors with oversight from Board Committees and the Executive Committee; implemented by designated Group functions.
  - Alignment with relevant regulations and standards (IDD, Directive (EU) 2016/97, EU Delegated Directive 2021/1269 – MiFID 2 ESG); publicly available on the Group website.
  - A Credit Policy (approved February 2025) guides investments in companies advancing circular economy and efficient resource management.

- Strategic rationale: Recognizes the circular economy’s role in achieving EU 2050 climate neutrality and halting biodiversity loss; highlights how circular models can reduce emissions across sectors such as agribusiness, consumer goods, chemicals, transport, fashion/textiles, energy/utilities, and construction.

- Actions and instruments:
  - Positions sustainable finance as a lever to support circular economy and climate mitigation.
  - Offers dedicated credit solutions to firms engaged in material recovery, recycling, waste management, and reuse of raw/secondary materials.
  - Embeds ESG (including circular-economy factors) throughout the credit lifecycle—from origination to review—supported by an ESG Questionnaire used with corporate clients to collect data and steer lending toward circular and decarbonization goals.
  - Participates in national ecological transition initiatives:
    - NRRP (Green Revolution and Ecological Transition) to fund circular-economy projects.
    - SACE Green New Deal guarantees (about 80% coverage) to catalyze low-impact, transition-aligned investments.
    - Convention with the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, Invitalia and ABI enabling escrow mechanisms that facilitate subsidized purchases under Sustainable Investments 4.0.
    - Convention with the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, CDP and ABI to grant subsidies for R&D and innovation supporting the ecological and circular transition under the Italian Green New Deal.
  - These initiatives are part of routine operations and are monitored and renewed annually; further dedicated actions and ongoing regulatory/market monitoring are planned.

- Targets:
  - No specific quantitative targets yet for managing downstream resource outflows.
  - Potential future adoption of dedicated targets; current approach is embedded within the Group’s broader decarbonization targets aligned with NZBA commitments.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group recognises the importance of the transition to a circular economy and sustainable resource management to achieve the EU’s climate neutrality goal by 2050 and to halt biodiversity loss.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes the importance of the circular economy and sustainable resource management to achieve EU climate neutrality by 2050 and halt biodiversity loss, noting environmental pressures from resource extraction and production.
- Positions sustainable finance as a lever to promote circular economy models and support corporate clients’ net‑zero transitions, including expanding financial products to meet counterparties’ needs.
- Provides dedicated credit solutions for companies in material recovery, recycling, waste management, and reuse of raw and secondary materials.
- Integrates ESG factors, including circular economy criteria, throughout the credit lifecycle (from origination to review), using an ESG Questionnaire to gather qualitative and quantitative data and steer lending in line with decarbonization and circularity goals.
- Participates in national ecological transition initiatives:
  - National Recovery and Resilience Plan (focus on Green Revolution and Ecological Transition).
  - SACE Green New Deal guarantees to incentivize low‑impact projects and the ecological transition.
  - Conventions with the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, Invitalia and ABI to facilitate SME access to subsidized facilities (e.g., Sustainable Investments 4.0) via escrow mechanisms.
  - Convention with the Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, CDP and ABI to support R&D and innovation for the ecological and circular transition under the Italian Green New Deal.
- Treats these initiatives as part of normal operations, with annual monitoring and renewal based on regulatory and market developments.
- Future focus on defining additional actions to accelerate circular and ecological transitions for key customers, alongside close monitoring of evolving regulations and stakeholder expectations.
- Targets status: no specific quantitative goals yet for downstream resource outflows; potential future target setting is under evaluation, while the broader decarbonization framework aligned with NZBA membership currently guides the commitment.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: To date, the Group has not defined specific quantitative targets for the management of resource outflows related to products and services with reference to the downstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasizes the Group’s commitment to circular economy and sustainable resource management as key to EU climate neutrality by 2050 and biodiversity protection.
- Describes how circular approaches can curb emissions across priority sectors (agribusiness, consumer goods, chemicals, transport, fashion/textiles, energy/utilities, construction).
- Positions sustainable finance as a lever to support corporate clients’ transition to net zero and expand products aligned with circular economy needs.
- Details dedicated credit solutions for material recovery, recycling, waste management, and reuse of raw/secondary materials, with ESG-integrated credit processes from origination to review.
- Uses an ESG Questionnaire to collect qualitative and quantitative data on clients’ circular economy practices, guiding lending consistent with circularity and decarbonisation objectives.
- Lists participation in national ecological transition initiatives:
  - NRRP “Green Revolution and Ecological Transition” projects supporting circular economy.
  - SACE Green New Deal guarantees (renewed in 2024) to back loans covering about 80% of amounts for projects reducing environmental impact.
  - Convention with Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, Invitalia, and ABI enabling escrow mechanisms for subsidised goods and facilitating SME investments (Sustainable Investments 4.0) toward circularity.
  - Convention with Ministry for Business and Made in Italy, CDP, and ABI to grant subsidies for R&D and innovation for ecological/circular transition under the Italian Green New Deal.
- Notes these initiatives are part of ordinary operations, reviewed and renewed annually in line with regulatory and market changes.
- Future outlook: plan to define additional actions for key clients’ ecological/circular transition and closely monitor evolving regulations and stakeholder expectations.
- Objectives: no specific quantitative downstream resource-outflow targets yet; potential future targets under evaluation; current approach anchored in broader decarbonisation targets aligned with NZBA membership.
- Introduces EU Taxonomy disclosure framework:
  - Explains the six environmental objectives and the distinction between taxonomy-eligible and taxonomy-aligned activities.
  - Cites delegated acts: 2021/2139 and 2023/2485 (climate objectives), 2023/2486 (other four objectives), and 2022/1214 (fossil gas and nuclear inclusion with added obligations).
  - References reporting KPIs per 2021/2178, differentiated by financial institution type.
  - Notes interpretative FAQs issued by the European Commission (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024).
  - Confirms the Group has prepared the required disclosures under this framework.

nodes.title: Disclosure pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation)
nodes.heading: Disclosure pursuant to Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 (Taxonomy Regulation)
nodes.start_phrase: The European Taxonomy is a classification system created by the European Union to determine whether an economic activity can be considered environmentally sustainable.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope of EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures within the 2024 Sustainability Reporting of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena.
- Overview of the EU Taxonomy framework: definition of environmentally sustainable activities and the six environmental objectives.
- Explanation of delegated regulations establishing eligible and aligned activities and technical screening criteria:
  - 2021/2139 and 2023/2485 for climate change mitigation and adaptation.
  - 2023/2486 for water/marine resources, circular economy, pollution prevention, and biodiversity.
- Reporting KPIs and sector-specific obligations per 2021/2178, distinguishing financial institutions’ requirements; addition of fossil gas and nuclear activities and related disclosures via 2022/1214.
- Reference to European Commission FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024) guiding interpretation and implementation; confirmation that the Group prepared the required disclosures accordingly.
- Transition to ESRS S1 (Own workforce) within Section 3 – Social Information:
  - Coverage includes impacts, risks, and opportunities from a double materiality perspective; policies, actions, and targets; worker involvement and channels for concerns; and monitoring metrics.
  - Scope includes all Group employees (permanent/temporary, full-time/part-time).
  - Approach: review of internal/public documents, existing safeguards and initiatives (e.g., a dedicated D&I function), with protections often exceeding minimum regulatory standards to build trust and attract/retain talent.
  - Material findings:
    - Positive impacts in Own Operations from measures ensuring adequate working conditions, equal treatment/opportunity, and privacy.
    - Opportunities to enhance reputation and stakeholder trust through protections on working hours, salary adjustments, social dialogue, training and skills development, freedom of association and collective bargaining, presence of works councils, work-life balance, health and safety protections, equal treatment, and prevention of workplace violence and harassment.

nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Section 3 – Social Information (ESRS S1: Own workforce) of Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s Sustainability Reporting. Coverage includes all Group employees (permanent/temporary, full-time/part-time).
- Approach: Double materiality assessment used to identify workforce-related impacts, risks, and opportunities. Mapping drew on internal/public documentation and existing employee-protection initiatives (e.g., a dedicated Diversity & Inclusion function). The Group notes safeguards that often exceed regulatory minima, supporting employee trust and talent attraction/retention.
- Material topics identified: 
  - Working conditions and employee rights: secure employment, working hours, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association and collective bargaining, work-life balance.
  - Health and safety.
  - Equality, inclusion, and conduct: gender equality and equal pay, diversity, inclusion of people with disabilities, measures against workplace violence and harassment.
  - Training and skills development.
  - Privacy.
- Impacts and opportunities:
  - Positive impacts within own operations from measures ensuring adequate working conditions, equal treatment, and privacy.
  - Opportunities to enhance reputation and stakeholder trust via protections on working hours, pay adjustments, social dialogue, training/upskilling, freedom of association, works councils, work-life balance, health and safety, equal treatment, and prevention of violence/harassment.
- Value chain scope: The materiality focus is primarily on own operations, with consideration of upstream/downstream relevance noted in the framework.
- Policies, actions, and targets: The section introduces policies, actions, and targets across five areas: 
  1) Safeguarding Working Conditions (secure employment, working hours, adequate wages, social dialogue, freedom of association, work-life balance),
  2) Health and Safety,
  3) Training and Skills Development,
  4) Diversity and Inclusion (gender equality and equal pay; inclusion of people with disabilities; anti-violence and harassment; diversity),
  5) Privacy.
- Key policy instruments and governance:

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group is committed to ensuring adequate working conditions in compliance with current legislation, addressing and managing issues such as safe employment, working hours, fair pay, social dialogue, freedom of association, collective bargaining and work-life balance.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Protection of working conditions across secure employment, working hours, fair pay, social dialogue, freedom of association and collective bargaining, and work-life balance.
- Policies:
  - Group-wide commitment to compliance with law and collective agreements, risk assessment, and prevention/protection measures.
  - 100% of employees covered by national sector CCNL and company Level II bargaining.
  - Human Resources Management Directive sets principles, responsibilities, and activities to optimize skills, support business, and foster professional development in line with inclusion and the Gender Equality Policy; applies to Parent Company and Group (Widiba, MPS Fiduciaria); approved by the CEO; available on the intranet.
  - Remuneration Policy aims at sustainable long-term value, motivation, retention, and attraction, aligned with risk governance; applies to Parent Company and all Group companies; designed with Compliance, Risk Management, and Internal Audit; compliant with Consob and Bank of Italy rules; published on the corporate website.
- Actions and safeguards:
  - Collective bargaining ensures stable employment, wage adequacy, social dialogue, and freedom of association; company bargaining enhances welfare, economic integration, training, and professional development.
  - Recent agreements include activation of company bonus (also usable as welfare), higher company contributions to supplementary pension funds, and increased meal voucher value.
- Psychosocial risk management:
  - Longstanding psychological counseling service (since 2016) extended Group-wide; from 3 June 2024, enhanced anonymous “listening and counseling” service covering work and personal/family issues.
  - Work-related stress risk assessment updated via focus groups with Workers’ Safety Representatives; facilitated by Group Health Service and Prevention/Protection leadership; representative sampling by role, gender, age, geography.
  - Positive feedback on mitigation measures with noted improvement areas; further assessments planned to monitor perceptions of work content and context.
- Work-life balance, families, and leisure (aligned with the 2024–2028 Business Plan):
  - Expanded flexibility tools through ongoing managerial and union dialogue.
  - Family-oriented welfare: medical expense coverage extended to family members; accident policy; medical leave.
  - MPSolidale solidarity fund (donated hours/days and portions of management remuneration) prioritizing childcare and serious personal/family needs.
  - Parenthood support: “Parents’ Profession Project,” initiatives for children’s education (including tailored study paths), sports and psycho-physical wellbeing programs via online platforms.
  - Learning benefits: foreign language study for employees and family members; university enrollment agreements; study leave.
  - Additional benefits: digital corporate library for employees and families; private offers platform; recreational/sports/cultural activities via staff social organizations (CRAL).
  - Plan to recruit family members of employees who died in service or while using the solidarity fund.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In response to the aforementioned policies in place, the Group has put in place and planned multiple actions to protect the working conditions of its workforce.
nodes.summary:
- Group-wide protections through collective bargaining: 100% of employees covered by CBAs, with company-level bargaining enhancing welfare, economic integration, training, professional development, bonuses (including welfare options), higher company pension contributions, and increased meal vouchers.
- Management of psycho-social risks: longstanding psychological counseling expanded Group-wide; from 3 June 2024 a new anonymous listening and counseling service launched for work and personal issues. Work-related stress mitigation assessed via focus groups with Workers’ Safety Representatives; positive feedback on measures with identified improvement areas; further assessments planned.
- Work-life balance and family support (2024–2028 horizon): expanded flexibility and targeted welfare for employees and families, including medical expense coverage to family members, accident policy and medical leave; MPSolidale solidarity fund prioritizing childcare; parenthood support (Parents’ Profession Project), customized study paths for children, sports and wellbeing programs via online platforms; language learning and university agreements; study leave; digital corporate library; discounts platform; CRAL recreational/cultural activities; plan to recruit family members of deceased employees; continued support to historic employee Welfare Fund and Mutual Assistance Association.
- Supplementary pensions and financial benefits: employer contribution of 2.5% to Corporate Pension Funds (membership open to dependents), rising to 3% from January 2025 per 2024 union agreement; insurance for death and disability; subsidized loans and favorable terms on banking/financial/insurance products, including renegotiation initiatives.
- Human Resources objectives: empower resources by aligning roles to skills and expectations and providing appropriate training; ensure coherence between appraisals, development paths, and incentives; monitor corporate climate and satisfaction; allocate resources per sizing models and Business Plan targets; control personnel-related budgets; define performance indicators for management activities.
- Occupational health and safety governance: certified Occupational Health and Safety Management System (ISO 45001) guided by an internal supervision document and a Group-wide Safety Policy; comprehensive Risk Assessment Document (RAD) updated to 30 June 2024 in line with Italian Legislative Decree 81/08; regular internal and external audits; policies communicated via intranet and website.
- Safety policy highlights: commitment to accident/illness prevention, continuous improvement, stakeholder communication, and legal compliance; applies to Parent and all Group companies; approved by the Board; implementation led by Top Management; aligned with national/EU law and UNI ISO 45001; publicly available.
- Safety actions and monitoring: external audits by RINA Services (Dec 2023–Apr 2024) confirmed ISO 45001:2018 certification, with next audit in March 2025; improvement programs defined; ongoing engagement with Workers’ Safety Representatives through statutory consultations, periodic meetings, and training.
- Safety targets: no specific numerical targets set; continuous monitoring ensured via audits, improvement programs, and structured dialogue with Workers’ Safety Representatives.
- Training and skills development: commitment to upskilling/reskilling and professional growth aligned with market and sustainability needs; proactive needs analysis to prevent skill gaps; HR Development, Reskilling, and Change Management governed by internal “Professional Development Pathways.”

- Focus area: Training and skills development
  - Strategy: enhance skills and support professional growth aligned with market and sustainable development needs; prevent skill mismatches to maintain service quality.
  - Governance documents:
    - Professional Development Pathways: combines experiential steps, planned mobility, and training to build technical and soft skills; applies to the Parent Company; approved by the first-level function “Professional Development, D&I and Training”; available on intranet.
    - Reskilling and Change Management plans: detail needs identification, skills assessment, activity monitoring, and results tracking; applies to Parent Company and all Group companies; approved by the same function; available on intranet.
  - Training model and planning: annual, cross-functional planning prioritizing initiatives; each activity linked to corporate processes and risks; MPS Academy classifies high-risk areas (Credit, Anti-Money Laundering and Financial Crimes, Customer Protection and Transparency, Data Governance, Data Protection, Legislative Decree 231, Cyber Security).
  - Assessment tools: annual Risk Assessment (role-based risk exposure) and Skills Gap Analysis (employee training needs).
  - Key initiatives:
    - MiFID II/Consob Intermediaries’ Regulation training: ~10,000 customer-facing staff; ~30 hours per capita; synchronous sessions for Premium Managers focused on needs analysis and financial protection tools.
    - Risk Culture info-training: intranet article series with Learning Cards (including ESG content, reaching ~16,000 people); dedicated intranet section; annual “Culture of Risk” event chaired by the Chairman of the Board of Statutory Auditors with CEO and senior leadership participation.
    - Multimedia risk training: ongoing courses covering Wealth Risk Management, Operational Risk, Anti-Money Laundering, and other risk domains.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s training model aims to respond proactively and dynamically to the new cognitive challenges posed by the markets and by continuous developments in the banking system, and business processes, as well as by and the impacts derived from it.
nodes.summary:
- Policies and governance: The Group formalizes Professional Development Pathways and Reskilling & Change Management plans. Both are approved by the first-level function “Professional Development, D&I and Training,” available to all employees on the corporate intranet. The Professional Development policy applies to the Parent Company; the Reskilling/Change Management plan covers the Parent Company and all Group companies. No direct references to external standards are cited.
- Training model and methodology: Annual, risk-driven planning links every course to business processes and specific risks (Credit, AML/Financial Crimes, Customer Protection/Transparency, Data Governance, Data Protection, Legislative Decree 231, Cybersecurity). Two core levers: role-based Risk Assessment and individual Skills Gap Analysis.
- Risk culture and compliance focus: Ongoing information-training via intranet articles and Learning Cards (including ESG topics, reaching ~16,000 people); annual “Culture of Risk” event chaired by governance bodies; multimedia and mandatory courses on Code of Ethics, Legislative Decree 231/2001, anti-corruption and market abuse.
- Scale and outcomes in 2024: MiFID II training for ~10,000 front-line staff (≈30 hours per capita). AML training for ~11,000 and Credit for ~4,300 via e-learning, webinars, coaching; ~800 back to classroom in Credit. Cybersecurity/data governance/data protection/Decree 231 training for >3,900 central resources (≈60% attendance).
- IT security awareness: Courses for all staff on key cyber threats; specialist training and certifications for control functions and IT (AIIA for Internal Auditors, ISACA and other certification bodies, SWIFT CSP, business continuity).
- Board engagement: Induction for Board members and Statutory Auditors on cybersecurity.
- Digital enablement: Training supporting core applications (consumer finance, mortgage workflows, etc.). “Digital Agility” project aligned with DigComp 2.0 for >1,000 central staff by April 2025 via webinars. “New Innovation and Technology Academy” for IT on architecture modernization, AI, and low-code.
- Network and role-based upskilling: Induction and reinforcement tied to network reorganization (POE value role: ~1,000 people x 10 hours; SB managers: ~870 people x 11 hours). Managerial training for new and experienced branch managers; induction for key network roles; CRO newcomers’ path (10 sessions co-designed with Deloitte).
- Commercial excellence: “Being advisor” for Premium Managers; “Objective Value” for Value Added teams (consumer credit process) rolled out to initial seven retail head offices in 2024; “Private Academy” progressive pathway to full role mastery with specialization/certification.
- Transparency and sector specialization: Enhanced “Transparency” program content following skills gap review; agri-food market training (≈320 people, 14 webinars, 1.5 hours each) with Santa Chiara Next and sector institutes (INIPA, ISMEA, QUALIVITA).
- Remediation training: Targeted post-audit training for branches with significant gaps (~100 staff) using webinars and adaptive e-learning.
- Innovation in delivery: “Regulation & Risk Culture” mobile app releases monthly content (video with AI avatar plus text) produced by Deloitte Risk Advisory.
- MPS Academy: Central hub for design, planning, monitoring, and financing of training since 2012; drives ESG awareness via online courses, workshops, seminars, and bespoke initiatives tied to skills gaps; also covers DEI topics.
- “MPS Sviluppa” people development program: Enhances skills, engagement, and growth with equal-opportunity access. Tools include digital coaching, assessments, 360 feedback; structured reskilling from central structures toward network and control roles; annual Talent Academy to identify and prepare high performers for greater responsibility.
- Objectives and monitoring: HR sets annual qualitative/quantitative targets (training coverage, alignment of performance/potential with development and incentives), tracked via process KPIs.
- Diversity and inclusion: Commitment to gender equality and equal pay for equal value, inclusion of persons with disabilities, prevention of workplace violence and harassment, and broader protection of diversity.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s organisation model and structure envisage that all corporate structures are responsible for basing their conduct on ethics and risk culture principles, as well as promoting a corporate culture based on ethics, inclusion, accountability and legality, in compliance with the Code of Ethics.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on an ethics- and risk-based corporate culture that respects human rights, promotes inclusion, accountability, legality, and enforces zero tolerance for discrimination across all protected grounds.
- Codification of commitments through key Group policies:
  - Rules on Inclusion: sets commitments to diversity, inclusion, equity and parity across the employee lifecycle, organization, operations, and communications; applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies; approved by the CHCO Directorate; aligned with EU and international frameworks (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, UN Declaration of Human Rights, SDGs/2030 Agenda, Principles for Responsible Banking) and relevant EU/Italian regulations (CRD V, EBA guidelines, EU 2023/970, Bank of Italy Circular 285, Law 162/2021).
  - Gender Equality Policy: promotes fairness, equality and an inclusive climate of listening and respect for all stakeholders; approved by the Board of Directors; aligned with UNI/PdR 125:2022.
  - Rules on Preventing and Combating Gender-Based Harassment: defines non-tolerated conduct and principles to ensure a workplace free from discrimination, violence, and harassment; applies Group-wide; approved by the CHCO Directorate; compliant with Law 4/2021 and ILO Convention 190/2019.
  - Group Guidelines on the Management of Whistleblowing Systems: governs reporting and handling of actual/potential non-compliance including breaches of equal opportunity and inclusion; applicable to Parent Company and Group entities; drafted in line with CRD IV, Legislative Decree 72/2015 (Art. 52-bis TUB), Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th/34th updates), and EU Directive 2019/1937. 
  - All documents are accessible via the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Reporting and remediation mechanisms:
  - Whistleblowing system for EU law and regulatory breaches, including equality and inclusion violations.
  - Additional channel via a Protection Committee for inappropriate workplace behavior.
  - Defined governance for implementing documents, managing deviations/non-conformities, and issuing specific reports.
- Continuous training for all new hires on mandatory topics (privacy, AML, Legislative Decree 231/2001, Code of Ethics, safety, Corporate Governance Code, etc.).
- Gender Equality Management System:
  - Updated for monitoring compliance and managing recommendations with corrective actions.
  - Establishes a Strategic Plan on gender equality with objectives and actions based on indicator analysis; overseen and approved by a Top Management Steering Committee.
  - Commitment to KPIs that track implementation of the Gender Equality Policy and support cultural change in diversity and inclusion.
- Ongoing Group-wide initiatives (2024–2028) covering employment and inclusion of people with disabilities, prevention of workplace violence and harassment, and promotion of diversity, applicable to all personnel.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: To ensure the monitoring of gender equality activities and areas, with particular reference to compliance management, the Gender Equality Management System was updated.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Group Guidelines on the management of whistleblowing systems for handling actual or potential non-compliance, including breaches of equal opportunities, fairness, and inclusion in the Code of Ethics, as well as violations of EU law and internal/external regulations.
- Applicability and governance: Applies to all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (Banca Widiba, Monte Paschi Fiduciaria). Implementation to be notified to the Directorate of Corporate Reporting; Staff CAE and Government Audit Subsidiaries; Organisation Partner; and Organisation Function. Documents available in the Group website Sustainability section.
- Regulatory framework: Aligned with Directive 2013/36/EU (CRD IV), Italian Legislative Decree 72/2015 (Article 52-bis TUB), Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU (EU whistleblowing).
- Reporting channels: Whistleblowing system covers non-compliance; inappropriate workplace behavior may also be reported to a Protection Committee per the Rules on preventing and combating gender-based harassment and the Gender Equality Management System.
- Training and compliance culture: New recruits receive ongoing training on contractual, regulatory, and ethical obligations (privacy, AML, Legislative Decree 231/2001, Code of Ethics, safety, Corporate Governance Code).
- Gender Equality Management System: Updated to monitor gender equality activities, define recommendations and corrective actions, and manage a Strategic Plan (2024–2028) with objectives and actions approved by a Top Management Steering Committee. Nonconformities are managed with specific reporting.
- KPIs and objectives: Adoption of specific D&I KPIs to track progress; key KPI is the share of positions of responsibility held by women—target 35% by 2023 exceeded (37%); 37.6% at end-2024; target >40% by 2028. Continuous monitoring with corrective measures as needed.
- Group-wide initiatives (ongoing over 2024–2028): 
  - Plural Management Project (D&I awareness, gender and disability focus).
  - Growth Together (evolution of the Women Leadership Program; 609 women managers since 2020).
  - Top Management training on gender equality and anti-harassment (Fondazione Libellula).
  - “Safe at work” specialist training on harassment prevention (Fondazione Libellula).
  - Disability LAB network participation (Wise Growth) on disability management topics.
  - “I’m Possible” trainings to build inclusive team awareness (disability focus).
  - Unconscious Bias course (97% completion) and Gender Equity course (92% completion) for all staff.
  - Anti-harassment awareness: ABI “Words of Inclusion” podcasts; “Financial Education: an empowerment tool” to counter economic violence.
  - D&I intranet page with interactive content and an inclusive glossary.
  - D&I induction for new recruits.
  - Inclusion Week (March 2024) on harassment prevention and disability; publication of a disability manifesto.
  - Participation in “Open Jam 2024” (The European House – Ambrosetti) to foster intergenerational dialogue.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The focus on issues related to diversity and inclusion is reinforced with an enrichment of performance indicators in line with the “Rules on Inclusion” document and with constant monitoring of existing indicators.
nodes.summary:
- Diversity and Inclusion initiatives: The Group ran extensive training and awareness programs on gender equality, disability inclusion, harassment prevention, and unconscious bias. Key actions included:
  - Plural Management Project training (2,633 managers trained overall; 210 in 2024) on diversity, inclusion, and Gender Equality Policy.
  - “Growth Together” leadership development for women (609 participants since 2020).
  - Top management engagement and training on gender equality and anti-harassment by Fondazione Libellula; a “Safe at work” session for specialists on harassment prevention/management.
  - Ongoing Disability LAB meetings (Wise Growth) on disability management, detection, and team support; “I’m Possible” sessions to build inclusive team awareness.
  - Unconscious Bias training offered to all staff (97% completion) and a “Gender Equity” course (92% completion).
  - Awareness efforts on preventing gender harassment and economic violence, including joining ABI’s “Words of Inclusion” and financial education courses as empowerment tools.
  - A continually updated D&I intranet hub with resources and an inclusive glossary; D&I modules in new hire induction.
  - Inclusion Week virtual classrooms (harassment prevention and disability) culminating in a disability manifesto with proposals; participation in “Open Jam 2024” to foster intergenerational dialogue.

  - Core KPI: share of positions of responsibility held by women—targeted at 35% by 2023 (achieved 37% in 2023; 37.6% at end-2024); goal set at >40% by 2028 under the 2024–2028 Business Plan.

- Privacy governance and practices: A dedicated section outlines protection of employees’ personal data through the Group’s Data Protection Policy.

Compliance aligns with GDPR, the Italian Privacy Code (as amended), and guidance from the Italian Data Protection Authority and EDPB. Policy is published on the corporate website (Sustainability section).
  - Methodological approach: Privacy by design/technology, data subject rights management, Records of processing, and data breach handling; defined roles/responsibilities, information flows, planning/reporting, and employee empowerment.

nodes.title: Privacy
nodes.heading: Privacy
nodes.start_phrase: This paragraph relates to Privacy, i.e. the protection of the confidentiality of the personal data of the Group’s people.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Protection of personal data confidentiality for the Group’s people through a structured privacy framework.
- Core policy: “Data Protection Policy” sets safeguards and employee concern-raising channels to prevent privacy violations.
- Methodological approach:
  - Privacy by design and by default in projects and technology use.
  - Upholding data subject rights.
  - Maintenance of Records of processing activities.
  - Data breach prevention, detection, and management.
  - Clear roles and responsibilities, privacy information flows, planning/reporting, and employee empowerment.
- Scope: Currently applies to the Bank, with plans to extend to other Group companies.
- Governance: Board of Directors oversees the privacy compliance system, approves policies/processes, and sets strategic direction.
- Compliance standards: EU GDPR (Reg. 2016/679), Italian Privacy Code (Leg. Decree 196/2003 as amended by 101/2018), and guidance from the Italian Data Protection Authority and EDPB, plus other applicable regulations.
- Transparency: Policy available in the Sustainability section of the Group’s website.
- Training and culture: Ongoing training at induction, during role changes, and when new personal data tools are introduced; promotes a pervasive data protection culture.
- Training content: Regulatory compliance (privacy rules, confidentiality, breach handling) and technological risk topics (e.g., phishing and scam techniques).
- Access control: Only authorized personnel process personal data on a strict need-to-know basis; access to IT and paper records is restricted; user accounts and authorization profiles are aligned to role, assigned tasks, and operational unit (least privilege/RBAC).

nodes.start_phrase: In order to prevent the violation of data privacy rights, data protection safeguards and channels for employees to raise concerns are ensured through the “Data Protection Policy”.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Protection of personal data confidentiality for the Group’s people, with safeguards and channels for employees to raise privacy concerns.
- Core policy: Data Protection Policy outlining a methodological approach covering:
  - Privacy by design/technology and compliance with data protection principles.
  - Respect for data subject rights.
  - Maintenance of Records of Processing Activities.
  - Data breach management.
  - Defined roles and responsibilities, privacy information flows, planning, reporting, and employee training/empowerment.
- Scope: Currently applies to the Bank, with plans to extend to other Group companies.
- Governance: Board of Directors oversees the privacy compliance system, approves policies/processes, provides strategic guidance, and issues implementation instructions.
- Compliance framework: Adherence to EU GDPR, Italian Privacy Code (Legislative Decree 196/2003 as amended by 101/2018), and guidelines/decisions from the Italian Data Protection Authority, EDPB, and other relevant regulations.

- Actions and controls: Ongoing employee training at onboarding, role changes, and new tool introductions; content spans regulatory obligations and technological risks (e.g., phishing, scams).

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In order to ensure that employees are trained in data protection issues, the Group provides for employee training, i.e. initiatives to promote a data protection culture.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Privacy protection of employees’ personal data within Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, as part of the 2024 Sustainability Report.
- Policy framework: A Group Data Protection Policy outlines:
  - Operational and privacy controls to ensure compliance from project/design and technology use stages, protection of data subject rights, maintenance of processing records, and data breach management.
  - Defined roles and responsibilities, privacy information flows, planning/reporting of activities and controls, and employee training/empowerment.
  - Current scope limited to the Bank with plans to extend to other Group companies.
  - Governance by the Board of Directors; compliance with GDPR, Italian Privacy Code (as amended), and guidance from the Italian Data Protection Authority and EDPB.
  - Public availability in the Group website’s Sustainability section.
- Actions and controls:
  - Ongoing employee training on regulatory aspects (privacy compliance, confidentiality, data breach handling) and technological risks (phishing and scams), provided at induction, during role changes, and upon introduction of new data-processing tools.
  - Strict access management based on necessity and role-specific authorization profiles for the Bank’s Information System; definition of “persons authorised to process data.”
- Objectives and monitoring:
  - No specific quantitative privacy targets set; effective oversight maintained.
  - Compliance Function conducts Level II checks: remote/on-site audits, reporting non-compliance to Internal Audit and DPO Staff, verifying DPIAs, and supporting DPO reporting to senior management.
- Worker involvement and industrial relations:
  - Respect for freedom of association and ILO-aligned practices; robust engagement with trade unions through Level II bargaining.
  - Structured consultations and disclosures during reorganizations, mobility, and changes in work organization; negotiation windows up to 50 days per the National Collective Labour Agreement.
  - Industrial relations managed by the First Level Company Function, ensuring compliance and active dialogue.
  - Joint Committees (Commercial Policies, Welfare, Training, Equal Opportunities, Environmental Sustainability) met 11 times in 2024 to address material issues and promote development.
  - The Equal Opportunities Committee sets female employment indicators and empowerment policies; the Corporate Observatory monitors workplace interactions, communication quality, and risks to worker dignity.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The group has not, to date, defined specific objectives for dealing with employee privacy issues.
nodes.summary:
- Employee privacy governance: No specific objectives set yet, but ongoing Level II compliance monitoring by the Compliance Function, including remote/on-site audits, reporting non-compliance to Internal Audit and the DPO, verification of DPIA execution, and support to the DPO in management reporting.
- Worker engagement and representation: The Group supports freedom of association in line with the Italian Constitution and ILO principles, encouraging active dialogue with trade unions.
- Collective bargaining and consultation: Level II bargaining emphasizes ongoing social dialogue, information, and consultation rights to support long-term sustainable growth and a positive corporate climate.
- Change management: In cases of restructuring or reorganization, the Group provides required disclosures and conducts negotiations with trade unions (up to 50 days) before implementing measures, aiming to limit impacts and safeguard working conditions.
- Industrial relations oversight: Managed by the First Level Company Function, which plans and conducts consultation procedures and ensures compliance with laws and collective agreements.
- Joint Committees: Company–union bodies central to Level II bargaining; met 11 times in 2024; focus areas include Commercial Policies, Welfare, Training, Equal Opportunities, and Environmental Sustainability.
- Equal Opportunities Committee: Sets female employment indicators and develops empowerment policies, advancing diversity as a driver of cultural and social growth.
- Corporate Observatory: Joint body monitoring workplace interactions and communication, aiming to preserve individual dignity and quality of life, and to identify situations that could harm worker dignity.

nodes.title: Listening to employees
nodes.heading: Listening to employees
nodes.start_phrase: For the Group, listening to people is an essential element of the relationship with employees and is carried out systematically by applying different internal tools and channels.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on systematic employee listening as a core element of the employer–employee relationship, using multiple internal tools and channels.
- CEO engagement throughout 2024: 14 in‑person meetings in Italy with 4,000+ colleagues to share 2024–2028 Business Plan and encourage dialogue; six additional in‑person sessions with Talent Academy participants and new hires; four all‑staff conference calls on financial results with live Q&A and follow‑up FAQs on the intranet.
- Division leadership outreach: 24 live meetings by Commercial C‑levels to explain divisional priorities and gather questions/remarks via live and post‑event channels.
- Sales function listening: 45 targeted sessions (often with business partners) to present market outlooks and collect feedback.
- “A Day at the Branch” (July 2024): managers from central structures visited 60+ branches, engaging ~2,500 employees for practical, network‑focused dialogue; attended by the CEO and Deputy Chief Commercial Officer; key insights compiled and shared via a structured intranet article.
- Measuring effectiveness and continuous feedback: internal climate surveys, focus groups, post‑event satisfaction questionnaires, and interactive intranet features (comments, likes, shares); new “Did you find this article useful?” prompt to assess content relevance and clarity.
- Open channels for all employees to express views on work life, applications, and initiatives; ongoing one‑to‑one meetings with HR Managers, including upon employee request.
- Targeted listening for new employees: early‑tenure satisfaction questionnaires and probation‑period feedback interviews to surface needs and areas of attention.

nodes.title: The effectiveness of involvement
nodes.heading: The effectiveness of involvement
nodes.start_phrase: Internal climate surveys and feedback collection are carried out by means of focus groups and employee satisfaction questionnaires after events, as well as interactive functions on the company intranet (comments, likes, shares).
nodes.summary:
- Employee listening and engagement: The Group systematically gathers employee input through multiple tools and channels. In 2024, the CEO held 14 in-person meetings across Italy with over 4,000 colleagues to share the 2024–2028 Business Plan, plus six sessions with Talent Academy participants and new hires, and four companywide calls on financial results with Q&A. Follow-ups included HR-led deep dives and intranet FAQs.
- Leadership dialogue across the organization: Commercial C-levels ran 24 live divisional meetings with open Q&A. Sales functions hosted 45 listening sessions, sometimes with business partners, to discuss market outlooks. The “A Day at the Branch” initiative in July 2024 brought central managers to over 60 branches (about 2,500 participants), including attendance by the CEO and Deputy Chief Commercial Officer; key takeaways were shared with all staff via the intranet.
- Measuring effectiveness of involvement: The Group uses climate surveys, focus groups, post-event satisfaction questionnaires, and interactive intranet features (comments, likes, shares, and a “Did you find this article useful?” prompt). HR Managers conduct systematic one-to-one meetings, including at employee request. New hires receive targeted listening through early-tenure questionnaires and probation-period feedback interviews.
- Channels to raise concerns and remediation processes: The Group encourages open dialogue through territorial meetings and formal structures. It operates a confidential Whistleblowing system (IT platform and telephone) for employees and qualified external personnel to report suspected misconduct, managed by the Fraud Audit department, with dedicated training—including a new multimedia course in 2024—plus additional training for control owners and new employees.

nodes.summary: Overview of social protection for Group employees with Italian contracts, detailing legal and collective bargaining coverage by entity. For the Parent Company and Widiba Bank, protections derive from Italian law, the Credit Sector National Collective Bargaining Agreement (CCNL), and the MPS Supplementary Agreement, covering: illness (salary/job preservation up to 36 months by seniority, NASPI indemnity for 24 months after dismissal, child/spouse recruitment on premature death); unemployment (NASPI 24 months); work injury/disability (salary/job preservation up to 36 months, indemnified disability leave, benefits for approaching retirement, NASPI 24 months, insurance for permanent disability/death, child/spouse recruitment on premature death); parental leave (job protection, indemnity, and CCNL salary top-ups); and retirement (extraordinary income support allowance within 5 years of AGO pension entitlement via the credit sector fund, allowance per AGO rules, and supplementary pension via MPS Pension Funds/MPS Fund). For MPS Tenimenti and MPS Magazzini Generali Fiduciari, coverage under their adopted National Collective Bargaining Agreements and Italian law includes similar protections, generally with indemnities of 12/24 months, parental leave with job protection and indemnity (no salary top-ups noted), and retirement allowances per AGO pension rules (no supplementary pension specified).

nodes.title: MPS Pension Funds
nodes.heading: MPS Pension Funds
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the welfare system provided for by the Group, in relation to the loss of income due to retirement, the MPS Pen- sion Fund and the MPS Welfare Fund have been introduced from 2020 as forms of supplementary pension system, with the possibility of membership also extended to the tax-dependent family members of Group employees.
nodes.summary:
- Social protection framework: Employees in Italy across the Group are covered for income loss through Italian law, sector collective agreements (Credit Sector CCNL), and MPS supplementary agreements. Coverage areas include illness, unemployment (NASPI), work injury/disability, parental leave, and retirement, with specifics varying by company.
- Parent Company and Widiba: Enhanced protections such as salary and job preservation up to 36 months (seniority-based), NASPI for 24 months post-dismissal, indemnified disability leave, accident insurance for permanent disability/death, child/spouse hiring in case of premature death, parental leave indemnities with CCNL salary top-ups, and pre-retirement/retirement benefits including extraordinary income support and supplementary pension payments.
- MPS Tenimenti and MPS Magazzini Generali Fiduciari: Similar protections aligned to their applicable national agreements, generally including salary/job preservation based on seniority, indemnities for 12/24 months post-dismissal, disability leave, accident insurance, parental leave protections, and retirement allowances per AGO rules.
- MPS Pension and Welfare Funds: Group supplementary pension schemes (open to employees and tax-dependent family members) managed with ESG criteria; signatories to UN PRI; published policies on stewardship and sustainability risk integration; defined ESG monitoring and reporting. In 2024, aligned with Laws 220/2021 and 122/2022 introducing policies against financing producers of anti-personnel mines/cluster munitions; MPS Pension Fund advanced strategic allocation into private markets via Article 8 and Article 9 SFDR strategies.
- Inclusion of persons with disabilities: 6% of employees are persons with disabilities (52% men, 48% women), hired under Italy’s Law 68/1999 with roles compatible with their conditions. Annual compliance checks determine required hires, coordinated with Employment Centres. The Group also employs other protected categories under Article 18 (e.g., orphans of workers deceased due to work, refugees).
- Training and performance reviews: Near-universal performance review coverage in 2023 across included companies (Parent Company, Widiba, MPS Fiduciaria, MPS Tenimenti, MGFM). By gender: 99.67% of women (8,840) and 99.39% of men (7,663) reviewed; overall 99.54% (16,503 of 16,579). nodes.title: Work-life balance metrics
nodes.heading: Work-life balance metrics
nodes.start_phrase: The Group is committed to welfare policies, which aim to create value for people and improve the corporate climate: every aspect of welfare in the Group is aimed at supporting colleagues and their families in financial, social and work/life balance terms, contributing to the increase in satisfaction, wellbeing, loyalty and productivity.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on employee welfare and work-life balance: comprehensive policies support employees and their families financially, socially, and in balancing work and life, aiming to boost satisfaction, wellbeing, loyalty, and productivity.
- Collective relations: welfare is central to Level II bargaining with trade unions; extended to employees using the sector Solidarity Fund; benefits apply to all employees regardless of contract type or hours and have expanded over time to cover evolving needs of employees, retirees, and families (over 50,000 people).
- Parental/family leave: available to all; job preservation guaranteed on return; leave can be taken for children up to age 12.
- 2024 parental leave usage: 1,452 employees (28% of eligible) took leave—325 men (14% of eligible men) and 1,127 women (37% of eligible women). Return-to-work rate after leave ~94%; 12-month retention ~98% (99% women, 98% men), with shortfalls due to voluntary resignations.
- Gender pay equality: overall gender pay gap (average gross hourly male vs. female) is 11.35% for 2024. By role: executives 14.80%; middle managers 6.82%; white-collar -0.91%. The gap has narrowed in recent years.
- Equal pay governance: objective job weighting and measures aligned with EBA Equal Pay Guidelines to promote gender balance and ensure gender-neutral remuneration.
- Pay methodology: gross hourly pay derived from Gross Annual Total Remuneration (ATR) divided by 1,554 theoretical annual hours, neutralizing part-time effects. ATR includes base pay, allowances, benefits (fringe, pensions, insurance), and variable pay for 2023 paid in 2024.
- Pay ratio: Total Remuneration rate of 8.97 (highest-paid employee vs. median of others).
- Human rights and complaints: no lawsuits or extrajudicial proceedings on gender equality violations; eight workplace harassment reports; no judicial/extrajudicial cases on severe human rights incidents.

Gross hourly pay is derived from Gross Annual Total Remuneration (ATR) divided by 1,554 theoretical hours, neutralizing part‑time effects; ATR includes base pay, recurring allowances, fringe benefits, company pension and insurance contributions, and variable pay. Highest-to-median Total Remuneration ratio is 8.97.

- Incidents and human rights: no lawsuits or extrajudicial proceedings on gender equality or serious human rights incidents; eight workplace harassment reports recorded.

- Workers in the value chain (ESRS S2): describes policies, actions, monitoring, and channels for concerns for workers in the value chain, based on a double materiality assessment. Identifies:

  - Positive upstream impacts: practices safeguarding health and safety and privacy, and preventing child and forced labour.

  - Commitment to UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and principles against child and forced labour; alignment with ILO and OECD standards.
  - Compliance structures: internal control system; Organisation, Management and Control Model under Italian Legislative Decree 231/01 for supplier selection and offence prevention.
  - Additional policies: Occupational Health and Safety Policy; Sustainability and ESG Policy; procurement practices that protect worker H&S, the environment, and people.
- Supplier management and engagement:

  - Ongoing stakeholder engagement with suppliers via the Purchasing Department’s Stakeholder Management process; channels for concerns are referenced through this process.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group’s Code of Ethics is the document that governs the guiding principles, values and rules of conduct that complement the legal and regulatory obligations for workers in the upstream value chain.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus: Addresses workers in the upstream value chain only, covering working conditions and other labour-related rights identified as material impacts.
- Core policies:
  - Group Code of Ethics governs supplier conduct, requiring explicit acceptance and alignment; emphasizes fairness, transparency, integrity, and avoidance of conflicts of interest; commits to UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights, including principles on Child and Forced Labour.
  - Organisation, Management and Control Model pursuant to Italian Legislative Decree 231/2001 guides supplier selection and prohibits relationships without 231 compliance.
  - Procurement approach prioritizes occupational health and safety and environmental protection; supported by Group Health & Safety Policy (aligned with UNI ISO 45001) and Group Sustainability & ESG Policy integrating ESG into strategy, risk indicators, and stakeholder engagement.
  - Governance: Policies approved/overseen by the Board and top management; references to recognized standards (ISO 45001, IDD, MiFID 2 ESG); documents available on the corporate website/intranet.
  - Stakeholder engagement with suppliers managed by the Purchasing Department.
- Actions and controls:
  - Supplier pre-qualification and contracting include checks on labour law compliance, application of National Collective Labour Agreements, DURC (contribution regularity), ESG certifications, 231 compliance statements, anti-mafia documentation, and alignment of supplier Codes of Ethics.
  - Heightened due diligence for categories where worker protection is critical (authorizations, safety measures, training).
  - 100% of counterparties informed of anti-corruption policies and procedures.
  - Annual updates and document reviews for suppliers’ social sustainability; Purchasing Department manages Supplier Register qualification.
  - Control functions assess data protection programs of suppliers; privacy roles and clauses embedded in contracts.
  - No serious human rights incidents reported in the upstream value chain.
- Monitoring, metrics, and targets:
  - No specific quantitative targets yet for value chain workers; effectiveness ensured via indicators, Supplier Register re-verifications, and Control/Internal Audit activities.
  - In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria in line with international standards; continuous verification for each new supplier.
  - Future evaluation of setting specific targets to drive continuous improvement.
- Compliance status: No detected cases of non-compliance with the UN Guiding Principles, ILO Declaration, or OECD Guidelines regarding upstream workers.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The following initiatives involve the majority of the Group’s suppliers and external service providers, including professionals, companies and foreign businesses, and are part of the Group’s normal practice regarding the management of supply relationships.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Initiatives cover most suppliers and external providers (including foreign businesses) as part of routine supply relationship management; double materiality analysis found only potential, not actual, negative impacts.
- Supplier selection and compliance: Suppliers are evaluated during pre-selection, award, and contract finalization for compliance with labor regulations, National Collective Labour Agreement application, DURC (Single Document of Contribution Regularity), ESG certifications, and alignment with the Group’s Code of Ethics (counterparties’ Codes must not conflict).
- Mandatory documentation: During registration, suppliers provide the 231 Model Compliance Statement (including anti-corruption references) and anti-mafia documentation, plus responses on certifications and ethics; new lawyers must sign contractual documentation.
- Model 231 requirements: Suppliers must declare knowledge of and compliance with Legislative Decree 231/2001; for higher-risk product categories, enhanced due diligence covers economic/financial soundness, permits/authorizations, worker safety measures, and specialized training.
- Anti-corruption and data protection: 100% of suppliers with commercial relations are informed of anti-corruption policies; Control functions annually verify suppliers’ data protection programs, and contracts include privacy role clauses.
- Governance and monitoring: Purchasing Department leads collection/verification for Supplier Register enrollment; annual checks ensure updated social sustainability documentation; Control and Internal Audit functions perform oversight.
- Human rights: No serious human rights issues reported in the upstream value chain to date.
- Objectives and performance: No specific targets yet for value chain workers; effectiveness ensured via indicators, post-contractual re-verification of Supplier Register requisites, and control/audit activities. In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria aligned with international standards; continuous verification applies to each new supplier. Future adoption of specific targets is under evaluation.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has not, to date, defined any specific targets to deal with the issue of value chain workers.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Management of supplier and external service provider relationships across the Group within the sustainability framework; double materiality analysis indicates only potential impacts to date, with no actual negative impacts requiring remediation.

- Supplier selection and compliance: Multi-stage assessment (pre-selection, award, contract finalization) includes checks on labor law compliance, National Collective Labour Agreement application, DURC (contribution regularity), ESG certifications, Model 231 (Legislative Decree 231/2001) and anti-mafia compliance, and alignment with the Group Code of Ethics. All suppliers are informed of anti-corruption policies and procedures (100% coverage).

- Heightened due diligence for certain categories: For products/services where worker health, safety, and dignity are critical, the Group assesses suppliers’ financial soundness, authorizations/permits, prevention and safety measures, and specialized training.

- Governance and controls: The Purchasing Department manages documentation collection and verification for the Suppliers Register; annual updates of suppliers’ social sustainability documentation; Control and Internal Audit functions conduct monitoring. Data protection compliance of suppliers/partners is verified and reinforced via contractual privacy roles and clauses.

- Monitoring and outcomes: No serious human rights problems reported in the upstream value chain. While no specific targets for value chain workers are set yet, effectiveness is tracked through indicators, ongoing verifications after initial contracting, and internal controls. In 2024, 100% of new suppliers (114) were assessed against environmental criteria aligned with international standards; setting explicit targets will be evaluated in the future.

- Worker involvement: No formal engagement process with suppliers’ workers; indirect assessment via supplier questionnaires, scoring that favors certified suppliers, and self-certification of adoption of applicable national/regional collective agreements.

- Grievance and remediation: An open Whistleblowing system is available to external parties and supplier personnel to report violations of laws, internal rules, procedures, and the Code of Ethics, with safeguards for whistleblowers referenced elsewhere in the report.

nodes.title: Process of involving workers in the value chain on impacts
nodes.heading: Process of involving workers in the value chain on impacts
nodes.start_phrase: Although the Group does not have a formalised process for involving suppliers’ workers, either directly or through representatives, it does believe that the requirements assessed when signing contracts with suppliers make it indirectly possible to assess respect for the rights of the suppliers’ workers.
nodes.summary:
- The Group lacks a formal process to directly involve suppliers’ workers or their representatives but indirectly assesses respect for their rights through supplier onboarding and evaluation.
- During supplier evaluation, a questionnaire assesses qualifications, with certified suppliers receiving higher scores that influence contract awards.
- At registration, suppliers must self-certify adoption of applicable national/regional collective labor agreements.
- To address and remediate potential negative impacts on workers in the value chain, the Group offers accessible reporting channels, notably a Whistleblowing system open to external parties.
- The Whistleblowing system supports compliance with laws, internal regulations, and the Code of Ethics, reinforcing sustainability, integrity, and fairness.
- Access is available via institutional channels to non-Group employees, including staff of companies providing goods or services to the Group; details on protections and effectiveness are provided in the “Protection of Whistleblowers” section within Governance Information.

nodes.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for workers in the value chain to raise concerns
nodes.heading: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for workers in the value chain to raise concerns
nodes.start_phrase: In order to prevent and/or remedy the concerns of workers in the value chain, the Group provides channels of free access also to external parties, such as the Whistleblowing system.
nodes.summary:
- Supplier and value-chain worker involvement: The Group lacks a formalized process to directly engage suppliers’ workers, but indirectly assesses respect for their rights through supplier onboarding and selection. A questionnaire-based supplier evaluation gives higher scores and weight to certified suppliers, and all suppliers must self-certify adoption of applicable national/regional collective agreements.

- Remediation and grievance channels: A free-access Whistleblowing system is available to internal and external parties, including employees of suppliers and third-party contractors. It supports risk prevention, compliance with laws and internal rules, and upholds the Code of Ethics, contributing to sustainability and integrity. Protections for whistleblowers are detailed in the Governance section.

- Affected communities (ESRS S3): Using a double materiality approach, the Group mapped impacts, risks, and opportunities by reviewing internal/public documentation and existing initiatives (e.g., cultural, scientific, social, environmental programs; youth employability and work-orientation activities; collaborations with local institutions; support for the agri-food sector). Material outcomes identified include:
  - Positive impacts in own operations from initiatives that protect and enhance territories (urban, cultural) and promote youth employability.
  - Positive downstream impacts from actions supporting employability in key national sectors.
  - Opportunities in the downstream value chain to expand products and services that support companies in sectors critical to the national economy, including financing for the national production fabric.
  - Relevant scopes span own operations and the downstream value chain. Policies, actions, and targets on territorial impacts are indicated to follow in subsequent sections.

  - Opportunities in the downstream value chain to broaden products and services that support companies in strategic sectors of the national economy; community engagement may also create financing opportunities for the national production fabric.

- Governance and oversight: Policies ensure structured planning, authorization, and oversight of community-related activities, with roles for Top Management and the Board of Directors.
- Key policies described:
  - Group Directive on Communication and External Affairs: Sets governance for external communication (media, social media, events, sponsorships, heritage), requires approvals, aligns with Italian legal/regulatory provisions (Legislative Decree 39/2010, ABI Circular 15/2010, Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013), and is accessible to all employees.
  - Historical Archive Management: Regulates creation, archiving, and transfer of documents of historical interest; supervised by the Archival Superintendency for Tuscany; aligned with the Code of Cultural Heritage (Legislative Decree 42/2004) and includes safeguards to prevent liability under Legislative Decree 231/2001 for cultural heritage offences; accessible to employees.

nodes.summary:
- Focus: Territory-related impacts and the Group’s policies, processes, and safeguards to support local communities in urban development, culture, youth employability, and selected economic sectors.
- Community support actions: professional development and orientation events, financial education initiatives, targeted support for vulnerable groups, and enhancement/preservation of banking and national artistic heritage. Oversight is ensured through formal policies.

Key policies and governance:
- Group Directive on Communication and External Affairs:
  - Establishes governance and responsibilities for external communication via a Strategic Communication Plan (media relations, social media, advertising, corporate image, events, sponsorships, heritage).
  - Aims to enhance the Group’s image and give visibility to territorially relevant events and community initiatives, with specific authorization procedures.
  - Governance flow: plan drafted by External Communication, Institutional Relations and Sustainability in line with Board strategies; review by Steering Committee; approval by the Board.
  - Compliance/alignment: Legislative Decree 39/2010, ABI Circular 15/2010, Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013 (Board oversight of public information/communication).
  - Availability: corporate intranet.

- Historical Archive Management:
  - Regulates creation, repository archiving, and transfer of documents of historical interest.
  - Supervision by the Archival Superintendency for Tuscany; Maximum Preservation Schedule approved by the Bank’s Board and the competent Ministry.
  - Managed by the Historical Heritage function.
  - Compliance: Code of Cultural Heritage and Landscape (Legislative Decree 42/2004); includes safeguards to prevent liability under Legislative Decree 231/2001 for cultural heritage offences introduced by Law 22/2022.
  - Availability: corporate intranet.

- Artistic Heritage Management:
  - Governs cataloguing, preservation, enhancement, and protection of the Bank’s movable artworks of particular cultural interest (per Art. 10(3)(a), Legislative Decree 42/2004).
  - Managed by the Historical and Artistic Heritage function.
  - Compliance: Italian Constitution and Legislative Decree 42/2004.
  - Availability: corporate intranet.

Overall, the document segment outlines how BMPS embeds community support and cultural stewardship into formal, Board-validated policies aligned with Italian regulatory frameworks, ensuring transparent communication, preservation of cultural assets, and structured community-oriented initiatives.

- Policy framework: A set of Group directives governs external communication, sponsorships and fundraising, sustainability/ESG integration, and the management of historical archives and artistic heritage. These policies:
  - Define roles, approval flows and oversight by Top Management/Board.
  - Align with Italian regulations and sector standards (e.g., Legislative Decree 39/2010, ABI Circular 15/2010, Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013, Legislative Decree 42/2004, Legislative Decree 231/2001 as amended by Law 22/2022).

- MPS Orienta program (2024): Career guidance, soft-skills development, financial education, and school–university engagement to strengthen the education–work bridge and employer branding.
  - Agreements with universities, master’s and specialist schools nationwide for curricular and non-curricular internships.
  - 40 internships activated in specialized functions (avg. 6 months), with some hires.
  - Participation in 2 University of Siena career days.
  - Education benefits for employees/families via Unitelma: 43 undergraduate and 184 post-graduate enrollments since 2020; agreement renewed for 2025–26.
- Support to the agri-food sector: Tailored financial services and strategic advisory to bolster local business sustainability.
  - MPS AgriDOP supports ecological transition and PDO/PGI, organic and environmental certifications; long-term value-chain and consortium support.
  - Expansion of specialized Agrifood Centres from 15 to 21 across key Italian districts, offering financing, protection solutions and expert advisory.
  - Proactive mapping of subsidy measures; guidance on innovation, digitalization and sustainability aligned with Italy’s NRRP.
- Sector engagement and visibility: Sponsorships and participation in major industry events (Gambero Rosso’s Guida Oli d’Italia 2024, Vinitaly, MASAF’s States General of Olive Growing, Divinazione Expo including the G7 Agriculture).

Consumers and end-users
[ESRS S4]
This section provides, in relation to the management of “consumers and end-users”, a description of the impacts, risks and 
opportunities found to be material from the double materiality analysis. Below, the section outlines the policies and actions 
taken to manage the issue, to mitigate risks and negative impacts, to seize material opportunities, and the targets set to

and their representatives on identified impacts that affect them, as well as the mechanisms for remedying negative im-
