Impacts, Risks and Opportunities

nodes.title: Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.heading: 3.4.1 Impacts, Risks and Opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The process to map impacts, risks and opportunities with reference to this standard includes the specific aspects related to the Group’s operational and commercial activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: ESRS S4 Consumers and end-users for Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena, covering double materiality (impacts, risks, opportunities), policies, actions, targets, stakeholder engagement, grievance/remedy channels.
- Stakeholders in scope: institutional, corporate, and retail customers, along with business partners and suppliers (as end-users of products/services).
- Key impact areas: data protection and privacy, accessibility and inclusion in financial services, quality and transparency of information, freedom of expression, personal safety, non-discrimination, and responsible business practices.
- Material impacts and scope:
  - Negative: potential inadequacy of safeguards for customer/end-user information (Own Operations and Downstream Value Chain).
  - Positive: business practices supporting freedom of expression (e.g., complaint mechanisms), clear and transparent product information, personal safety, social inclusion, and process digitalisation (e.g., enhanced user authentication) within Own Operations.
- Risks: operational and reputational risks from potential personal data protection violations across Own Operations and Downstream Value Chain.
- Opportunities: strengthen stakeholder trust via robust privacy and expression safeguards (Own Operations); expand inclusive products/services and enhance privacy protections (Downstream Value Chain).
- Sub-topics mapped under S4: privacy, freedom of expression, access to quality information, health and safety, non-discrimination, access to products and services, responsible business practices; assessed for impact and financial materiality across own operations, upstream, and downstream.
- Privacy and IT security governance:
  - Data Protection Policy: defines privacy controls by design/by default, data subject rights, processing records, data breach management, roles/responsibilities, information flows, planning/reporting, and employee training. Approved by Board of Directors; applies to Parent Company, Widiba, and fiduciary entities; aligned with GDPR, Italian Privacy Code, EDPB guidance; public on the Group website.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance: establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS), roles, and responsibilities; centralized governance by the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation with IT; aligned with ISO/IEC 2700x; available on intranet; applies to all Group companies.
- ISMS approach: lifecycle protection of data and information, risk assessment, and preventive/protective measures to meet regulatory and asset protection requirements.
- Next sections (not fully shown): actions and targets for privacy, customer listening and complaint handling, product information quality, personal safety, non-discrimination, accessibility (including digitalisation), and responsible business practices.

nodes.title: Policies, Actions and Targets for consumers and end users
nodes.heading: 3.4.2 Policies, Actions and Targets for consumers and end users
nodes.start_phrase: This section deals with privacy issues, with reference to the policies, processes and controls defined by the Group to ensure IT security and protect the personal data of customers and end users from unauthorised access and loss of data.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Consumer and end-user protection through privacy and IT security at Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group.
- Key policies:
  - Data Protection Policy (privacy compliance management):
    - Ensures privacy-by-design/default, handling of data subject rights (access, rectification, deletion, etc.), Records of Processing Activities, and data breach management.
    - Defines roles/responsibilities, privacy information flows, planning/reporting, and staff training/empowerment.
    - Scope: Parent Company, Widiba, and fiduciary companies; approved by the Board of Directors.
    - Compliance: GDPR, Italian Privacy Code (Leg. Decree 196/2003 as amended by 101/2018), guidance from the Italian DPA and EDPB; publicly available on the Group website.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance:
    - Establishes the organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for the Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect information assets and set medium/long-term strategy.
    - Scope: All Group companies; centralized governance in the Parent’s Information Security function; implementation by Information Security and IT; company-level adoption via top management.
    - Alignment with ISO/IEC 2700x standards; available on the corporate intranet.
- Overarching approach:
  - Data and information are protected across their entire lifecycle in line with regulatory requirements.
  - The ISMS is risk-based, with prevention and protection measures planned and implemented to minimize risks and safeguard company assets and personal data.

nodes.title: Privacy
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.1 Privacy
nodes.start_phrase: This section deals with privacy issues, with reference to the policies, processes and controls defined by the Group to ensure IT security and protect the personal data of customers and end users from unauthorised access and loss of data.
nodes.summary:
- The excerpt focuses on consumer and end‑user protection through privacy and IT security, ensuring data and information are safeguarded across their entire lifecycle in line with regulatory requirements and corporate asset protection.
- It presents two cornerstone Group policies:
  - Data Protection Policy: establishes privacy governance and operational controls, including privacy by design/default, management of data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, etc.), maintenance of Records of Processing Activities, data breach management, defined roles and responsibilities, privacy information flows, planning/reporting, and staff training/awareness. Scope covers the Parent Company, Widiba Group, and Fiduciaria companies. It is approved and overseen by the Board of Directors and aligned with GDPR, the Italian Privacy Code (as amended), and guidance from the Italian Data Protection Authority and EDPB. Publicly available on the Group website (Sustainability section).
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance: sets the organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for logical security via an Information Security Management System (ISMS), providing a medium/long‑term strategic direction to protect information assets. It applies to all Group companies, with local adoption via company resolutions. Governance is centralized in the Parent Company’s Information Security function, with implementation by Information Security and IT functions. It references internal and external standards, including ISO/IEC 2700x, and is available on the corporate intranet.
- The ISMS underpins both policies with a risk‑based approach: assessing all relevant risks and implementing preventive and protective measures to minimize them, ensuring adequate protection of personal data and company information throughout their lifecycle.

nodes.title: Privacy - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.1 Privacy
nodes.start_phrase: This section deals with privacy issues, with reference to the policies, processes and controls defined by the Group to ensure IT security and protect the personal data of customers and end users from unauthorised access and loss of data.
nodes.summary:
Privacy
This section deals with privacy issues, with reference to the policies, processes and controls defined by the Group to 
ensure IT security and protect the personal data of customers and end users from unauthorised access and loss of data.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.1.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: In the context of customer and end-user protection, privacy protection and IT security safeguards play a key role in ensuring that data and information, throughout their entire lifecycle, are adequately protected, in accordance with regulatory requirements on the protection of personal data and safeguarding of company assets.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Customer and end‑user privacy and IT security, ensuring protection of personal data and information assets throughout their lifecycle in line with regulatory requirements.

- Key policies:
  - Data Protection Policy: Defines privacy controls (privacy by design/by default), data subject rights management, records of processing, data breach management, roles/responsibilities, information flows, planning/reporting, and employee training. Scope: Parent Company, Widiba Group, Fiduciaria companies. Governance: Approved and overseen by the Board. Compliance: GDPR, Italian Privacy Code, guidance from the Italian DPA/EDPB. Availability: Group website (Sustainability section).
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance: Establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS), organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for logical security across all Group companies. Centralized governance by the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation with Information Security and IT. Aligns with ISO/IEC 2700x. Availability: Corporate intranet.

- ISMS approach and coverage:
  - Risk‑based management of security across ICT service lifecycle; integrated into all processes and channels across the Group.
  - Objectives: Confidentiality, integrity, availability, verifiability, accountability.
  - Activities: Define security architecture and requirements; incident management; fraud prevention; emergency communications; change management; monitoring, audit facilitation, and continuous improvement.
  - Staff awareness and training are central to effectiveness.

- Review cadence: Directive reviewed annually and updated at least every three years or upon significant changes (laws, standards, internal/outsourced processes, threat landscape, technologies, organization).

- Actions completed in 2022–2024:
  - Firewall configuration review to align with international frameworks, remove non‑compliant rules, and enforce updated standards.
  - “Zero password” initiative introducing passwordless customer authentication (e.g., push notifications, biometrics).

- Ongoing initiatives: Regular employee training programs on information security, with needs identified via the 3D approach model.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.1.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Parent Company, with the support and cooperation of all the corporate functions and Group companies, has established the Information Security Management System (ISMS), for areas under its responsibility: a set of organisational structures, processes, procedures and technological solutions adopted for the purpose of protecting the Group’s own information assets and the information that Customers and end users exchange with the Group.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and governance: The Group mandates comprehensive information security across the entire ICT service life cycle, all Group companies, and all forms of personal data, regardless of channel or data subject. The security directive is reviewed annually and updated at least every three years or upon significant regulatory, standards, process, threat, technology, or organizational changes.
- ISMS establishment: The Parent Company leads a Group-wide Information Security Management System covering structures, processes, procedures, and technologies to protect Group and customer information. It formalizes security requirements, defines security architecture, ensures confidentiality, integrity, availability, verifiability, and accountability, manages incidents/fraud/emergency comms/change, drives staff awareness and training, and enables monitoring, audits, and continuous improvement.
- 2022–2024 initiatives completed in 2024:
  - Firewall configuration review aligned with international frameworks, removing non-compliant rules and adding standards-based ones.
  - “Zero password” rollout to enable passwordless authentication (e.g., push notifications, biometrics) for customers and users.
  - Ongoing employee security awareness and training based on the Group’s 3D approach.
- 2024–2028 Information Security Strategic Plan and 2025 focus:
  - Complete projects launched in 2024, including actions from Cyber Resilience Stress Tests.
  - New initiatives to reinforce security processes and platforms.
  - Strengthen security safeguards: advanced data security and IAM, stronger perimeter defenses, improved detection and incident management, enhanced device controls.
  - Strengthen digital resilience: technological/organizational measures for operational resilience, stronger business continuity management, and more robust application/data availability infrastructure.
  - Transpose regulatory requirements: continuous alignment with supervisory expectations and findings; standardize and fortify systemic resilience.
  - Increase cybersecurity awareness: customer-focused training and periodic communications to elevate risk awareness and defense practices.
- Performance measurement: Quarterly assessment of IT security via a proprietary maturity framework, reviewing security posture and integrating new implementations/design changes.
- Freedom of expression and customer voice:
  - Policy commitment (Code of Ethics) to timely, thorough, and free complaint handling; clear guidance on filing/handling complaints and access to out-of-court resolution bodies.
  - Group Policy on managing complaints, ABF and ACF appeals emphasizes complaints as:
    - Essential to maintaining satisfactory customer relationships.
    - Tools to identify critical issues and improve product/service quality.
    - Safeguards for customer protection, fostering amicable resolutions and, if needed, informing positions for potential judicial proceedings.
- Stakeholder alignment: Targets are set considering key stakeholder interests as part of the Group’s stakeholder engagement process.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.1.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The main objectives in the area of information security have been defined in the Information Security Strategic Plan 2024-2028.
nodes.summary:
- Sets Information Security objectives within the 2024–2028 Strategic Plan; in 2025 the Bank will complete projects begun in 2024 (notably those stemming from Cyber Resilience Stress Tests) and launch new initiatives to bolster security processes and platforms.
- Planned cybersecurity initiatives:
  - Strengthen security safeguards: deploy advanced data security and identity & access management, reinforce perimeter defenses, enhance incident detection/response, and tighten corporate device controls.
  - Enhance digital resilience: implement tech/organizational measures for operational resilience, reinforce business continuity management, and improve infrastructure supporting application/data availability.
  - Ensure regulatory alignment: continuously adapt to supervisory requirements and findings to standardize and strengthen system resilience.
  - Raise cybersecurity awareness: deliver customer training and periodic communication campaigns on cyber risks and defenses.
- Incorporates stakeholder interests as identified in the Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Assesses IT security performance quarterly using a proprietary maturity framework reviewing the Group’s security posture and recent implementations.
- Addresses customer freedom of expression through robust complaint management:
  - Per the Code of Ethics, respond promptly and thoroughly to customer and consumer-association complaints via clear, timely communications; interactions are clear and free of charge.
  - Provide transparent information on complaint submission/handling and access to out-of-court dispute resolution bodies.
  - Group Policy on handling complaints, ABF and ACF appeals: complaint management is essential to customer relations, a tool to identify issues and improve service quality, and a safeguard to foster amicable resolutions or clarify positions prior to judicial proceedings.

nodes.title: Freedom of expression
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.2 Freedom of expression
nodes.start_phrase: Issues relating to the freedom of expression of customers, with particular reference to the processes of listening to customers and the submission of complaints by them, are dealt with in this paragraph.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024–2028 Information Security Strategic Plan and 2025 priorities. It details planned initiatives to: strengthen cybersecurity safeguards (advanced data security, identity and access management, perimeter defenses, incident detection/response, and device controls); enhance digital and operational resilience, including business continuity and infrastructure availability; ensure ongoing compliance with evolving supervisory and regulatory requirements; and increase customer cybersecurity awareness through training and communications. It notes stakeholder considerations in setting targets and a quarterly, proprietary maturity assessment of the Group’s security posture. A separate section addresses customer freedom of expression via complaints handling: the Group’s Code of Ethics and policies commit to timely, thorough, and free complaint management; clear guidance on filing and handling complaints and access to out-of-court resolution (ABF/ACF); and the use of complaints as a tool to strengthen customer relationships, identify and resolve issues, improve service quality, and conduct preliminary investigations before any judicial escalation.

nodes.title: Freedom of expression - Introduction
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.2 Freedom of expression
nodes.start_phrase: Issues relating to the freedom of expression of customers, with particular reference to the processes of listening to customers and the submission of complaints by them, are dealt with in this paragraph.
nodes.summary:
Freedom of expression
Issues relating to the freedom of expression of customers, with particular reference to the processes of listening to  
customers and the submission of complaints by them, are dealt with in this paragraph.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.2.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: As set out in the Code of Ethics, the Group is committed to responding to complaints aired by customers and their protection associations by using appropriate and timely communication systems.
nodes.summary:
- Information security strategy and objectives:
  - Framed by the Information Security Strategic Plan 2024–2028, with 2025 focused on completing 2024 initiatives (including those stemming from Cyber Resilience Stress Tests) and launching new projects to reinforce processes and platforms.
  - Key initiatives:
    - Strengthening security safeguards to enhance the Group’s cybersecurity posture: advanced data security and identity/access management, stronger perimeter defenses, improved incident detection/response, and tighter controls on corporate devices.
    - Strengthening digital resilience: measures to ensure operational resilience, reinforce business continuity management, and bolster infrastructure supporting application and data availability.
    - Transposing regulatory requirements: ongoing alignment with supervisory authorities’ expectations and findings to standardize and reinforce system resilience.
    - Increasing cybersecurity awareness: customer-focused training and periodic communication campaigns on cyber risks and defenses.
  - Performance measurement via a proprietary maturity framework reviewed quarterly, reflecting new implementations and the current security posture.
  - Stakeholder interests are considered through the Group’s Stakeholder Engagement process.

- Freedom of expression and customer complaints management:
  - Policy commitments (Code of Ethics and Group Policy on handling complaints, ABF and ACF appeals): timely, clear, and free-of-charge responses; transparent information on complaint procedures and access to out-of-court dispute resolution; complaints used to improve services and resolve disputes amicably, with preliminary investigation before judicial escalation.
  - Governance and scope: policy approved by the Parent Company’s Board of Directors; applies to the Bank and Group companies (Widiba, MPS Fiduciaria); aligned with relevant laws and regulations (e.g., Consolidated Law on Banking, Bank of Italy, Consob); publicly available via the Group website (Sustainability section).
  - Operational process for complaints: receipt, logging/take-over, preliminary investigation (gathering information and forming a settlement proposal), resolution (rejected/upheld/partially upheld), customer communication, and accounting.
  - Assessment criteria during handling: event reconstruction, marketing and customer information adequacy, compliance with internal rules and contracts, potential internal fraud, documentation completeness, commercial/credit considerations, inputs from relevant functions, established ABF/ACF and judicial guidelines, litigation and compliance risks, and proportionality of customer claims to actual issues or damages.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.2.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The operational procedures for handling complaints adopted by the Group outline the responsibilities assigned to the various corporate structures and define at least the following activities:
nodes.summary:
- Context and governance: Policies are defined with consideration of stakeholder interests and approved at Parent Company Board level, with clear scopes across Group entities and references to applicable laws and standards. Public availability is ensured via the Group website and intranet.

- Complaints management, ABF and ACF appeals and petitions:
  - Aims: provide prompt, clear, complete responses; reduce disputes; conduct preliminary investigations to define parties’ positions; gather feedback to identify operational criticalities and improvements.
  - Scope: Bank and Group companies (Widiba, MPS Fiduciaria).
  - Governance and compliance: approved by the Parent Company’s Board; aligned with the Consolidated Law on Banking, Bank of Italy provisions, and relevant Consob resolutions; accessible via the Sustainability section of the website.
  - Operational procedures: receipt, registration and intake, investigation, resolution (upheld/partially upheld/rejected), customer communication, and accounting.
  - Assessment criteria: event reconstruction, marketing and customer information quality, adherence to internal rules/contract terms, potential internal fraud, documentation completeness, commercial/customer relationship (including credit), inputs from consulted functions, ABF/ACF and court orientations, compliance and litigation risk, and congruity of customer claims.
  - Monitoring and objectives: no quantitative targets under “freedom of expression,” but ongoing quantitative and qualitative monitoring of processing times, outcomes of grievances, and arbitration decisions to enhance customer experience.

- Health and safety for customers and end users:
  - Focus: ensure products/services and on-site activities protect health and safety; prevent injuries and illnesses; foster a strong safety culture through information and training.
  - Safety Policy: central reference for risk assessment, objective-setting and review; commitment to prevention, continuous improvement, stakeholder communication, and compliance with legal and other requirements.
  - Scope and governance: applies to the Parent Company and all Group Companies; approved by the Parent Company’s Board; implemented under Top Management and Management responsibility.
  - Standards and availability: compliant with national/EU legislation and UNI ISO 45001; summary available on the corporate website and Suppliers Register; full access on the intranet; includes informing employees, suppliers, and customers about safety organization, emergency management, risks, and prevention/protection standards.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.2.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: In the area of “freedom of expression”, the Group has not planned to identify measurable quantitative targets.
nodes.summary:
- Customer experience and grievance oversight: In the “freedom of expression” area, the Group sets no quantitative targets but enforces policies and actions to ensure service quality and continuously improve customer experience. It conducts ongoing quantitative and qualitative monitoring of the Complaints and Mediation Department, tracking compliance with processing times, effectiveness, and outcomes of grievances and arbitration decisions (upheld/partially upheld/rejected; favourable/partially favourable/unfavourable).

- Health and safety focus: Protects the health and safety of customers and end users in relation to products and services, and within offices and branches, aiming to prevent injuries and illnesses. Emphasizes information, training, and building a broad “safety culture” across the workforce.

- Safety Policy framework: The occupational Health and Safety Policy guides risk assessment and the setting/review of objectives. Commitments include accident and illness prevention, continual improvement of H&S management and performance, communication of principles to stakeholders, and compliance with applicable legal and voluntary requirements.

- Scope and governance: Policy applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies. It is approved by the Parent Company’s Board of Directors, with implementation led by Top Management and company management.

- Standards and compliance: Implemented in line with national and EU workplace health and safety laws and aligned with UNI ISO 45001 (replacing OHSAS 18001 as of March 2021), which informs the company’s general management objectives.

- Stakeholder consideration: Policy content reflects interests identified through the Group’s Stakeholder Engagement process.

- Accessibility: A summary is available in the Sustainability section of the corporate website and the Suppliers Register; the policy is accessible to employees via the corporate intranet.

nodes.title: Health and safety
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.3 Health and safety
nodes.start_phrase: This section deals with issues related to the protection of the health and safety of customers and end users, i.e. the set of policies, measures and procedures adopted by the Group to ensure that the use of the products and services offered is in compliance with the protection of their health and safety and with reference to the activities carried out by the Group and within its Offices and Branches by preventing injuries and illnesses.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group’s approach to two areas: customer-related “freedom of expression” and health and safety. For freedom of expression, the Group sets no quantitative targets but ensures service quality and continuous customer-experience improvement by closely monitoring the Complaints and Mediation Department’s timeliness and effectiveness, tracking upheld/partially upheld/rejected grievances and arbitration outcomes. The health and safety section focuses on protecting customers and end users in the use of products/services and within offices and branches, emphasizing prevention of injuries and illnesses. It highlights training and information for employees to strengthen a safety culture, and a Group Safety Policy that guides risk assessment and the setting/review of objectives, committing to prevention, continuous improvement, stakeholder communication, and compliance with legal and other requirements. The policy applies to the parent and all Group companies, is approved by the Board of Directors, and is implemented under Top Management’s guidance. It aligns with national/EU laws and UNI ISO 45001 (replacing OHSAS 18001 from March 2021). Summaries are available on the corporate website (Sustainability section), the Suppliers Register, and the internal intranet, and the Group undertakes to inform employees, suppliers, and customers about safety governance, risks, and prevention standards, with stakeholder interests considered via the Stakeholder Engagement process.

nodes.heading: 3.4.2.3 Health and safety

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.3.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The protection of customers and end users is a primary objective for the Group, in order to guarantee the safety of its customers and contribute to a lasting relationship of trust.
nodes.summary:
- Freedom of expression/customer experience: No quantitative targets set; focus on ensuring service quality and continuous improvement via ongoing quantitative and qualitative monitoring of the Complaints and Mediation Department. Key metrics tracked include complaint processing times, outcomes of grievances (upheld/partially upheld/rejected), and arbitration decisions (favourable/partially favourable/unfavourable).

- Health and safety for customers and end users: Describes policies, measures, and procedures to ensure safe use of products and services and to prevent injuries/illnesses within offices and branches. Emphasizes workforce training, awareness, and a strong safety culture.

- Health and Safety Policy: Group-wide policy approved by the Board, led by Top Management, committing to accident/illness prevention, continuous improvement, stakeholder communication, and compliance with legal requirements. Implemented in line with national/EU laws and UNI ISO 45001. Policy information is accessible on the corporate website, suppliers register, and intranet.

- Actions: Deployment and progressive integration of an Occupational Health and Safety Management System across the Group; initiatives to spread safety culture, enhance cross-structure cooperation, and ensure traceability of responsibilities.

- Health and safety objectives: No measurable targets for consumer/end-user protection; effectiveness assured through external audits, improvement programs, and ongoing dialogue with Workers’ Safety Representatives to continuously monitor the OHS management system.

- Non-discrimination: Addresses equal access to products and services. The Rules on Inclusion formalize commitments to diversity, inclusion, equity, and respect (aligned with the Code of Ethics), guiding staff conduct toward customers with sensitivity and helpfulness, including those with disabilities or from foreign countries.

- Inclusion policy governance and standards: Applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies; implementation overseen by relevant corporate functions. Aligned with international frameworks (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, UN Declaration of Human Rights, UN 2030 Agenda, Principles for Responsible Banking). Available in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.

- Stakeholder engagement: Both safety and inclusion policies consider the interests of key stakeholders as outlined in the Group’s stakeholder engagement process.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.3.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In order to build solid technical and organisational safeguards in the banking sector, as regards corporate safety management, the Parent Company has taken every step necessary to develop an “Occupational Health and Safety Management System” and to gradually incorporate it into the other management systems implemented, as well as extending it to the other Group companies.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s actions to build and roll out an Occupational Health and Safety Management System across the banking Group, integrating it with other management systems.
- Highlights initiatives to spread a culture of workplace health and safety, improve cooperation among corporate structures, enhance business efficiency in safety, and ensure responsibility traceability.
- Notes that, while no measurable targets have been set for consumer/end-user health and safety, effectiveness is ensured through external audits, improvement programs, and ongoing dialogue with Workers’ Safety Representatives for continuous monitoring.
- Refers readers to the Own Workforce section for further details on corporate health and safety actions.
- Addresses non-discrimination for customers and end consumers, committing to inclusion, fairness, equality, respect, and attentive listening in customer interactions.
- Specifies staff conduct: adopting a respectful, helpful, and non-intrusive approach tailored to individuals’ specific needs (e.g., physical disabilities, foreign customers).
- Outlines the Rules on Inclusion policy: commitments to valuing diversity, inclusion, equity, and parity throughout employees’ business life cycle; applicable to the Parent Company and all Group companies.
- Explains implementation governance: companies must notify the relevant reporting Unit and the Professional Development, D&I, and Internal Communication functions; the policy aligns with recognized international principles (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, UN Declaration of Human Rights, 2030 Agenda, and Principles for Responsible Banking).
- States the policy’s public availability in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.3.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: In the area of consumer and end-user health and safety protection, the Group has so far not set any measurable targets.
nodes.summary:
- The Group is developing and integrating an Occupational Health and Safety Management System across the Parent Company and other Group companies, promoting a safety culture, cross-structure collaboration, efficiency in safety processes, and clear responsibility traceability.
- Continuous monitoring of occupational health and safety is ensured through external audits, improvement programs, and ongoing dialogue with Workers’ Safety Representatives; no measurable targets have yet been set for consumer/end-user health and safety.
- A commitment to non-discrimination ensures equitable access to products and services for all customers and end consumers.
- The Rules on Inclusion formalize commitments to diversity, inclusion, equity, and parity, guiding employee conduct to be respectful, attentive, and supportive—especially for people with disabilities and customers from foreign countries—without being intrusive.
- The Inclusion policy applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies, with implementation oversight involving Professional Development, D&I, and Internal Communication functions.
- The policy aligns with international frameworks (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, UN Declaration of Human Rights, 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and the Principles for Responsible Banking).
- Policy details are available in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website, and stakeholder engagement informs policy content.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.4.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Rules on Inclusion define the Group’s commitment to inclusion, fairness and equality, respect and listening, values that inspire the Group and are confirmed in the Code of Ethics.
nodes.summary:
- Occupational health and safety: The Parent Company is building and integrating an Occupational Health and Safety Management System across all Group companies, promoting a safety culture, clear responsibility traceability, and efficiency through interaction among corporate structures. Effectiveness is monitored via external audits, continuous improvement programs, and dialogue with Workers’ Safety Representatives. No measurable targets are set yet; further details are in the Own Workforce section.

- Non-discrimination and inclusion: The Group’s Rules on Inclusion commit to valuing diversity, equity, and inclusion in all phases of business, guiding staff to use respectful, supportive, and non-intrusive behavior with all customers, including those with disabilities and people from abroad. The policy applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies, is overseen by Professional Development, D&I and Internal Communication functions, aligns with international standards (EU Charter of Fundamental Rights, UN Declaration of Human Rights, 2030 Agenda/SDGs, Principles for Responsible Banking), and is publicly available on the corporate site.

- Inclusive communication standards: Corporate guidelines promote inclusive, accessible language; imagery reflecting gender, social, ethnic, and cultural diversity; clear, accessible channels; and events designed for balanced gender representation and venue accessibility. Compliance references include EU Directive 2006/54 and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. For “freedom of expression,” no quantitative targets are set; effectiveness is monitored via customer feedback and engagement processes.

- Digital access to products and services: The Group advances digitalisation to broaden products, services, and channels, improving access for less digitalised customers and enhancing overall customer experience. The Group Directive on ICT Governance and Strategy sets an IT strategy for operational excellence—stability, performance, quality, and satisfaction—enabling anytime, any-device banking through enabling technologies.

- IT governance and security policy: The Group Policy on Governance and definition of the IT strategy establishes the organisational model, principles, and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance to protect information assets and support the Digital Operational Resilience Strategy. It applies to the Bank and all Group companies, requires formal transposition notifications to relevant units (IT and Organisation), aligns with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013, and is available on the corporate intranet.

- Stakeholder engagement: Policy content is shaped with consideration of key stakeholders, as outlined in the Report’s Stakeholder Engagement section.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.4.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: Communication, a fundamental means of sharing corporate information, is developed with a language that helps to counteract the formation of stereotypes and prejudices and to eliminate discrimination towards customers and the general public.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on inclusive, non-discriminatory corporate communication to counter stereotypes and ensure equal treatment, in line with EU Directive 2006/54/EC and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.
- Communication guidelines include: audience-appropriate, inclusive and accessible language; imagery reflecting gender, social, ethnic, and cultural diversity; clear, accessible channels promoting inclusion and combating prejudice; inclusive event management with gender-balanced speakers/participants and accessible venues.
- In the “freedom of expression” area, no quantitative targets are set; effectiveness is monitored via feedback and consumer/end-user involvement processes.
- Access to products and services: ongoing digitalization to broaden products, services, and channels; improve inclusivity for less digitalized stakeholders; and enhance overall customer experience.
- ICT governance and strategy aim for operational excellence (stability, performance, quality, satisfaction) and a bank-customer model enabling access anytime, from any device, leveraging technologies to provide distinctive service and anticipate needs; stakeholder interests are integrated through formal engagement processes.
- Group Policy on IT governance and strategy: establishes the organizational model and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance, protects information assets, and guides medium/long-term Digital Operational Resilience Strategy; applies to the Bank and all Group companies; implementation involves corporate reporting units, IT, and the Organization Area; aligned with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013; available to employees on the corporate intranet.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.4.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: In the area of “freedom of expression”, the Group has not planned to identify measurable quantitative targets.

Peer-to-peer communication is promoted to ensure equal representation, listening, and treatment.

- In the “freedom of expression” area, no quantitative targets are set; effectiveness is monitored through feedback collection and consumer/end-user involvement processes.
- Access to products and services: continued digitalization of customer interactions to expand products, services and channels; improve access for less digitally skilled users; and deliver a seamless, satisfying, anytime/any-device customer experience. Stakeholder interests inform policy design.
- ICT governance and strategy: a Group Policy defines the organizational model and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance to protect information assets and guide medium/long-term Digital Operational Resilience objectives, targeting operational excellence (stability, performance, quality, satisfaction).
- Scope and compliance: policy applies to the Bank and all Group companies, with responsibilities assigned to corporate reporting units, IT, and the Organisation Area; implemented in line with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013. The policy is available to all employees on the corporate intranet.

nodes.title: Access to products and services in terms of digitalisation of supply
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.5 Access to products and services in terms of digitalisation of supply
nodes.start_phrase: This section covers the issues of access to products and services with regard to customers and end users in terms of offering digitalised products and services are covered in this section.

- In the “freedom of expression” area, no quantitative targets are set; effectiveness is monitored through feedback collection and consumer/end-user involvement processes.
- Access to products and services: ongoing digitization of customer interactions to expand offerings and channels, enhance access for less digitally experienced stakeholders, and deliver a smoother, omnichannel, any-time/any-device customer experience.
- ICT governance and strategy: a Group Directive defines an IT strategy focused on operational excellence (stability, performance, quality, user satisfaction) and a relationship model enabling customers to reach the bank anytime from any device, using enabling technologies to anticipate needs; stakeholder interests are incorporated via the Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Group Policy on Governance and definition of the IT strategy (Logical Security Governance) sets the organizational model, principles, and responsibilities to protect information assets and support the Digital Operational Resilience Strategy; applies to the Bank and all Group companies; requires notification to corporate reporting units, IT, and the Organization Area; implemented in line with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013; available to employees on the corporate intranet.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.5.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group, operating in a context of continuous evolution and transformation, continues its initiative to digitalise customer interactions by expanding the range of products, services and access channels offered and improving access to banking services and products for less digitalised stakeholder categories, ensuring a smoother and more satisfying experience for all customers, regardless of their degree of familiarity with digital technologies, with the ultimate aim of optimising the customer experience.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on inclusive, non-discriminatory corporate communication aligned with EU Directive 2006/54/EC and the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Guidelines cover inclusive language, diverse and respectful imagery, clear and accessible channels, and event organization with gender balance and accessible venues. Effectiveness is monitored via feedback and consumer involvement; no quantitative targets set under “freedom of expression.”

- Strategy to improve access to products and services through digitalization, ensuring a smooth experience for all customers, including less digitally skilled stakeholders. The Group Directive on ICT Governance and Strategy defines an IT strategy focused on operational excellence, customer reach “anytime, any device,” and protection of information assets, aligned with Bank of Italy Circular 285/2013. Policy applies across the Group and is available on the corporate intranet.

- Actions to enhance alternative distribution channels and inclusion:
  - ATM and e-money: Ongoing ATM migration (completion by 2025) to boost security and compatibility; extended audio guide functionality for visually impaired users across debit/credit cards; expansion of Apple Pay and Google Pay to Parent Company and Widiba customers.
  - Internet banking: Continued optimization of the multi-channel platform, enhanced protection tools, expanded online services, improved branch–online integration, and rollout of paperless processes to save time and reduce paper use. Commitment to accessibility with assistive technologies, periodic usability checks, and support from specialized providers/associations. Open banking enhancements planned (payment cancellation, bulk payments) and efforts to reduce friction in third-party payment authorizations.

- Governance and oversight: While no measurable quantitative targets are set for digital access, effectiveness is monitored by the Body with Strategic Supervision Function (OFSS), which annually assesses the adequacy, functionality, and reliability of the information system and services.

nodes.summary:

  - Establishing processes and rules to protect customers in line with regulatory requirements.
  - Setting commercial marketing plans (strategy, objectives, pricing, products, promotions, communications).
  - Overseeing customer relationship management.
- Product design, development, and marketing aligned with customer needs and legal standards on transparency and fairness to prevent unfair practices.
- Code of Ethics ensures procedures to offer suitable products/services and provide clear, comprehensive pre-contractual information for informed choices.
- Special attention to vulnerable customers: promoting access to banking, informed credit use, and prevention of over-indebtedness.
- Creation of sustainable, inclusive products and services addressing basic financial needs to support social welfare.
- Adherence to Sustainability and ESG Guideline: respect for human rights, fairness and inclusion, labor standards (including child and forced labor), health and safety, and good governance.
- Exclusion and enhanced due diligence policies for high social impact sectors under the Sustainability and ESG Directive, particularly:
  - Arms sector: exclusion of financing/brokering related to arms per Law 185/90, with limited support only for transactions authorized by relevant authorities and compliant with laws.
  - Prohibition on relationships and transactions involving controversial/banned weapons (nuclear, biological, chemical, cluster bombs, depleted uranium, landmines).
  - No support for transactions linked to sanctioned/embargoed countries, active conflicts, or governments responsible for serious human rights abuses.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: Meeting customer needs is a fundamental condition for the Group in conducting its business activities and an inescapable requirement in maintaining and improving a relationship of trust with customers.
nodes.summary:
- Emphasis on responsible business practices centered on transparent, continuous, and non-discriminatory customer communications, meeting customer needs, and maintaining trust.
- Strong focus on social inclusion: facilitating access to banking, promoting informed credit use, preventing over-indebtedness, and tailoring sustainable products for vulnerable customers and broader society.
- ESG and human rights commitments embedded in the Sustainability and ESG Guideline, including exclusion and enhanced due diligence for high social impact sectors:
  - Armaments: exclusions aligned with Law 185/90 and bans on controversial weapons; no dealings with sanctioned/embargoed countries or severe human rights violators.
  - Tobacco: due diligence based on corruption/media risk, state ownership, and tobacco-derived revenues (including pharmaceutical tobacco).
  - Gambling: extended due diligence for online platforms, gambling halls, machinery, and marketing.
- Robust policy framework with defined scopes, Board-level approvals, Compliance pre-validation, and alignment with external regulations/standards (e.g., GDPR, MiFID II, EBA Guidelines, IDD, IVASS, EBA/EIOPA rules):
  - Group Policy on Commercial Policies.
  - Group Products Policy (conception, acquisition, control; Board and risk committee involvement).
  - Rules for ESG qualification of investment products to prevent greenwashing (SFDR compliance).
  - Governance and Control of Customer Banking Products (end-to-end product lifecycle, target market, RAF impact, delisting).
  - Governance and Control of Customer Financial Products (MiFID II product governance).
  - Distribution of Protection Insurance Products and Supplementary Pension Schemes (IDD/IVASS-aligned).
  - Sustainability and ESG Policy (community impact: digital inclusion, disaster support, regional and female entrepreneurship, anti-usury).
- Governance, oversight, and review cadence: strategic policies reviewed at least triennially; risk policies annually; involvement of the Board, Risk Management Committee, Risk & Sustainability Committee, and the Investment and Product Steering Committee.
- Product design actions grounded in customer intelligence and regulatory/sustainability compliance: assessing suitability/appropriateness, pricing within usury rules, precise target market definition, and system/process impact analysis.
- Social inclusion products and initiatives:
  - MPS Mio Futuro Account and Free Savings Service for under-18s (financial inclusion and education under parental oversight).
  - First Home Fund–guaranteed mortgages via Consap for primary residences, including young couples, single parents with minors, low-income tenants, and under-35s with non-standard contracts.
  - Participation in SACE Garanzia Futuro to finance company growth, infrastructure, supply chains, communities, and female entrepreneurship.
  - Sustainability Linked Loans with ESG covenants tied to pricing; 27 loans with social covenants totaling EUR 188.5 million in 2024.
  - Anti-usury financing via partnerships (e.g., Fondazione Toscana per la prevenzione dell’usura Onlus, Adiconsum), totaling about EUR 1.7 million in 2024.
- Attention to stakeholder interests through formal engagement processes; policy availability on the corporate intranet and selected overviews on the corporate website.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 3.4.2.6.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the wider process of designing its products and services, the Group ensures that product characteristics are determined taking into account the findings of customer intelligence analyses.
nodes.summary:
- The Group embeds customer intelligence in product and service design, using behavioral segmentation, MiFID profiles, portfolio analyses, demand assessment, and feedback from customer interactions.
- Product governance ensures: assessment of investment product risk for suitability/appropriateness; pricing aligned with regulations (including anti-usury) and internal policies; clear target-customer definitions; adherence to Group directives on product governance and target market; and compliance with sustainability requirements across risk, business effectiveness, tools/processes, IT impacts, and regulations.
- Social inclusion offerings:
  - MPS Mio Futuro Account and Free Savings Service: launched 16 Dec 2024, a bundled current account for under-18s promoting financial inclusion and savings education under parental oversight.
  - First Home Fund–guaranteed mortgages (Consap): continued in 2024, up to 100% LTV for main-home purchase/renovation, targeting eligible customers including young couples (one ≤35), single parents with minors, tenants of low-income housing associations, and under-35s with non-standard contracts.
  - SACE Garanzia Futuro: joined in 2024 to finance company growth in Italy and abroad, infrastructure, supply chains, local communities, and female entrepreneurship.
  - Sustainability Linked Loans: made available in 2024, linking ESG KPIs (social, environmental, governance) to improved pricing; 27 loans with social covenants disbursed, totaling EUR 188.5 million.
  - Anti-usury financing: dedicated funding with pilot agreements (Fondazione Toscana per la prevenzione dell’usura Onlus, Adiconsum); about EUR 1.7 million disbursed in 2024.

- Supports regional development and entrepreneurship:

- Provides disaster-relief finance:

nodes.title: Consumer and end-user involvement processes
nodes.heading: 3.4.3 Consumer and end-user involvement processes
nodes.start_phrase: The management of material impacts entails that the Group should have its own employee engagement processes in place to take their views into account.
nodes.summary:
- Customer-centric commitment: The Group’s Code of Ethics prioritizes customer satisfaction through transparency, innovation, and personalization, placing customers at the center of commercial strategies and monitoring satisfaction and loyalty targets.
- Active listening and omnichannel engagement: Continuous collection of feedback and proposals from customers and stakeholders; delivery of a personalized, accessible banking experience via an omnichannel model combining digital tools and qualified assistance.
- Contact Centre structure:
  - Network Hub: Commercial/specialist assistance via MIA Chatbot (handles 44% of requests autonomously) and human consultants managing the remaining 56% (70% via chat, 30% via phone).
  - Customer Hub: Information, transaction assistance, and outbound consulting through phone, email, webform, certified email, and call-back; about 420,000 calls and 70,000 non-call enquiries annually.
- Digital Banking feedback: App ratings (1–5 stars) on Apple and Google stores; Level II Customer Service monitors and replies using business-approved templates validated by Communications, escalating to tailored responses when needed; evaluations drive app and UX improvements.
- Banca Widiba specifics: Continuous customer rating and comment system (1–5 scores with suggestions); 2024 average of ~16,000 comments/month, 97.2% positive; feedback systematically analyzed to enhance offerings and service quality.
- Negative impact remediation and dispute channels: Structured, uniform dispute management across the Group (including Widiba) covering:
  - Complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decree 28/2010), assisted negotiation (Legislative Decree 132/2014).
  - Access to Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) and Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF) for unresolved or late-handled issues.
- Consumer channels and definitions:
  - Applications: Written requests/reports of logistical, relational, or commercial nature from customers or non-customers.
  - Complaints: Verbal objections about services or contractual/pre-contractual matters, relational issues with staff, objections via web/social, and media/journalist inquiries on products/services or inefficiencies.
- Complaints management process:
  - Transparency and accessibility via website, contract documents, branches/specialist centers.
  - Submission methods: In-branch delivery, postal mail, online form, email/certified email to the Complaints Function.
  - Operational oversight by the Complaints and Mediation Department.
  - Procedure steps: Receipt and transmission; registration in the GRB application; investigation with branches or competent functions; independent decision-making; accounting and settlement when customer reimbursement is due.

nodes.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.heading: 3.4.4 Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the processes to manage material negative impacts on customers and end users, the Group has processes in place to remedy and manage concerns expressed by customers.
nodes.summary:
- Section outlines the Group’s processes for remediating negative customer impacts and the channels available for consumers and end-users to raise concerns, within a structured, uniform dispute management framework tailored to each business (including Banca Widiba).
- Recognized dispute avenues include complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decree 28/2010), assisted negotiation (Legislative Decree 132/2014), and escalation to the Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) for banking/financial services and the Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF) for investment services and collective asset management when complaints are unresolved or overdue.
- Consumer communication types are distinguished as:
  - Applications: written requests or reports of a logistical, relational, or commercial nature from customers or non-customers.
  - Complaints: verbal objections related to bank services or contractual/pre-contractual relations; verbal issues concerning staff conduct; objections via web/social channels about products/services; and media/journalist requests for clarification or remarks.
- The Group promotes transparent and accessible grievance channels via its website, contractual documentation, and direct communications at branches and specialist centres.
- Submission channels include in-person delivery at branches/specialised centres, postal mail, an online form on the institutional website, standard email, and certified email to the Complaints Function.
- Operational oversight of complaints, ABF/ACF appeals, mediation, and assisted negotiations is centralized in the Complaints and Mediation Department.
- Complaint handling process steps: receipt and forwarding to the department; registration in the Complaints Management application (GRB); investigation with the relevant branch or specialist function; independent decision-making; and accounting/settlement where compensation to the customer is due.

nodes.title: Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns - Introduction

nodes.heading: 3.4.4 Processes to remediate negative impacts and channels for consumers and end-users to raise concerns
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the processes to manage material negative impacts on customers and end users, the Group has processes in place to remedy and manage concerns expressed by customers.
nodes.summary: Overview of Group-wide processes to remediate negative impacts and handle customer/end-user concerns through a structured, uniform dispute management framework across businesses (including Banca Widiba). Dispute mechanisms include complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation under Legislative Decree 28/2010, assisted negotiation under Legislative Decree 132/2014, and escalation—after unsuccessful or untimely responses—to the Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) for banking/financial product and service disputes and the Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF) for obligations of diligence, fairness, information, and transparency in investment services and collective asset management. Channels include formalised management of written applications from customers and non-customers, and complaints submitted verbally, via web or social media, or by journalists/media, covering service/contract matters (including pre-contractual), relational issues with staff, product/service objections, and requests for clarification.

nodes.title: Complaints management
nodes.heading: 3.4.4.1 Complaints management
nodes.start_phrase: The Group seeks maximum transparency and accessibility of grievance channels, actively informing consumers of their existence through its institutional website, contractual documentation and direct communication at branches and specialist centres.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: How the Group manages, remediates, and tracks customer and end‑user concerns and negative impacts, within its sustainability and governance framework.

- Dispute pathways: Internal grievance handling and external resolution routes, including complaints to Supervisory Authorities, mediation (Legislative Decrees 28/2010 and 132/2014), and recourse to the Financial Banking Arbitrator (ABF) and Financial Disputes Arbitrator (ACF).

- Channels and definitions: Formalized processes for:
  - Applications/requests from customers and non‑customers (mainly logistical/relational/commercial).
  - Complaints, including verbal objections about services or pre‑contractual issues, relational issues with staff, web/social media objections, and media/journalist requests.

- Accessibility of grievance channels: Multiple submission methods—branch delivery, mail, online form, and email/PEC—communicated via website, contracts, and in‑branch notices.

- Governance and process ownership: The Complaints and Mediation Department oversees end‑to‑end monitoring, including ABF/ACF appeals, mediation, and assisted negotiation; operates independently from marketing to avoid conflicts of interest.

- Complaint handling workflow: Receipt, registration in dedicated systems (GRB/CRM), investigation with business support, independent decision‑making, and settlement/accounting when due; multi‑level (I/II/III) escalation with standardized ticket taxonomy and defined outcome categories (sustained/partially accepted/not sustained) and customer feedback steps.

- Regulatory response timeframes: Maximum times to reply—60 days (banking/financial/investment services), 45 days (insurance brokerage), 30 days for CIS Code of Conduct matters (with specific GDPR‑based exceptions/possible extensions), and 15 business days (payment services).

- Confidentiality and non‑retaliation: Protection for individuals using complaint mechanisms; commitment to transparency, fairness, and clear guidance so customers can exercise their rights.

- Monitoring and reporting: Quantitative/qualitative tracking of processing times, upheld/partially upheld/rejected rates, and ABF/ACF outcomes; annual public report on complaint handling per Bank of Italy provisions; issues and risks escalated to relevant functions, including Compliance and Risk.

- Stakeholder involvement: No direct customer involvement in procedure design/review; effectiveness gauged via indicators such as repeat complaints and ABF/ACF filings, alongside internal KPIs.

- Banca Widiba specifics: Customer Care via Mediacenter and advisors; formal complaint submission by mail/email/advisor with required identification and case details; a “Complaints Register” aligning with Group standards using ABI classification to census and monitor all complaints, including verbal, web/social, and media‑initiated objections.

- Human rights and customer protection: Commitment to trust, transparency, fairness, integrity, and respect; adherence to internal rules, external codes/agreements, contracts, and applicable laws/regulations across all geographies and activities.

nodes.title: Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
nodes.heading: 3.4.5 Protecting the human rights of consumers and end users
nodes.start_phrase: In line with the significance identified in the Double Materiality Analysis of issues related to consumers and end users, the Group is committed to developing relationships of trust and mutual and lasting satisfaction with customers, marked by va- lues of transparency and fairness.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s complaints and mediation framework, noting no formal stakeholder involvement in procedure design or review, but systematic tracking of effectiveness via customer complaints, appeals (ABF/ACF), complaint reiterations, and outcomes as proxies for satisfaction.
- Details quantitative and qualitative monitoring of the Complaints and Mediation Department, including adherence to processing times and effectiveness metrics (upheld/partially upheld/rejected complaints, and arbitration decisions by outcome).
- Confirms annual public reporting on complaint handling in line with the Bank of Italy’s Supervisory Provisions on transparency and fairness, and highlights the department’s organizational independence from marketing to avoid conflicts of interest.
- Outlines Banca Widiba’s specific grievance-handling pathway: initial recourse to Customer Care via Mediacenter or the customer’s advisor; if unresolved, formal written complaints via mail, email (reclami@widipec.it), or delivery through the advisor, with required contents (identification, relationship details, contact, issue description, supporting documents).
- Introduces the “Complaints Register” to standardize complaint management with Group procedures, enable early resolution, classify cases per ABI standards, and ensure ongoing monitoring.
- Defines what constitutes a complaint, including verbal objections on services/contractual relations, written objections via web channels (chat, social media), and clarification requests from journalists/newspapers.
- Sets out commitments to protect the human rights of consumers and end users: transparency, fairness, compliance with internal/external rules and laws, counterparty due diligence to avoid links to illegal or harmful activities, and adherence to the UN Global Compact and UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking.
- Specifies minimum sustainability criteria and exclusions: no financing where evidence of human rights or labor violations, fraud, money laundering, corruption, terrorism financing, or involvement with controversial/internationally banned weapons; no support for transactions involving sanctioned/embargoed countries, armed conflict contexts, or governments committing serious human rights violations.
- Introduces Governance Information – Business Conduct (ESRS G1): scope includes impacts, risks, opportunities; preventive/mitigative policies and actions; targets and metrics to assess effectiveness.
- Highlights governance mechanisms: a Board-approved Code of Ethics integrated with the 231 Compliance Programme; dissemination to subsidiaries/partners; monitoring via internal controls; and the presence on governing bodies of members with specialized expertise in business conduct and Legislative Decree 231/2001.

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: Material Group policies on corporate culture include the Group’s Code of Ethics and the Group Policy on Governance Security Logic.
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: G1 Conduct of Enterprises in the Sustainability Report, covering corporate culture, whistleblower protection, anti- and active/passive corruption (with links to cybersecurity), and connections to AML/CFT.
- Materiality highlights:
  - Negative impacts: potential lack of adequate cybersecurity safeguards for Group IT and network systems.
  - Risks: reputational risk from inadequate cybersecurity and potential breaches of customer privacy/information by employees.
  - Opportunities: stronger stakeholder confidence through effective whistleblower protection.
  - Scope: considerations span own operations and the upstream/downstream value chain; outcomes addressed for both impact and financial materiality.
- Corporate culture policies:
  - Code of Ethics: sets principles, values, and conduct rules for internal and external relations, supports sustainability objectives, and aligns Group goals with societal interests.
  - Governance and oversight: Code is part of Model 231, approved by the Board; compliance and internal audit manage confidential reporting, assessment, and escalation to corporate bodies and the 231 Supervisory Board.
  - Applicability and standards: applies Group-wide across geographies and stakeholders; aligned with internal rules, external codes/agreements, and legal/regulatory obligations; publicly available on the corporate website.
- Cybersecurity framework:
  - Strategic stance: IT security as a core cultural pillar to ensure resilience, robustness, and responsiveness.
  - Policy/Directive on Logical Security Governance: establishes the Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect information across its lifecycle; defines organizational model, principles, roles, and long-term direction.
  - Governance model: centralized at the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implemented by Group companies via top-management resolutions; supported by Information Security and IT functions.
  - Standards and transparency: ISMS managed in line with internal/external standards, notably ISO/IEC 2700x series; overview available on the corporate website.
- The section introduces the Group’s Policies, Actions, and Targets related to whistleblower protection, prevention of corruption, and cybersecurity safeguards.

nodes.title: Cybersecurity
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.2 Cybersecurity
nodes.start_phrase: IT security is one of the fundamental pillars of the Group’s culture, which is committed to ensuring the resilience, robustness and responsiveness of its digital system.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: Governance policies and actions within the Group’s Sustainability Reporting, centered on the Code of Ethics and Cybersecurity/Logical Security Governance, plus related training and implementation measures.
- Code of Ethics:
  - Objectives: define standards of good conduct; inform employees of required behavior; support implementation of Group sustainability policies; align Group objectives with civil society interests.
  - Scope: addressed to the entire corporate population across all geographies and value chain stages; stated as applicable to all customers.
  - Governance and validation: approved by the Bank’s Board of Directors; implementation ensured via the internal control system.
  - Commitments and references: adherence to internal rules and procedures; external codes and agreements (including international); contractual, legal, and regulatory obligations in each operating context.
  - Availability: published in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Cybersecurity and Logical Security Governance:
  - IT security positioned as a fundamental pillar to ensure resilience, robustness, and responsiveness of digital systems.
  - Group Directive/Policy defines and implements an Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect data and information across their lifecycle and all company activities.
  - Group Policy on Logical Security Governance:
    - Defines organizational model, principles, and responsibilities for Logical Security Governance and sets a medium/long-term strategic direction.
    - Scope: applies to the Parent Company and all Group companies.
    - Validation and implementation: adopted by Group companies through top management resolutions, with adaptation to company size/characteristics; governance centralized in the Parent Company’s Information Security function; implementation guided by Information Security and IT functions.
    - Standards: managed in line with internal rules and external standards, notably ISO/IEC 2700x series.
    - Availability: overview available in the Sustainability section of the corporate website.
- Actions and training:
  - Mandatory, structured compliance training for all employees, updated with regulatory/procedural changes; enrollment campaigns, monthly monitoring, reminders; courses require passing a final test.
  - Multidimensional training model to strengthen risk culture, integrated with Model 231/01, assigning relevance levels to material topics.
  - ISMS established with cooperation across all corporate structures and Group companies to protect Group and customer information assets; additional cybersecurity actions referenced under “Privacy” in the Consumers and End Users chapter.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.3 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: In order to guarantee and ensure that all employees are aware of and understand the values and principles underpinning the Group’s activities, a structured training model is in place which sets out that all employees complete their assigned courses.
nodes.summary:
- Mandatory, structured training program to ensure all employees understand the Group’s values, principles, and risk culture, with courses updated by Compliance after regulatory/procedural changes, monitored monthly, and closed by a mandatory final test.
- Multidimensional training model integrated with Model 231/01, identifying material topics and assigning relevance levels to strengthen risk culture.
- Establishment of an Information Security Management System (ISMS) to protect Group and customer information, with further cybersecurity actions referenced under the Privacy section.
- 2024 training coverage shows near-universal participation (about 99–100%) in both 231-relevant and anti-corruption courses across employees, executives, middle managers, CEOs/C-levels, and major functions, with geographic breakdowns; 16,433 employees trained on 231 topics and 16,159 on anti-corruption.
- Internal control system ensures compliance with the Code of Ethics; corporate functions manage operational risks including non-compliance, while Control Functions and Internal Audit verify operations, risk evolution, and assess the adequacy and reliability of the internal control system.
- Clear information security governance with defined roles, responsibilities, and separation of duties to prevent overlap.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 4.1.3.4 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The internal control system, which is a fundamental element of the overall and ordinary governance system of the Group, ensures compliance with the Code of Ethics.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on 2024 training coverage across the Group on “231-relevant” compliance topics and anti-corruption, showing near-universal participation (generally 99–100%).
- Headline figures: 16,433 Group employees trained on 231-relevant topics (99%); 16,159 trained on anti-corruption (99%).
- Detailed breakdowns by role and geography:
  - Executives, CEOs and direct reports, middle managers, and employees, with regional splits (Northeast, Northwest, South Central, Islands) all at 99–100% coverage.
  - Function-specific participation and coverage for key C-level areas (Audit, Compliance, Finance, HR, Lending, Operations, Risk, Safety & Security, Legal) and Commercial divisions (Enterprises & Private, Retail, Large Corporate & Investment Banking), with most at 99–100% and a noted 97% for HR.
- Governance objectives: the internal control system underpins Code of Ethics compliance; each function manages and monitors risks, including non-compliance risks.
- Control Functions and Internal Audit: verify regular operations, track risk evolution, and assess the adequacy, functionality, and reliability of the organizational and internal control system.
- Information security: defined roles and responsibilities to ensure separation of duties; an ISMS with security frameworks and indicators for guidance, control, and monitoring; active coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Whistleblower protection: a formal internal reporting system and Group Directive enable employees and qualified external parties to report fraud, business irregularities, and violations of banking rules and EU law; employees are expected to uphold high ethical standards and report concerns.
- Policy specifics:
  - Scope: all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria).
  - Oversight: Board of Directors approves the internal reporting system; Board of Statutory Auditors supervises it.
  - Compliance references: Directive 2013/36/EU, Italian Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU.
  - Availability: policy accessible in the Sustainability section of the Group’s corporate website.

nodes.title: Protection of whistleblowers - Introduction
nodes.heading: 4.1.4 Protection of whistleblowers

Protection of whistleblowers
