nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.4.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: With regard to reports of violations received through the Whistleblowing channel, the Group has set up an internal system, defi- ning a procedure for the management of reports that employees and qualified external parties may make in relation to events of fraud, as well as irregularities in the conduct of business or violations of the rules governing banking activity and of European Union law.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the Group’s Information Security Management System (ISMS), which sets security frameworks and indicators to guide, control and monitor protection measures, and maintains ongoing coordination with authorities and industry associations for alignment and information sharing.
- Details the whistleblower protection framework, governed by the Group Directive on Internal Violation Reporting Systems, emphasizing ethical conduct, stakeholder considerations, and clear procedures for reporting violations of laws, regulations, internal rules, and EU law.
- Outlines the Group Policy on the management of whistleblowing systems: applies to all personnel of the Parent Company and Group companies (including Banca Widiba and Monte Paschi Fiduciaria); implementation notifications to designated corporate functions; strategic oversight by the Board of Directors and system-wide supervision by the Board of Statutory Auditors; compliance with Directive 2013/36/EU, Legislative Decree 72/2015, Bank of Italy Circular 285 (11th and 34th updates), and Directive 2019/1937/EU; policy available on the corporate website.
- Specifies reporting channels and eligibility: a dedicated internet-accessible IT platform and a telephone line; reporters can include employees, suppliers, consultants, former employees, candidates, shareholders, and persons with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Explains case handling: the Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports; acknowledges receipt within 7 days and provides feedback within 3 months; produces Special Investigation Reports and, where responsibilities are found, follows publication requirements.
- Affirms protections: confidentiality of whistleblowers and reported individuals, protection against retaliation or discrimination for good-faith reports, and penalties for breaches of confidentiality, retaliatory acts, or obstruction.
- Clarifies governance and objectives: the Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the entire system; a Head of Internal Reporting Systems (within Internal Audit) ensures process integrity and reports annually to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management; no quantitative targets set.
- Introduces the anti-corruption framework addressing active and passive corruption and the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing: internal procedures and conduct guidelines for all staff; a rule document providing prevention guidelines that complement the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures for signatory powers, expenditure cycle, and supplier relations.
- Notes the scope of reportable matters includes administrative, accounting, tax, AML/CFT, market abuse, investment services irregularities, and data privacy violations.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 4.1.4.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: Through the dedicated IT platform, which can also be accessed via the internet by “qualified external persons”, or orally via a dedicated telephone service, staff and qualified external persons can report negligent, unlawful, irregular or improper cir- cumstances and conduct relating to their work - which they suspect or have become aware of in the course of their duties.
nodes.summary: The excerpt outlines the Group’s whistleblowing framework and anti-corruption governance. It describes a dedicated IT and phone reporting system accessible to employees and qualified external parties (including suppliers, consultants, former and prospective staff, shareholders, and individuals with administrative, management, or control roles) to report suspected negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct. Reportable matters include administrative and accounting/tax irregularities, AML/CTF violations, market abuse, investment service irregularities, and data privacy breaches. The Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, acknowledges receipt within seven days, provides follow-up within three months, and issues Special Investigation Reports, including publication when required. The Group guarantees confidentiality and protects whistleblowers from retaliation or discrimination, with penalties for breaches or obstruction. Oversight is provided by the Board of Statutory Auditors, while the Head of Internal Reporting Systems ensures process integrity and reports annually to key governance bodies; no quantitative targets are set. The section also covers active and passive corruption, including AML/CTF, and details policies promoting transparency, accountability, and integrity through anti-corruption procedures and a guideline document that complements the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relationships.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 4.1.4.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: The supervisory role over the entire system is guaranteed by the Board of Statutory Auditors of the Parent Company.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing framework: Accessible IT platform and dedicated phone line for employees and qualified external parties to report negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct related to work.
- Eligible reporters: Employees; suppliers, contractors, consultants; former staff (information gained during employment); job candidates (information from selection process); shareholders; individuals with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Reportable issues include: Administrative, accounting, and tax irregularities; violations related to anti–money laundering and counter–terrorist financing; market abuse (insider trading, manipulation); irregularities in investment services; data privacy violations.
- Investigation process: Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, confirms receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up within 3 months; prepares Special Investigation Reports and discloses per applicable standards when responsibilities are found.
- Protections: Strict confidentiality for whistleblowers and reported persons; prohibition of retaliation or discriminatory actions; penalties for breaching confidentiality, retaliation, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and oversight: Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the system; Head of Internal Reporting Systems (within Internal Audit) ensures proper operation and reports annually to key governance bodies (Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director overseeing internal control and risk management); no quantitative targets set.
- Anti-corruption and financial crime: Coverage of active and passive corruption, money laundering, and terrorist financing.
- Policies and controls: Group promotes transparency, accountability, and integrity; has issued a rule document with guidelines for preventing corruption, complementing the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relationships, alongside staff procedures and training.

nodes.title: Active and passive corruption
nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Active and passive corruption
nodes.start_phrase: This paragraph covers active and passive corruption issues, including the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing, are covered in this paragraph.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing system and channels: dedicated IT platform (also for qualified external persons) and a telephone line for reporting negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct encountered in work contexts.
- Eligible reporters: internal personnel and qualified external parties, including suppliers, self-employed workers, freelancers/consultants, former employees (for information acquired during employment), job candidates (for information acquired during selection), shareholders, and individuals with administrative, management, or control roles.
- Scope of reports: includes administrative, accounting and tax irregularities, AML/CFT violations, market abuse (insider trading, manipulation), irregularities in investment services, and data privacy breaches.
- Handling of reports: the Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives reports, conducts preliminary checks and investigations, acknowledges receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up feedback within 3 months.
- Outcomes and documentation: Special Investigation Reports summarize findings; if employee responsibilities are identified, reports are prepared and published per applicable standards.
- Whistleblower protections: safeguards against retaliation, discrimination, or unfair treatment; confidentiality of the report and personal data is ensured; penalties apply for breaching confidentiality, retaliating, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and oversight: Board of Statutory Auditors oversees the system; a Head of Internal Reporting Systems (in Internal Audit) ensures proper operation and annually reports to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management. No quantitative targets are set for whistleblower protection.
- Anti-corruption framework: addresses active and passive corruption, including AML and counter-terrorist financing; promotes transparency, accountability, and integrity in dealings with public administrations and external staff.
- Policies and controls: a rule document provides guidelines for preventing corruptive events, complementing the Group’s anti-corruption policy through the Code of Ethics, Model 231, and procedures governing signatory powers, the expenditure cycle, and supplier relations; staff receive internal anti-corruption procedures and training.

nodes.heading: 4.1.5 Active and passive corruption
nodes.start_phrase: This paragraph covers active and passive corruption issues, including the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing, are covered in this paragraph.

Active and passive corruption
This paragraph covers active and passive corruption issues, including the fight against money laundering and terrorist

nodes.title: Policies
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.1 Policies
nodes.start_phrase: The Group promotes the principles of transparency, accountability and integrity in its relations with public administrations and external staff by adopting internal anti-corruption procedures and courses of action for all personnel.
nodes.summary:
- Whistleblowing system: Accessible via a dedicated IT platform (including for qualified external persons) and a telephone line to report negligent, unlawful, irregular, or improper conduct related to work. Eligible reporters include employees, suppliers, self-employed workers, consultants, former employees (for information acquired during employment), job candidates (for information acquired during selection), shareholders, and those with administrative, management, or control roles. Covered issues include administrative/accounting/tax irregularities, AML/CFT violations, market abuse, investment services irregularities, and data privacy breaches.
- Reporting process and protections: The Fraud Audit unit within Internal Audit receives and investigates reports, acknowledges receipt within 7 days, and provides follow-up within 3 months. Findings are documented in Special Investigation Reports. The Group guarantees confidentiality, protects whistleblowers from retaliation or discrimination, and imposes penalties for breaching confidentiality, retaliatory acts, or obstructing reports.
- Governance and objectives: The Board of Statutory Auditors supervises the system. A Head of Internal Reporting Systems within Internal Audit oversees process execution and submits an annual report to the Board of Auditors, Board of Directors, Risk and Sustainability Committee, and the Director responsible for internal control and risk management. No quantitative targets are set for whistleblowing.
- Anti-corruption and AML/CFT policies: The Group adopts a zero-tolerance approach to active and passive corruption, including AML/CFT. Key documents include the Group Anti-Corruption Policy and the Group Policy on Combating Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing, both approved by the Board of Directors and available on the corporate website. Policies apply to all Group personnel and entities acting on the Group’s behalf, with control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions. Policies align with national and EU laws and international standards and commitments (Italian Civil and Criminal Codes, OECD, UN, G20, Transparency International, Wolfsberg Group, UN Global Compact, UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking) and consider stakeholder interests via the stakeholder engagement process.
- Actions and risk management: The Group conducts periodic self-assessments of corruption risk, at least biennially identifies high-risk areas, and strengthens processes with preventive controls. Violations may trigger disciplinary measures up to termination. Sensitive areas include supplier appointments, joint ventures/M&A, gifts and entertainment, events and sponsorships, hiring, credit disbursement, expenditure cycle, consultancy, subsidised finance/public service transactions, political contributions, donations, membership fees, non-profit activities, and management of public services.

nodes.title: Actions
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.2 Actions
nodes.start_phrase: The Group operates in line with its values and with a sense of responsibility towards society by applying “zero tolerance” towards any corrupt practice (direct or indirect, public or private, external or within the organisation, instigated, attemp- ted, committed), to ensure that its staff and all persons working for it comply with anti-corruption regulations, adopting all measures necessary to prevent and effectively counter the risk.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Governance, policies, actions, controls, training, and oversight related to anti-corruption and the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing (AML/CTF) within Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena Group, as part of its Sustainability Reporting.
- Policy framework:
  - Group Anti-Corruption Policy: Sets principles and conduct rules for all employees and third parties acting for the Group; approved by the Board; control activities assigned to Corporate Control Functions; aligned with UN Global Compact, UNEP Principles for Responsible Banking, and guidance from OECD, UN, G20, Transparency International, and the Wolfsberg Group; available on the corporate website.
  - Group AML/CTF Policy: Defines the Group’s global AML/CTF approach for the Parent Company and all subsidiaries; Board approves the policy and annual AML report (including ML/TF risk self-assessment and activity plan); aligned with national, EU, and international standards; available on the corporate website.
- Stakeholders: Policy design considers interests identified through the Group’s Stakeholder Engagement process.
- Zero tolerance and disciplinary regime: The Group applies zero tolerance to all forms of corruption (public/private, internal/external, direct/indirect) and foresees disciplinary actions up to termination for violations.
- Risk assessment and scope:
  - Periodic self-assessments of corruption risks across all business processes; biennial identification of high-risk areas (e.g., suppliers, JVs/M&A, gifts/entertainment, events/sponsorships, hiring, credit disbursement, procurement, consultancy, subsidised finance, political contributions/donations/memberships/non-profit, management of public services).
  - Latest 2024 assessment found potential risks across structures but no need for additional measures beyond existing safeguards.
  - Explicit prohibition of political contributions and heightened controls in dealings with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program and training:
  - Ongoing risk self-assessments by functions and employee awareness/training.
  - Training content updated by the Training function with Compliance validation upon regulatory/procedural changes or audit findings.
  - Specialized training for Internal Audit’s Fraud Audit staff (including international certification paths such as CFE).
  - Board induction for subsidiaries on administrative liability and Group 231 Models.
- AML/CTF controls:
  - Identification of applicable regulations, impact assessment, and updates to internal rules.
  - IT systems for risk management, due diligence, data retention, continuous customer/transaction monitoring, detection of potentially suspicious activity, and reporting to the Financial Information unit.
  - Ongoing assessment of risk management processes and internal control adequacy.
  - Mandatory AML/CTF training for all employees.
- Roles and responsibilities:
  - Compliance Function: Identifies corruption-risk processes and evaluates safeguards; coordinates rule application and training; provides advisory support; partners with HR on info-training programs.
  - 2024 Compliance Plan: Approved 6 Feb 2024; 797 audits executed vs 692 planned; 758 conformity opinions and 649 validation opinions issued.
  - Internal Audit: Performs third-level controls within the Internal Control System.
  - AML Function (Parent Company) and Chief Risk Officer’s department (Group level): Monitor AML/CTF risks; CRO reports directly to the Board and centralizes duties for Italian subsidiaries.
- Targets: The Group ensures prevention of active and passive corruption (including AML/CTF) but has not set quantitative targets.

nodes.title: Objectives
nodes.heading: 4.1.5.3 Objectives
nodes.start_phrase: On 6 February 2024, the Bank’s Board of Directors resolved on the programme of activities and controls (2024 Compliance Plan), which the Compliance function undertook to complete during the 2024 financial year.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Anti-corruption, anti–money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CTF) governance, controls, training, and metrics within the Group’s 2024 Sustainability Reporting.
- Risk assessment and policy: Corruption risks are assessed across all business processes; 2024 results found potential risks everywhere but deemed current safeguards adequate. Strict prohibition on political contributions or any support to political causes, with heightened focus on interactions with Public Administration.
- Anti-corruption program: Periodic risk self-assessments by functions; employee training and awareness plans. Training content is updated by the Training function under Compliance validation when regulations/procedures change or audits reveal gaps.
- Specialized training: Internal Audit’s Fraud Audit team receives targeted training (including “training pills” and structured courses) and may pursue international certifications (e.g., CFE). Subsidiary Boards receive induction on entities’ administrative liability and the Group’s Model 231 framework.
- AML/CTF controls: Ongoing regulatory scanning and internal framework updates; IT procedures for risk management, due diligence, recordkeeping, continuous monitoring, suspicious activity detection, and FIU reporting; periodic assessments of risk management and internal controls; AML/CTF training for all employees.
- Governance and responsibilities: Compliance Function identifies corruption-risk processes, assesses safeguards, coordinates rule application and training, advises on anti-corruption, and supports HR with info-training. Internal Audit performs third-level controls. The Parent Company’s AML function monitors AML/CTF risks; at Group level, the Chief Risk Officer (reporting to the Board) centrally oversees these duties for Italian subsidiaries. Corporate bodies are involved with defined roles per the Internal Control System. No quantitative prevention targets are set.
- 2024 Compliance Plan execution: Approved on 6 Feb 2024. Of 692 planned audits, 797 were performed; 758 conformity opinions and 649 validation opinions on internal regulations were issued.
- Training metrics (2024): 100% of Parent Company staff are enrolled due to universal exposure to corruption risk. Training recipients included 16,321 workers in functions at risk (out of 16,439 total), 155 executive managers, and 7 members of administrative/management/supervisory bodies. Delivery included classroom (e.g., 19.0 hours for functions at risk; 5.0 for administrative bodies) and computer-based training (e.g., 12,227.0 hours for functions at risk; 116.3 for executives; 2.0 for administrative bodies). Topics covered definitions, policies, and suspicion/detection procedures. Training frequency generally once per year where required.
- Outcomes: No confirmed incidents of corruption involving the workforce in 2024, and no legal/regulatory non-compliance cases resulting in penalties (monetary or non-monetary).

nodes.title: Metrics
nodes.heading: 4.1.6 Metrics
nodes.start_phrase: The metrics used to monitor the effectiveness of the measures taken to manage business conduct, in relation to anti-corruption training and active and passive bribery cases, are reported in this section.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on governance and controls: The Group’s Internal Control System assigns clear roles to corporate bodies to mitigate business conduct risks, including corruption and bribery.
- Metrics and monitoring: The document reports metrics on anti-corruption training coverage and any active or passive bribery cases to assess effectiveness.
- Risk mapping and scope: Compliance maps “functions at risk,” and all corporate structures are considered potentially exposed; 100% of Parent Company staff are enrolled in anti-corruption training.
- 2024 training coverage:
  - Functions at risk: 16,321 training recipients (out of 16,439 total at-risk workers).
  - Administrative, management and supervisory bodies: 155 recipients.
  - Other workers: 7 recipients.
- Training delivery and hours (2024):
  - Functions at risk: 12,227.0 hours e-learning; 19.0 hours classroom; 12,246.0 total.
  - Administrative/management/supervisory bodies: 116.3 hours e-learning; no classroom; 116.3 total.
  - Other workers: 2.0 hours e-learning; 5.0 hours classroom; 7.0 total.
  - Training frequency: annual where required.
- Training content: definition of corruption, relevant policies, and suspicion/detection procedures.
- Outcomes: In 2024 there were no legal or regulatory non-compliance cases, no penalties, and no confirmed instances of corruption involving the workforce.

nodes.title: Training on the fight against corruption and bribery
nodes.heading: 4.1.6.1 Training on the fight against corruption and bribery
nodes.start_phrase: As part of the periodic activities carried out by the Group in order to identify the main areas considered to be “at risk of corruption”, within which the mapping of functions at risk carried out by the Compliance function takes place, potentially all corporate structures are exposed to “corruption risk”.
nodes.summary:
- Governance and controls: The Group’s Internal Control System and Corporate Bodies have clearly defined roles to mitigate business-conduct risks, including corruption and bribery, with effectiveness monitored through specific metrics.
- Anti-corruption training: All Parent Company staff are considered potentially exposed to corruption risk and are enrolled 100% in the anti-corruption training campaign. Training covers definitions of corruption, internal policies, and suspicion/detection procedures, is required annually, and is delivered via classroom and computer-based modules.
  - Participation and hours (2024): Functions at risk trained total about 16,3k people; executives 155; administrative/management/supervisory bodies 7. Training hours: functions at risk 12,246; executives 116.3; administrative/management/supervisory bodies 7. Delivery included approximately 19 classroom hours for functions at risk and 5 for administrative/management/supervisory bodies, with the remainder via e-learning.
- Incidents and compliance (2024): No cases of legal/regulatory non-compliance (monetary or non-monetary) and no confirmed instances of corruption involving the workforce.
- EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosures (KPIs for credit institutions):
  - Green Asset Ratio (GAR) at 31 Dec 2024: turnover-based 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023), capex-based 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023). Total GAR assets: EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
  - Data limitations: GAR depends on counterparties’ published non-financial data; exposures to entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, reducing the numerator.
- Methodology:
  - KPIs aligned with Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178. GAR = taxonomy-aligned exposures over total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers).
  - Counterparties under NFRD: For exposures where use of proceeds is not known, taxonomy eligibility/alignment is weighted by counterparties’ reported turnover and capex KPIs across the six environmental objectives, using an external data provider. Following EC FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD are included. Where use of proceeds is known, no eligible/aligned exposures were identified under the screening criteria.
  - Guaranteed household loans: Only loans secured by residential real estate considered eligible. Loans for building renovations and motor vehicles excluded due to insufficient data to identify “green loans.” Alignment applies technical criteria differentiating buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre-2020 buildings not holding EPC class A, alignment may be met if in the top 15% of national/regional building stock for primary energy demand, using studies by private entities.

structure.title: Annexes
structure.heading: Section 5 - Annexes
structure.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
structure.summary:
- Context: Annex of the 2024 Sustainability Report outlining credit institutions’ KPIs required under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and its Disclosures Delegated Act.
- Purpose: Enhance transparency on sustainability and support the low‑carbon transition by reporting eligibility and alignment of activities with the EU Taxonomy, focused on the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
- Scope and data dependency: GAR relies on counterparties’ non-financial disclosures; entities outside the NFRD scope are excluded, which constrains the ratio.
- Reported results (31 Dec 2024): turnover-based GAR 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023); capex-based GAR 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
- Methodological framework: Based on Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178; GAR defined as exposures to taxonomy-aligned assets over total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- Key methodological choices:
  - Counterparties under NFRD and those not obliged to publish NFI: where use of proceeds is unknown, exposures are weighted by counterparties’ published turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives; where use of proceeds is known, no eligible/aligned exposures per Delegated Regulation 2021/2139. Following EC FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), counterparties whose parent companies are subject to NFRD are included (change vs 2023).
  - Guaranteed household loans: only residential real estate–secured loans considered eligible; renovation and motor vehicle loans excluded due to lack of “green loan” identification. Alignment applies technical screening criteria distinguishing buildings pre/post 31 Dec 2020; for pre‑2020 buildings lacking class‑A EPC, 2024 assessment uses the top 15% primary energy performance criterion based on private studies (not used in prior year).
- Cross-reference: Full regulatory framework discussed in the report’s Environmental Information section.

nodes.title: Key performance indicators (kpi) of credit institutions
nodes.heading: 5.1 Key performance indicators (kpi) of credit institutions
nodes.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Annex of the 2024 Sustainability Report detailing Article 8 EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852 and Delegated Reg. 2021/2178) disclosure requirements for credit institutions, focused on reporting eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance transparency and support the low‑carbon transition.
- Core KPI reported: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- 2024 results and comparatives: Turnover‑based GAR 1.06% (0.50% in 2023); CapEx‑based GAR 1.15% (0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (EUR 94,254 million in 2023). GAR is constrained by counterparty disclosures; entities outside NFRD are excluded, reflecting data gaps.
- Methodological framework: Based on Annex V of Delegated Reg. 2021/2178 and technical screening criteria in Delegated Reg. 2021/2139; uses counterparties’ published Taxonomy KPIs for the six environmental objectives.
- Key methodological choices:
  - Financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish NFI: For exposures with unknown use of proceeds (as per external data provider), weighting is based on counterparties’ turnover and CapEx Taxonomy KPIs from their non‑financial statements. No eligible/aligned exposures are recognized where the use of proceeds is known, per 2021/2139. Scope of NFRD counterparties expanded in 2024 to include entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD, per European Commission FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024).
  - Guaranteed household loans: Only loans secured by residential real estate are considered eligible; building renovation and motor vehicle loans are excluded due to lack of “green loan” identification. Alignment assessment distinguishes buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre‑2020 buildings not meeting EPC class A, alignment can be met via the “top 15%” primary energy performance criterion, now supported by private studies (not available in the prior year).
- Cross‑reference: Points to the Environmental Information section for a fuller regulatory discussion of Article 8 Taxonomy disclosures.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.heading: 5.1.1 Introduction
nodes.start_phrase: The tables below show the disclosure requirements under Article 8 of the Disclosures Delegated Act supplementing the EU Taxonomy Regulation (2020/852)57.
nodes.summary:
- Context: Annex section of a 2024 Sustainability Report outlining credit institutions’ KPIs under Article 8 of the EU Taxonomy Regulation and its Disclosures Delegated Act.
- Purpose: Explain disclosure obligations starting in 2023 for Taxonomy eligibility and alignment, enhancing transparency and supporting the low‑carbon transition.
- Key metric: Green Asset Ratio (GAR) defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (excluding trading book and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranationals).
- 2024 results: Turnover‑based GAR 1.06% (vs 0.50% in 2023); CapEx‑based GAR 1.15% (vs 0.53% in 2023); total GAR assets EUR 94,586 million (vs EUR 94,254 million in 2023).
- Data dependency: GAR calculation relies on counterparties’ reported Taxonomy KPIs; entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, affecting the ratio.
- Methodology basis: Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178 and technical screening criteria in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139; application reflects European Commission FAQs (Dec 2023 and Nov 2024).
- Methodological choices:
  - For financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish non‑financial information: when use of proceeds is unknown, exposures are weighted by counterparties’ turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives; no eligible/aligned exposures recognized where use of proceeds is known per screening criteria. NFRD perimeter broadened to include entities whose parents are subject to NFRD.
  - Guaranteed household loans: only loans secured by residential real estate considered eligible; building renovation loans and motor vehicle loans excluded due to insufficient green‑loan identification. Alignment applies screening criteria distinguishing buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020; for pre‑2020 assets not EPC class A, alignment may be met if in the top 15% of national/regional building stock for primary energy needs, supported by private studies (newly available in 2024).
- Cross‑reference: Points to a broader discussion of Article 8 disclosures in the Environmental Information section.

nodes.title: Methodology
nodes.heading: 5.1.2 Methodology
nodes.start_phrase: The main methodological choices adopted by the Group on the basis of current regulations are outlined below.
nodes.summary:
- Context and purpose: Part of the Sustainability Reporting section detailing Article 8 EU Taxonomy (Reg. 2020/852) disclosures for credit institutions. From 2023, financial firms must report eligibility and alignment KPIs to enhance transparency and support the low‑carbon transition. Scope follows the NFRD (2014/95/EU).

- Key metrics reported (as of 31 Dec 2024):
  - Turnover-based Green Asset Ratio (GAR): 1.06% (0.50% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Capex-based GAR: 1.15% (0.53% at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Total GAR assets (denominator): EUR 94,586 million (EUR 94,254 million at 31 Dec 2023).
  - Note: GAR depends on counterparties’ disclosed data; exposures to entities outside NFRD scope are excluded, which impacts the ratio.

- Methodological framework:
  - KPIs per Annex V of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2178.
  - GAR defined as exposures to taxonomy‑aligned assets divided by total covered assets (gross carrying amount of total assets excluding trading book exposures and exposures to central governments, central banks, and supranational issuers).

- Key methodological decisions:
  - Financial undertakings and entities not obliged to publish non-financial information:
    - Where use of proceeds is unknown (assessed with an external provider), exposures are weighted by counterparties’ reported Taxonomy turnover and CapEx KPIs across the six environmental objectives.
    - Where use of proceeds is known, no taxonomy-eligible and aligned exposures were identified under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139.
    - Following European Commission FAQs (21 Dec 2023 and Nov 2024), NFRD counterparties now also include entities whose parent companies are subject to NFRD, expanding scope versus 2023.
  - Guaranteed household loans:
    - Eligibility limited to loans secured by residential real estate.
    - Building renovations and motor vehicle purchases excluded due to insufficient data to tag “green loans.”
    - Alignment screening applies criteria for buildings constructed before/after 31 Dec 2020. For pre‑2020 buildings lacking EPC class A, the Group used the “top 15%” primary energy performance criterion based on private studies (new in 2024).
  - Flows: Defined as gross new exposures; only positive flows are counted (no netting of repayments or sales).
  - Assets under management (AuM): KPI calculated as the share of equity and debt issued by NFRD‑subject companies within total AuM equity and debt.

- Comparability note: Templates as of 31 Dec 2023 are disclosed, but year‑on‑year comparisons are not fully homogeneous due to 2024 scope changes (notably inclusion of entities with NFRD‑subject parent companies).

- Gas and Nuclear templates: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 (amending 2021/2139), the Group reports eligibility, alignment, and non‑eligibility for gas and nuclear activities. These templates cover only non‑financial companies that disclosed the relevant KPIs in their 2023 reporting.

nodes.title: Gas & Nuclear templates
nodes.heading: 5.1.3 Gas & Nuclear templates
nodes.start_phrase: In line with Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214 of 9 March 2022 amending Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/2139, the Group publishes templates for the alignment, eligibility and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities.
nodes.summary:
- Regulatory basis and methodology: Disclosures prepared under EU Taxonomy Regulation (EU) 2021/2178, with “flows” defined as new exposures at gross book value (only positive flows), and an Assets Under Management ratio limited to securities issued by companies subject to mandatory NFRD. Templates are referenced to 31 Dec 2023; 2024 scope changes make year-on-year comparisons non-homogeneous.
- Gas & Nuclear disclosures: In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, publication of templates on eligibility, alignment, and non-eligibility of gas and nuclear activities, limited to non-financial companies that reported the relevant KPIs in 2023.
- Key KPIs for credit institutions (Annex VI):
  - Main KPI Green Asset Ratio (GAR) – stock:
    - 2024: Environmentally sustainable assets €997m (Turnover) and €1,089m (Capex); % KPI 1.05% (Turnover) and 1.15% (Capex); coverage over total assets 75.77%; assets excluded from numerator 44.96% and from denominator 24.23%.
    - 2023: €467m (Turnover) and €496m (Capex); % KPI 0.50% and 0.53%; coverage 75.52%; excluded from numerator 49.52% and from denominator 24.48%.
  - Additional KPI GAR – flows:
    - 2024: €587m (Turnover) and €1,055m (Capex); % KPI 0.62% and 1.12%; coverage over total assets 6.54%.
    - 2023: €141m (Turnover) and €151m (Capex); % KPI 0.15% and 0.16%.
  - Trading book and fee/commission income: not applicable/blank. Financial guarantees and AUM show small aligned portions (e.g., 2024 FG 1.06% Turnover, 2.75% Capex; AUM 3.45% Turnover, 7.24% Capex).
- Detailed GAR stock breakdowns (2024 and 2023) by:
  - Counterparty type (financial undertakings, non-financial undertakings, households), product (loans and advances, debt securities, equity), and environmental objectives (CCM, CCA, WTR, CE, PPC, BIO).
  - Classification of aligned activities into use-of-proceeds, transitional, and enabling.
  - Households, especially residential mortgage loans, represent the bulk of taxonomy-eligible exposure (2024: €30.354bn eligible; €867m aligned).
  - Non-financial undertakings contribute to aligned amounts; financial undertakings show limited alignment; insurance negligible.
- Scope of assets in GAR:
  - Numerator exclusions captured (but included in denominator): SMEs/NFCs not subject to NFRD, non-EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on-demand interbank, cash and cash-like, and other assets.
  - Total GAR assets and assets not covered for GAR provided; the latter include central governments, central banks, and trading book exposures.
- Off-balance sheet exposures (to undertakings subject to NFRD): Reported aligned amounts for financial guarantees and AUM, with debt/equity splits.

nodes.title: Assets for the GAR (stock) - Capex calculation
nodes.heading: 1.Assets for the GAR (stock) - Capex calculation
nodes.start_phrase: In milion of Eur 2024
nodes.summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report (Sustainability Reporting) detailing EU Taxonomy and Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures.
- Presents the “Assets for the GAR (stock)” with a CapEx-based view and a comparative 2024 vs 2023 snapshot, in millions of euros.
- Breaks down GAR-covered assets (included in numerator and denominator) by counterparty and instrument: financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance), non‑financial undertakings, and households (notably mortgages collateralised by residential property). Also shows collateral obtained.
- For each exposure, reports taxonomy eligibility and alignment across the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
- Further classifies aligned exposures by “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” categories.
- Details assets excluded from the GAR numerator (but included in the denominator), including SMEs and NFCs not subject to NFRD disclosure, non‑EU counterparties not subject to NFRD, derivatives, on‑demand interbank loans, cash and cash‑related assets, and other assets (e.g., goodwill).
- Summarizes total GAR assets, assets not covered for GAR (central governments, central banks, trading book), and total assets for both 2024 and 2023.
- Includes off‑balance sheet exposures for undertakings subject to NFRD (financial guarantees and assets under management), with “of which” breakdowns for debt and equity and their taxonomy eligibility/alignment.
- Provides a sectoral (NACE 4‑digit) view of stock aligned exposures on a turnover basis, listing sectors such as electricity production/transmission/distribution, shipbuilding, machinery and equipment manufacturing, petroleum products, chemicals/synthetic fibres, electronics and instruments—showing gross carrying amounts and the portion environmentally sustainable under each objective.

nodes.title: GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Turnover
nodes.heading: 2. GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Turnover
nodes.start_phrase: 1 Credit institutions must report in this template information on exposures in the banking book with the sectors covered by the taxonomy (NACE sectors 4 levels of detail), using the relevant NACE codes on the basis of the counterparty’s principal activity.
nodes.summary:
- Extract from Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s 2024 Annual Report – Sustainability Reporting, focused on Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosure.
- Presents GAR sector information for the stock of taxonomy‑aligned exposures using two KPIs:
  - Turnover-based alignment.
  - Capex-based alignment (partial table shown).
- Granular breakdown by sector at NACE Rev. 2, 4‑digit code level, with line‑by‑line figures across numerous industries (manufacturing, energy and utilities, waste and remediation, construction and civil engineering, transport and logistics, telecoms and data services, real estate, business services, and other services).
- Discloses, in EUR million, for each sector and counterparty category:
  - Gross carrying amount.
  - “Of which environmentally sustainable” amounts under EU Taxonomy objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), and Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO), plus a total across all objectives.
- Counterparty segmentation distinguishes:
  - Non-financial corporates subject to NFRD.
  - SMEs and other non-financial corporates not subject to NFRD.
- Illustrative sector entries include electricity production/transmission/distribution, water collection/treatment/supply, waste treatment, shipbuilding, machinery and equipment, petroleum products, construction of roads, telecoms and data processing, and others, showing both gross exposures and the subset deemed environmentally sustainable; many sectors display low or zero alignment, with some notable aligned amounts in utilities, water services, waste management, shipbuilding, and telecoms.
- Provides a 2023 comparative table for turnover-based alignment to enable year‑on‑year sectoral comparison.
- Methodological notes specify:
  - NACE assignment is based on the immediate counterparty’s principal activity.
  - Joint exposures are classified by the borrower most relevant/decisive for granting the exposure.
  - Reporting must follow the required 4‑digit NACE disaggregation.
- Bilingual column headers (English/Italian) indicate “of which environmentally sustainable” values; figures are presented in EUR million.

nodes.title: GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Capex
nodes.heading: 2. GAR sector information of the stock aligned exposures - Capex
nodes.start_phrase: Breakdown by sector - NACE 4 digits level (code and label) Climate Change Mitigation
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena’s EU Taxonomy Green Asset Ratio (GAR) disclosures, with a sectoral view of taxonomy-aligned exposures based on Capex, and the GAR “stock” turnover calculation for 2024, plus a compact 2023 sectoral comparison.

- Scope and structure:
  - Detailed breakdown by NACE 4‑digit sector of gross carrying amounts (EUR million) and “of which environmentally sustainable” amounts for each of the six environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - Split by counterparty type: non‑financial corporates subject to NFRD vs SMEs/other NFCs not subject to NFRD.
  - Coverage spans energy, manufacturing, utilities, construction, transport/logistics, telecoms, real estate, and business services.

- 2024 sector highlights (examples from the extract):
  - Electricity networks and generation show notable aligned portions (e.g., transmission and distribution with high CCM alignment; electricity production with aligned amounts reported).
  - Water and waste utilities contribute aligned exposures (water collection/treatment/supply and treatment/disposal of non‑hazardous waste show aligned amounts across CCM, WTR, CE, and PPC).
  - Civil engineering and roads display some CCM‑aligned shares.
  - Transport‑related services (service activities incidental to land transport) include meaningful aligned exposures.
  - Selected manufacturing (e.g., measuring instruments, engines/turbines, cables) and telecoms (wired telecommunications) show exposures with modest aligned components.
  - Several sectors carry exposure but no aligned share (e.g., crude oil extraction, some retail/manufacturing activities).

- 2023 comparison:
  - A condensed table lists selected NACE sectors with gross vs aligned amounts, enabling a year‑over‑year view of taxonomy alignment for key activities (e.g., shipbuilding, machinery, electricity, gas trading, postal/courier).

- GAR “Total assets for the stock – Turnover (%)” (2024):
  - About 32.7% of total assets are GAR‑covered.
  - Taxonomy‑aligned shares are small overall, concentrated in CCM (≈1.06% of total assets), with limited alignment in CCA (~0.01%), WTR (~0.06%), and CE (~0.02%); PPC and BIO are negligible in the extract.
  - By counterparty:
    - Households (primarily residential mortgages) constitute the largest covered share and the bulk of the aligned CCM component (~0.93% via green/energy‑efficient mortgages).
    - Non‑financial undertakings contribute ~0.11% aligned.
    - Financial undertakings contribute ~0.02% aligned.
  - Instrument split includes loans and advances, debt securities (including use‑of‑proceeds), and equity; “use of proceeds,” “transitional,” and “enabling” flags are disclosed but minimal in the excerpt.

- Measurement notes:
  - Figures are gross carrying amounts (EUR million) for sector tables and proportions of total assets for the GAR turnover calculation.
  - Assets held for trading are excluded from the GAR scope.

  - Flow GAR based on Turnover (%): 2024 disclosure.
- Structure and scope:
  - Breakdowns by EU environmental objectives: Climate Change Mitigation (CCM), Climate Change Adaptation (CCA), Water and Marine Resources (WTR), Circular Economy (CE), Pollution Prevention and Control (PPC), Biodiversity and Ecosystems (BIO).
  - For each objective: “taxonomy-eligible” vs “environmentally sustainable (taxonomy-aligned)”, with flags for Use of Proceeds, transitional, and enabling activities.
  - Asset classes and counterparties covered: loans and advances, debt securities (including use-of-proceeds bonds), equity instruments; financial undertakings (credit institutions, other financial corporations, management companies, insurance undertakings), non‑financial undertakings, households (notably loans collateralised by residential property), local government financing, and collateral obtained.
  - Denominator and coverage details: “not HfT eligible for GAR calculation,” total GAR assets, and proportion of total assets covered.
- Main findings for Stock GAR (Capex):
  - Households—especially loans collateralised by residential immovable property—represent the largest share of covered assets.
  - Taxonomy alignment increases year over year: overall aligned share rises from 0.53% (2023) to 1.16% (2024).
  - Non‑financial undertakings show growth in alignment (roughly doubling from 2023 to 2024), with small aligned portions mainly in climate change mitigation and, to a lesser extent, circular economy and water.
  - Financial undertakings contribute marginally to aligned exposure; equity instruments are largely absent.
  - Use-of-proceeds, enabling, and transitional categories appear but remain minimal.

- Main findings for Flow GAR (Turnover) 2024:
  - Presents eligible and aligned shares with the same objective and sectoral breakdown.
  - Overall taxonomy-aligned share is modest (around 0.62%), with most contribution from households and non‑financial undertakings; financial undertakings add a small amount.
  - Use-of-proceeds, enabling, and transitional exposures remain limited.
- Cross-cutting observation:
  - Eligibility is higher than alignment; alignment is concentrated in climate change mitigation, with minor presence in adaptation, circular economy, and water; pollution and biodiversity exposures are negligible.
